Umrah · Health & SafetyUmrah with Diabetes: Medication, Insulin and Safety Tips for Pilgrims

Diabetes does not stop you from performing Umrah. Every week of the year, pilgrims with diabetes complete their Umrah safely. What it does demand is planning. The heat, the long walks, the changed meal times and the crowded Haram can all push blood sugar up or down, so the pilgrims who do best are the ones who prepare weeks before they travel. This guide covers the practical steps. It is general guidance only, and your own doctor's plan always comes first.

Start with your doctor, 4 to 6 weeks before: Book a review appointment four to six weeks before departure. Ask for a fitness check, an HbA1c test to set your baseline, and a clear plan for adjusting your insulin or tablets during the pilgrimage, because the extra walking often means doses need to come down. A common approach is to reduce insulin before a long walk, but never change a dose on your own. Ask your doctor for three pieces of paper: a short summary of your condition and treatment, a medication list that uses generic names rather than brand names, because brands differ between countries, and a signed letter on letterhead covering any injectable medicines, needles or devices you carry. Keep one copy in your hand luggage, one in your day bag, and photos of everything on your phone.

Packing your diabetes kit: Pack a dedicated bag that stays in your hand luggage and never leaves your side: all medicines in their original labelled packaging, with about 30 percent extra in case of delays, your glucometer with plenty of test strips and lancets, glucose tablets, and snacks such as dates or energy bars for low blood sugar. If you use insulin, carry it in a cooler bag. Never put medicines in checked luggage, where bags go missing and temperatures swing. Loose pills in an unmarked organiser are exactly what customs officers are trained to question, so keep everything labelled and declare it with your doctor's letter.

Insulin in the Saudi heat: Unopened insulin must stay between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, and insulin in use must stay below 30 degrees. In Makkah that takes care: use the hotel fridge for your stock, carry only the pen or vial you need for the day, keep it in a cooler bag, and never leave it in a hot car or in direct sun. Ask the hotel in advance about fridge access in your room. If your insulin has been sitting in heat above 30 degrees for hours, treat it as spoiled and do not use it.

Tawaf, Sa'i and low blood sugar: Tawaf is about 2 kilometres of walking and Sa'i about 3 kilometres, so check your blood sugar before you start and eat some extra carbohydrate, such as bread, before Tawaf. Carry glucose tablets or dates in your pocket. The warning signs of low blood sugar are sweating, shaking, a fast heartbeat, hunger and confusion. If they appear, stop and treat it at once with 2 to 3 dates, a spoon of honey, half a glass of juice or glucose tablets, then check your sugar again after 15 minutes. Tell your travelling companions in advance what low blood sugar looks like for you and where your glucose is kept. If you cannot manage the distance on foot, a wheelchair for Tawaf and Sa'i is fully valid.

Heat, water and feet: Heat and dehydration push blood sugar up and raise the risk of serious problems, so drink water and Zamzam often, rest in the shade between rites, and avoid the midday sun where you can. Check your feet every night: wash them, look for cuts or blisters, and wear comfortable shoes that are already broken in. Treat any small wound before you travel, because a small foot injury can become serious on a pilgrimage. Carry a medical ID card or bracelet that says you have diabetes, and travel insurance that covers it.

Food, timing and the journey home: Meal times will shift around prayers, so keep snacks in your day bag for delayed meals. Dates are ideal: quick sugar when you need it, and easy to carry. When you return home, book a check with your doctor within a week, because doses that were changed for the journey usually need changing back. Above all, do not let the worry take over the worship. With a doctor's plan, a packed kit and companions who know what to do, Umrah with diabetes is entirely possible.

Keep reading: packing list, summer heat safety, how long Umrah takes, elderly parents, Zamzam virtues.

Umrah · WomenUmrah During Pregnancy: Rules, Safety and Practical Tips

Thousands of women perform Umrah while pregnant every year. The ruling is reassuring: pregnancy does not stop a woman from performing Umrah, and no school of Islamic law forbids it. What changes is the planning, not the permission. New to Umrah? Start with our first-timers guide.

The Islamic ruling: Umrah is voluntary worship, and Islam never asks a person to risk their health for a voluntary act. All four Sunni schools permit a pregnant woman to perform Umrah. The guiding principle is that harm is to be removed, and the Quran says Allah does not burden a soul beyond what it can bear (Quran 2:286). If a doctor says the journey risks mother or baby, scholars say postponing is right, and the reward of the intention remains.

The best time to travel: the second trimester: Doctors and Umrah operators agree the second trimester, roughly weeks 14 to 27, is the most comfortable window. Morning sickness has usually settled and energy has returned. The first trimester brings nausea and the highest miscarriage risk, so most doctors discourage travel then. The third trimester is physically harder and brings airline restrictions, so late pregnancy Umrah needs a careful talk with your doctor first.

Flying while pregnant: airline rules: Airlines are stricter than most travellers expect. Saudia requires a medical certificate once a pregnancy passes 28 weeks, the certificate must be issued within 10 days of the flight, and Saudia refuses carriage from 35 weeks (32 weeks for twins). Other airlines are similar: a fit-to-fly letter from around 28 to 29 weeks and no boarding between 35 and 37 weeks. Check your airline's exact policy before you book, not after.

Talk to your doctor before you book: Get a full sign-off and carry a copy of your antenatal record. Saudi Arabia requires MenACWY meningococcal vaccination for an Umrah visa, given at least 10 days before arrival. UK public health guidance says pregnant women should receive it according to its licensed indications in pregnancy, but confirm with your own doctor. Check your travel insurance too: most policies exclude pregnancy, childbirth and related complications, so read the fine print.

Tawaf and Sa'i while pregnant: Tawaf and Sa'i are walking rites: the Mataf circuit is roughly 2 kilometres and Sa'i between Safa and Marwah is close to 3 kilometres. Walk slowly, rest between circuits, and use the outer rings or upper floors. A wheelchair Tawaf and Sa'i are fully valid, and many pregnant pilgrims use one for some or all of the rites with no reduction in reward; our elderly and disabled Umrah guide explains booking. Choose off-peak hours, after Isha or late at night, and keep a companion with you.

Heat, crowds and what to skip: Makkah heat is the most underestimated risk for a pregnant pilgrim, and summer temperatures regularly cross 45 degrees. Travel in the cooler months from November to February where possible, keep water with you inside the Haram, and never let the first day's enthusiasm set the pace for the trip. Do not attempt to kiss the Black Stone while pregnant: scholars agree the salute from a distance is enough, and the crush near the stone is a real risk. Our summer heat safety guide has more.

What to pack: Your doctor's fitness note and a copy of your antenatal record; loose, comfortable clothing and good walking shoes; a water bottle, light snacks and oral rehydration sachets; unscented toiletries for Ihram; and a small cushion for resting between rites. See our Ihram for women guide for clothing rules, our packing list for the rest, and our menstruation during Umrah guide if your period arrives mid-trip.

Duas for your baby: Tawaf is a known time for accepted duas. Two Quran duas parents make for their children are Quran 3:38, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring," and Quran 25:74, asking for spouses and offspring as a comfort to the eyes.

When to postpone: A high-risk pregnancy, a history of complications, bleeding, or a doctor's advice against travel are reasons to postpone. Postponing a voluntary act to protect a life is not falling short of worship. It is performing it correctly.

Sources: Al Sada Travels, HTG Travel, Sakina Wellbeing, Umrah.guide.

Umrah · Step by StepHow Long Does Umrah Take? A Realistic Timing Guide

First-time pilgrims often ask how long Umrah takes, and the honest answer is: the rites take hours, not days. Unlike Hajj, which takes five to six days, the four Umrah rites fit into a single session of a few hours. This guide gives a realistic rite-by-rite breakdown so you can plan your day. If you have never been, our first-timers guide explains the whole journey from home to Haram.

The short answer: In normal crowds, most pilgrims finish in 2 to 4 hours from entering the Haram to the haircut. First-timers usually take 3 to 5 hours because they move slowly, stop for duas, and learn the route as they go. In peak times, such as the last ten nights of Ramadan, the same rites can stretch to 5 or 6 hours.

Rite by rite: Entering Ihram: 30 to 60 minutes for bathing, changing into Ihram, two rak'ahs, intention and Talbiyah at the Miqat. Tawaf, seven circuits: 45 to 90 minutes on the ground floor Mataf when the crowd moves steadily; on the upper floors or roof, where the circuit is much wider, it can take 1.5 to 2 hours. Two rak'ahs and Zamzam: 10 to 15 minutes behind Maqam Ibrahim, then Zamzam water. Sa'i, seven lengths: 45 to 90 minutes at walking pace; the full Sa'i distance is about 3 kilometres. Haircut (Halq or Taqsir): 10 to 20 minutes at the barber stations near the Haram. Our guides to the Miqat points, Ihram rules, Tawaf and Sa'i cover each stage in full.

What makes it longer or shorter: Crowds are the biggest factor. A Tawaf that takes 30 minutes off-season can take 2 hours in peak season. Floor choice: the ground floor is the shortest distance but the most crowded; upper floors are longer but calmer. Timing: the Mataf is quietest between 8 and 10 in the morning and between 1 and 3 at night. It is fullest right after Fajr and Maghrib prayers, when prayer crowds merge with Tawaf. Fitness and mobility: elderly pilgrims and wheelchair users should allow extra time; an electric scooter for Tawaf and Sa'i can bring the total under 2 hours, as our elderly and disabled Umrah guide explains. Rest breaks: there is no rule against resting between rites. Sit, drink Zamzam, and continue when ready. Heat slows everything down too, so read our summer heat safety guide before a hot-season trip.

Is there a time limit? No. There is no fixed time limit on completing Umrah once you start. You remain in Ihram until you finish Sa'i and cut your hair, so most pilgrims finish in one continuous session rather than spreading it across days. Take the time you need.

Planning your trip around the timing: Do Umrah on your first day in Makkah, then keep 2 to 3 days in the city so you are not rushed. The rites are a few hours, but the journey deserves unhurried days for prayer at the Haram, rest and Ziyarat. Avoid doing Umrah the moment you land, exhausted from a long flight. Rest first, then enter Ihram fresh. Book your slot ahead with our step-by-step Nusuk Umrah permit guide.

Common first-timer mistakes: Counting fourteen Sa'i lengths instead of seven. One length from Safa to Marwah is one; Marwah back to Safa is two, and seven lengths end at Marwah. Rushing through Tawaf to beat the crowd and missing the duas. Choosing the busiest hour, right after Maghrib, for a first Tawaf.

Frequently asked questions: How long does Umrah take for the first time? About 3 to 5 hours including rest breaks. Can I split Umrah across two days? The rites are normally done in one session, but resting between rites is allowed, and there is no fixed deadline. Does the time include travel to Makkah? No. The hours above cover the rites inside the Haram only. Add your travel time from Jeddah or Madinah separately.

Sources: Wego blog, Reading Islam, Hisar Tour, Makkah Live.

Umrah · Health & SafetyUmrah in Summer Heat: Staying Safe in Makkah and Madinah

Summer Umrah, from June to August, is the cheapest and quietest time to travel, and many families choose it for the school holidays. The trade off is serious heat. Makkah's average daytime high in June is 43.9°C, and on the open marble of the Haram courtyard it feels hotter still. The heat is a planning problem, not a reason to cancel: with the right schedule, water, and rest, a summer Umrah is perfectly doable.

How hot it really gets: June averages a high of 43.9°C and a low of 29.3°C; July averages 43.2°C and 29.8°C; August averages 42.9°C and 30.1°C (World Meteorological Organization climate normals 1991-2020, Makkah station). The highest temperature ever recorded in Makkah is 51.8°C. Madinah is similar, with August averaging 43.8°C by day. Nights stay near 30°C, so there is little relief after dark. The white marble around the Kaaba reflects the sun and feels hotter than the air temperature, and the walk between hotel and mosque is where most people feel it.

Plan your rites around the sun: Do Tawaf and Sa'i before Fajr or after Maghrib and Isha, when the air is coolest and the courtyards are shaded. Keep 11 AM to 4 PM for rest, prayer inside, and sleep. The Haram interior and the Sa'i gallery are fully air conditioned, so indoor worship is comfortable at any hour. If you must cross the courtyard at midday, walk in the shade of the colonnades, carry water, and keep it short.

Drink before you feel thirsty: In 43°C heat you lose water fast, and thirst arrives late. Carry a refillable bottle and sip through the day. Zamzam water is available throughout both Harams. Pack oral rehydration salt sachets from home and use one if you have been sweating heavily. Go easy on tea, coffee, and soft drinks, which do not replace water.

What to wear and carry: Light, loose, breathable clothes in light colours. A white umbrella for the walk to the Haram, a hat or cap outside Ihram, sunglasses, and sunscreen. In Ihram, use unscented sunscreen and unscented toiletries, because scented products are not allowed in the state of Ihram. A small hand fan or a damp cooling towel helps on the courtyard. Wear comfortable sandals with grip, because hot marble is slippery when wet. Our full Umrah packing list covers everything else to pack.

Look after the vulnerable: Elderly pilgrims, small children, pregnant women, and anyone with heart, kidney, or breathing problems feel the heat first. Keep them in the shade, shorten their time outdoors, and consider a wheelchair for Tawaf and Sa'i on the air conditioned upper floors. Children dehydrate faster than adults and complain later, so offer them water on a schedule, not when they ask. See our guides to Umrah for elderly and disabled pilgrims and Umrah with kids for more detail.

Know the warning signs: Heat exhaustion comes first: tiredness, dizziness, headache, nausea, heavy sweating with pale clammy skin, cramps, and strong thirst. Move the person to a cool place at once, lay them down, loosen clothing, cool the skin with water, and give small sips of water. If they feel better within 30 minutes, they are recovering. Heatstroke is a medical emergency: a very high temperature, hot skin that has stopped sweating, a fast heartbeat, fast breathing, confusion, a seizure, or loss of consciousness. Call for help immediately and cool the person with a wet sheet or cold water while you wait.

Emergency numbers to save: 911 is the unified emergency number in Makkah and Madinah. 997 reaches the Saudi Red Crescent ambulance anywhere in the Kingdom. 998 is Civil Defence. Save all three in your phone before you travel.

If your dates are flexible, check our guide to the best time to go for Umrah, consider a day trip to Taif, in the mountains near Makkah, where the air is noticeably cooler, or plan the main rites for the night hours and keep the days for rest. Summer Umrah rewards the pilgrim who respects the sun: early mornings, late nights, water in hand, and the midday hours spent in the cool of the Haram.

Sources: World Meteorological Organization climate normals 1991-2020 (Makkah station); NHS guidance on heat exhaustion and heatstroke.

Umrah · WomenMenstruation During Umrah: What Women Can and Cannot Do

Many sisters worry about one thing above all when they book Umrah: what if my period comes during the trip? The ruling is clear, and it is merciful. Menstruation does not cancel your Umrah and does not stop you from travelling. It only pauses one rite, Tawaf, until you are pure again. This guide explains what you can do, what must wait, and how to plan.

Enter Ihram even while menstruating: If your period starts before you reach the Miqat, still enter Ihram there. Do ghusl, make the intention, and recite the Talbiyah like everyone else. Purity is not a condition for entering Ihram. The proof is Asma bint Umays, the wife of Abu Bakr, who gave birth at Dhul-Hulayfah, the Miqat of Madinah, during the Farewell Hajj. She asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, what to do, and he told her to do ghusl, tie a cloth, and enter Ihram. Menstrual blood carries the same ruling as postnatal blood here. Passing the Miqat without Ihram is not allowed, even while menstruating, so do not wait until you are pure to enter Ihram. Our Ihram for women guide covers the clothing and rules in full.

What must wait: Tawaf: A menstruating woman may not enter the mosque and may not perform any Tawaf until she is pure and has done ghusl. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told his wife Aisha when she menstruated during Umrah: "Do everything that the pilgrims do, but do not circumambulate the House until you become pure." (Sahih al-Bukhari 1650, Sahih Muslim 1211.) The same applies to the Rawdah in Madinah, because it is inside the Prophet's Mosque: a Rawdah visit must wait until purity, so rebook your permit in the Nusuk app for a later slot; see our Rawdah permit for women guide. When you are pure, our Tawaf guide walks through the rite step by step.

What you can still do: Sa'i between Safa and Marwa does not require purity according to the majority of scholars, so it is valid while menstruating; our Sa'i guide explains the rite. Note that some contemporary scholars advise waiting for Sa'i too, because the Sa'i area is now enclosed within the mosque building, so ask a trusted scholar about your situation if you want to follow that view. You can recite the Talbiyah, make dua, read Quran from memory, and do dhikr throughout. You can also visit the markets, rest, and prepare while you wait.

If your period starts after Tawaf: If you have already completed Tawaf and your period begins, go ahead with Sa'i, then cut a little hair and exit Ihram. Your Umrah is complete. Purity is not a condition for Sa'i, so there is nothing to redo.

If your period starts before Tawaf: Stay in Makkah and wait until your bleeding ends, then do ghusl and perform Tawaf. You remain in Ihram while you wait, so the Ihram restrictions still apply: no perfume, no cutting hair or nails, no marital relations. There is no penalty and no fidya for the wait itself. Use the days for rest, dua, and Quran, and keep your group informed so they can plan around you.

If your group must leave before you are pure: This is the hardest situation, and you should not decide it alone. Contact a scholar or mufti before your travel dates if this is a real risk, and speak to your group leader early. Some scholars, in genuine necessity where a woman cannot extend her stay, permit Tawaf in the state of menstruation followed by a sacrifice (dam) as expiation. This is a concession for necessity, not the normal ruling, so take personal guidance from a scholar rather than deciding it yourself.

Plan ahead: Track your cycle when you book, and try to place your Makkah days in the window after your period ends. Some women ask their doctor about medicine to delay their period for the trip: discuss this with your doctor well before you travel, never at the last minute. Pack enough sanitary supplies, because familiar brands may be hard to find, and keep a small bag ready for the wait in Makkah. If you are travelling without a mahram, our guide to women travelling alone for Umrah covers the current rules.

Sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1650; Sahih Muslim 1211.

Umrah Visa · Transit VisaUmrah on a Layover: The 96-Hour Saudi Transit Visa Explained

Short answer: Yes. If your flight connects through Saudi Arabia on Saudia or flynas, you can leave the airport, travel to Makkah and perform Umrah on the free Saudi stopover visa, as long as your layover is no more than 96 hours and you hold a booked Umrah slot on Nusuk before you travel. The rules are strict, so this guide explains them one by one. Travelling on a normal holiday instead? Start with our full Umrah visa guide.

What the visa is: The stopover (transit) visa lets you stay in Saudi Arabia for up to 96 hours, four days. It is single entry and cannot be extended. Once issued, it stays valid for entry for 90 days from the date of issue. The visa itself is free, but you still pay an application fee of about $10.50 plus mandatory medical insurance of about $29, roughly $39.50 in total. It covers tourism and Umrah, but it does not cover Hajj, and you get only one stopover per booking.

Who can get it: Only passengers booked on Saudia or flynas, on a single connecting ticket where Saudi Arabia is the stop in the middle and your final destination is a third country. No other airline offers this visa; fly with anyone else and you need a separate transit visa arranged in advance. You need a passport valid for at least six months, a confirmed onward ticket, and a visa or residence permit for your final destination if that country requires one. Compare the cost with a standard visa in our guide to visa fees.

How to apply: You apply during the airline booking flow, and it takes about three minutes. On Saudia, apply in the "Seats and Extras" section; on flynas, apply through its stopover visa page. The application goes to the national visa platform of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the visa and insurance papers arrive by email. Saudia asks for a square photo, 200x200 pixels and no larger than 20KB. Saudia also includes one free hotel night, claimed through Saudia Holidays after payment; flynas does not advertise one. An issued visa does not guarantee entry: passport control can still refuse you.

Umrah on this visa: The visa alone is not enough to perform Umrah. You must register on the Nusuk app or website and book your Umrah slot before you travel, and book a Rawdah permit the same way if you plan to visit Madinah. Our step-by-step Nusuk Umrah permit guide walks through the booking. The current 1448 AH Umrah season runs from 31 May 2026 to 7 April 2027, so finish your trip well before the season closes and check the cut-off dates on Nusuk first. You can also check your visa status online before departure.

Layovers under 12 hours: Short connections follow different rules. Saudia allows transit without a visa for up to 12 hours if you stay airside, inside the airport. But separate tickets, collecting your bags, or leaving the airside area can all require entry permission. A short layover is not a free Umrah trip: without the stopover visa and a Nusuk booking, you stay in the terminal.

A realistic 96-hour plan: Land in Jeddah and head straight to Makkah; our Jeddah airport to Makkah guide covers the Haramain high-speed train and taxi options. Perform Umrah on your first day while you are fresh, then rest. If time allows, add a day trip to Madinah for Ziyarah and a Rawdah visit with your booked permit. Be back at the airport well before the 96 hours run out: the clock starts when you enter the country.

Mistakes to avoid: Booking two separate tickets and assuming the stopover visa applies, when it only works on a single connecting ticket. Assuming any airline qualifies, when only Saudia and flynas offer it. Travelling without a Nusuk Umrah booking. Overstaying the 96 hours, which can bring fines and problems on future trips. And trying to use the stopover visa for Hajj, which it never covers.

Sources: Visit Saudi and the national eVisa platform, Saudia transit visa guidance, flynas stopover visa page, Wego travel blog Saudi transit visa guide (updated 12 Oct 2026), AlwaysPacked stopover visa guide (checked 13 Nov 2026), A Walk in the World transit Umrah guide (checked 13 Nov 2026).

Umrah · Farewell TawafTawaf al-Wada (Farewell Tawaf): Rules, Duas and Common Mistakes

Tawaf al-Wada, the farewell tawaf, is seven circuits around the Kaaba performed as your last act in Makkah before travelling home, once your Hajj or Umrah rites are complete. It is the pilgrim's goodbye to the House of Allah: you circle it one final time, pour out your duas, and then leave the city. It follows the same form as any other tawaf, which our Tawaf guide explains step by step.

The ruling: For Hajj pilgrims, Tawaf al-Wada is obligatory according to the majority of scholars, the Hanafi, Shafii and Hanbali schools; the Maliki school holds that it is sunnah. For Umrah-only visitors, it is not obligatory: it is sunnah and recommended, because the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not perform a farewell tawaf when he left Makkah after Umrat al-Qada. So if you are travelling for Umrah only, do not worry that your Umrah is incomplete without it. It is a beautiful recommended act, not a condition of acceptance.

The evidence: Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "None of you should depart until his last act is circumambulation of the House" (Sahih Muslim 1327). He also reported: "The people were commanded that the last thing they do should be to circumambulate the House, but an exception was made for menstruating women" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim 1328). These two reports are the basis of the ruling for Hajj, and of the exemption explained next.

Who is exempt: A woman in menstruation or postnatal bleeding does not perform Tawaf al-Wada and owes no expiation for leaving it. If she becomes pure while she is still in Makkah, she should perform it before she leaves. A person so ill that they truly cannot perform it is excused. But if you can manage it with help, or in a wheelchair, then do it: needing assistance does not remove the obligation after Hajj.

If you miss it after Hajj: If the farewell tawaf was forgotten or left out of ignorance, the ruling is to offer a sacrifice, a sheep slaughtered in Makkah and distributed to its poor, and there is no sin on you. If it was deliberately neglected, the sacrifice is still owed, and it is sinful once you have travelled beyond the distance at which prayers are shortened, about 83 to 85 km from Makkah. If you are still near Makkah, return and perform it. In every case your Hajj remains valid. Pilgrims preparing now can plan the farewell tawaf into their last day with our Hajj 2027 guide.

How to perform it: Exactly like any tawaf: seven circuits in a state of wudu, then two rakahs of prayer. There is no fixed dua written for the farewell tawaf. Recite the Tawaf duas you know, ask Allah to accept your Hajj or Umrah, and make it genuinely your last act in Makkah. Do not go back to long shopping trips or sightseeing afterwards; if you end up staying in Makkah much longer, repeat the farewell tawaf before you finally leave. It comes right at the end of your stay, after Sai and the other rites are complete.

Common mistakes: Skipping the farewell tawaf after Hajj, where it is obligatory for most pilgrims. Doing it days before departure and then staying on in Makkah, so it is no longer your last act. Believing it is compulsory after Umrah and worrying needlessly, when it is only recommended. And a menstruating woman attempting it instead of leaving without it, when the Prophet (peace be upon him) himself excused her. If this is your first journey, our first-time Umrah guide shows where the farewell tawaf fits in the full order of rites.

Sources: Sahih Muslim 1327 and 1328, Sahih al-Bukhari, Islamweb fatwa on Farewell Tawaaf, IslamQA on whether Tawaf al-Wada is necessary in Umrah, Office of the Mufti of the Federal Territory of Malaysia Al-Kafi #502.

Hajj 2027 · Packing ListHajj 2027 Packing List for First-Timers: What to Pack for Mina, Arafat and Muzdalifah

Hajj 2027 is expected around mid May 2027, with the Day of Arafat most likely on 15 May 2027 subject to moon sighting. First-timers usually overpack, then carry too much through the five days of Hajj. The fix is a three bag system: one main suitcase left at the hotel, one small day backpack for Mina, Arafat and Muzdalifah, and one secure pouch worn on the body for documents, phone and cash. See our Hajj 2027 Registration guide and the days of Hajj for the full picture.

The three bag system: Bag one is the main suitcase. It stays at your hotel with everything not needed during the five days: spare clothes, gifts and anything heavy. Bag two is the day backpack, small and light enough to carry all day, holding what you need for Mina, Arafat and Muzdalifah. Bag three is the body pouch, worn on your body for documents, phone and cash. Hajj means long walks, crowded buses and nights away from your hotel, so one heavy bag makes every ritual harder and buries your documents when you need them most.

Documents and money: These live in the body pouch, never in the suitcase. Pack your passport, valid at least six months beyond travel, printed copies of your Hajj visa and permit with photos of both saved on your phone as backup, and your Nusuk card. Keep group leader contact details and meeting points saved on paper and phone, because phones die and paper does not. Carry Saudi riyals in cash for small purchases, water and taxis, plus a bank card as backup, and tell your bank before travel so payments are not blocked.

Ihram and clothing: Men pack two or three sets of unstitched Ihram cloths, plus a simple Ihram belt with a pocket for cash and cards. Women pack loose, modest, breathable clothing in plain colours, with no special Ihram garment needed. Read the Ihram rules before packing anything scented. Pack broken in, comfortable sandals that leave the ankle bone uncovered for men in Ihram, and a spare pair if possible. Add extra socks and a light layer for cool nights.

The Mina, Arafat and Muzdalifah day bag: This is the heart of the article. Pack it the night before, and check it against each stop.

For Mina (tent stay):

  • The small day bag itself, packed light
  • Extra clothing and a small laundry bag
  • Personal toiletries and a small towel
  • Sun cream and a light umbrella
  • Phone, cable and power bank
  • A reusable water bottle
  • Earplugs and a sleep mask for shared tents

For Arafat (a long hot day outdoors):

  • Water
  • Medication
  • Phone with emergency numbers saved
  • Group meeting point details
  • Tissues and wipes
  • Hand sanitiser
  • Sun cream and umbrella
  • A light layer
  • Snacks such as dates and nuts

For Muzdalifah (an open air night under the sky):

  • A small foldable mat or thin sleeping bag
  • A light blanket or shawl
  • A pouch for the pebbles collected for the stoning at Jamarat
  • Comfortable footwear
  • Medicines needed overnight

Toiletries and health: Once you enter Ihram, scented products are not permitted, so pack unscented soap, shampoo, deodorant and sunscreen, plus unscented wet wipes. Bring basic medication with a copy of each prescription, rehydration salts for hot days, and a small blister kit. Check required vaccinations with your Hajj group well before travel.

What not to pack: Leave valuables beyond the minimum at home. Skip large bedding for Muzdalifah: a thin mat is enough for one night, and bulky bedding is hard to carry. Leave heavy books behind, and pack nothing scented for use during Ihram. The Saudi Ministry of Hajj advises keeping bags light with personal essentials only.

Checklist summary: three bags; documents, Nusuk card and riyals in the body pouch; two or three Ihram sets for men, plain breathable clothing for women; broken in sandals plus a spare pair; a day bag packed for Mina, Arafat and Muzdalifah; unscented toiletries; medication with prescriptions; nothing heavy, scented or precious. Also travelling for Umrah? Compare this list with our Umrah packing list. Then pack light, because every extra kilo is carried through heat, crowds and long walks.

Sources: halalexplore.com Hajj packing guide, haramainsafa.com Hajj checklist, travelways.pk packing list, Saudi Ministry of Hajj pre-travel guidance.

Madinah · Hotel GuideHotels Near Bab al-Salam Gate, Madinah: Best Stays by the Prophet's Mosque

Bab al-Salam, the Gate of Peace, is the historic western gate of Masjid an-Nabawi, the gate pilgrims use to greet the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Staying on this western side puts you closest to the Rawdah entrance and to the ladies entrance, which makes it the best base for women, elderly pilgrims and anyone planning several visits to the Rawdah. If your Madinah days are short, those saved minutes at every prayer add up to more time inside the mosque and less time walking across hot courtyards.

Closest hotels to Bab al-Salam: The hotels below sit on the western side of the mosque, listed with walking distances from UmrahMap.

HotelDistanceWalk
Manazeli Madinah Hotelabout 280 metres4 minutes on foot
Al-Madinah Goldenabout 280 metres4 minutes on foot
Rua Al-Andalus Hotelabout 300 metres4 minutes on foot
Nusk Al-Hijra Hotelabout 380 metres5 minutes on foot
Crowne Plaza Madinahabout 430 metres6 minutes on foot
Pullman Zamzam Madinahabout 430 metres6 minutes on foot
New Madinah Hotelabout 520 metres7 minutes on foot

Walking times vary with the entrance route used and with crowds at prayer times, so treat every figure here as a guide rather than a promise.

Five star stays on the western piazza: Pullman Zamzam Madinah is a 5 star hotel on the Bab al-Salam side, with rooms listed from around USD 149 per night, about 835 rooms, and a partial renovation completed in 2024. Madinah Hilton is a 5 star hotel on the western piazza with a view towards the Green Dome, rooms listed from around USD 299 per night, about 357 rooms, and a Rawdah permit assistance desk for guests. Anwar Al Madinah Movenpick Hotel is a 5 star stay about a 3 minute walk from the mosque, with about 1,295 rooms, close to the ladies entrance. Listed prices are from August 2026, and readers should check current rates before booking.

Budget picks near the gate: Manazeli Madinah and Al-Madinah Golden are the closest budget options, then Rua Al-Andalus and Nusk Al-Hijra, all a short flat walk from the gate. These simpler hotels are good for families and for pilgrims who spend most of the day at the mosque and use the room mainly for sleep, rest and a shower between prayers. What you give up in lobby size and breakfast choice, you gain back in location.

Why the west side suits women and elderly pilgrims: The ladies entrance, Gate 25, is on this side, a short walk from the hotels above. The walk is flat, shaded and level, with no steep streets to manage five times a day. The Rawdah entrance is near too, so a permit slot means a short walk instead of a long one across the courtyards. Book ahead, and if no scheduled slot appears, our Rawdah Instant Access guide explains the other route in.

Booking tips: Book early, because prices rise sharply in Ramadan and Hajj season. Compare the full stay total including meal plan before paying, not just the nightly rate. Confirm the actual entrance route from the hotel, not just the straight line distance on a map. Allow extra time at Fajr, Maghrib and Friday prayers, when the courtyards and gates fill quickly. Gates can be closed or made one way at prayer times, so follow mosque staff directions. For the wider choice across the city, see our Madinah hotels guide, plan your Madinah ziyarat days between prayers, and leave time for Jannatul Baqi, the historic cemetery east of the mosque.

Sources: maps.umrahcore.com Gate 1 As-Salam Gate page, hotelsinmakkah.com Pullman Zamzam Madinah, Madinah Hilton and Anwar Al Madinah Movenpick pages, opentravelguide.com Pullman ZamZam Madinah guide.

Nusuk App · Umrah PermitHow to Book Your Umrah Permit in the Nusuk App: Step by Step (2026)

Every pilgrim who enters Masjid al-Haram in Makkah to perform Umrah needs a permit, and the permit is issued inside Nusuk, the official app of the Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah. The permit is completely free. Never pay anyone for a permit: Nusuk issues it at no cost to every registered pilgrim with a valid visa, so anyone charging you for one is running a scam. This guide walks through the whole process in order, from creating your account to the QR code you show at the gate.

Step 1: download the real app. Install Nusuk from the Apple App Store or Google Play, and check that the developer is listed as the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah. Copycat apps with similar names exist, and only the official one can issue a permit that the gate scanners will accept.

Step 2: create your account. Open the app and choose your account type. Pick Visitor if you are an international pilgrim travelling on a visa. Pick Resident if you hold a Saudi Iqama; residents sign in through Nafath, the national single sign-on service. Visitors register with their passport number, full name exactly as printed on the passport, email address, mobile number with the country code, and a password. Type every detail slowly, because the app checks your entry against your visa record and one wrong digit can stop the match.

Step 3: verify and link your visa. Nusuk sends a one-time code (OTP) to confirm your account; enter it to finish registration. Then link your visa number and passport inside the app. If the app cannot find your record, your visa may not have synced yet: allow 24 to 48 hours after the visa is issued before trying again, rather than creating a second account.

Step 4: book the permit. On the home screen, tap Umrah, then Permits. Select yourself and add any companions travelling with you, so the whole group is on one booking. Pick a date, then a time slot. Slots are colour coded, and the green slots have the lightest crowds. Each time card also shows the prayer period it falls in, for example Before Maghrib or After Isha, so you can plan around the prayers.

Step 5: confirm the booking. The app shows a summary sheet titled "Your Blessed Umrah" with your name, date and time window. Read it carefully, agree to the terms, and tap Confirmed Booking. The permit is issued instantly, with a QR code, a reservation number and your time window. There is nothing to pay and nothing to print.

On the day: the QR code. The QR code appears in the app 2 hours before your slot. Save it offline and take a screenshot as a backup, because the connection inside the Haram can be slow. Officials scan the QR code at the Masjid al-Haram entry gates, so arrive inside your time window with the code ready on your screen. You can hold only one active Umrah permit at a time; if your plans change, cancel the existing permit first and then book the new slot.

Common problems. If the OTP never arrives, work through our Nusuk OTP Not Received? guide, which covers number formats, the email option and the old-account login loop. If registration fails, check for typing errors in your passport and visa numbers, digit by digit. And if you have only just received your visa, wait the full 24 to 48 hours for the sync before concluding that something is broken.

One permit does not cover Madinah. The Umrah permit is for Makkah only. Praying in the Rawdah inside the Prophet's Mosque needs its own separate permit, booked in the same app; our Rawdah Instant Access and Waitlist guide explains the scheduled permit, Instant Track and the waitlist. Book both permits from home before you travel, and your first days in the two holy cities will run to plan instead of to luck.

Sources: Wego Nusuk app guide (blog.wego.com/nusuk-app/) · Wego Umrah permit guide (blog.wego.com/permit-for-umrah/) · Saudi Life Guide Nusuk guide (saudilifeguide.com/nusuk-app/) · Umrahajj Nusuk guide (umrahajj.com/nusuk-app/). Checked 25 November 2026.

Travel · Getting AroundMakkah to Madinah Taxi Prices 2026: Fares by Car, Booking Tips

The road journey between Makkah and Madinah runs about 435 to 450 km along the Hijrah Highway and takes 4.5 to 5 hours by car, depending on traffic and stops. A private taxi is the door-to-door option: it collects you from your hotel in one city and drops you at your hotel in the other, with your luggage in the boot the whole way. Taxi fares on this route are charged per vehicle, not per person, and the price is fixed and agreed before you travel. The table below gives the one-way ranges found across private transfer providers, checked on 25 November 2026.

CarPassengersOne-way fare
Toyota Camry / Hyundai SonataUp to 4SAR 350–500
Hyundai Staria6–7SAR 430–560
Toyota HiAce10–11SAR 550–800
GMC Yukon XLUp to 7SAR 750–1,100
Toyota Coaster15–19SAR 800–1,150

Read the ranges honestly. Prices vary by provider and by season, and the same car can be quoted at both ends of its range in different months. The figures above are the going rates across several providers, not a tariff set by any authority. Tolls and parking are often not included in the first quote, so ask whether they are covered before you treat a fare as final. A quote far below the range for that car usually means a smaller car, a shared ride, or extras added later. If a company quotes you per person or in another currency, convert it back to one per vehicle figure in riyals before you compare it with the table.

Booking tips that save money and arguments:

  • Agree the full price on WhatsApp before the day, in writing, including any stops you plan to make on the way. A written agreement ends most disputes before they start.
  • Price any stop in advance: a detour to Badr adds roughly SAR 100 to the fare, and other ziyarat stops should be agreed the same way, not negotiated at the roadside.
  • Book a few days ahead in busy seasons: prices rise during Ramadan and Hajj, and the best cars go first, so a booking made in advance locks both the car and the fare.
  • Pay after the ride where the provider offers it; several companies let you pay the driver on arrival in Madinah, which keeps the risk on their side, not yours.
  • Confirm the exact car model, not just the price: a "7-seater" quote can mean very different vehicles, and five hours on the highway is a long time to spend in the wrong one.

Taxi or train? For a solo traveller, the Haramain high-speed train can be cheaper: economy fares run roughly SAR 49 to 250 per person, and the train is faster. But train fares are per seat, while a taxi fare covers the whole car, so for a family of four or more one fixed taxi fare is usually better value, with no station transfers at either end. Our general Makkah to Madinah transport guide compares the train, bus and taxi side by side, and the Haramain train guide covers stations, booking and luggage rules if you lean that way.

Whichever car you choose, agree the fare, the model and the stops in writing before the day, keep the driver's number saved, and give your Madinah hotel name clearly when you book, since most drivers know the hotels around the Prophet's Mosque well. Leave Makkah with time to spare. The Hijrah road is part of the journey, and a calm, fairly priced ride makes arriving in Madinah feel the way it should.

Sources: Makkah Umrah Taxi (makkahumrahtaxi.com/makkah-to-madinah-taxi/) · Mashaer Fleet (mashaerfleet.com) · Al Haram Cabs (alharamcabs.com) · Golden Alsham (goldenalsham.sa) · Kiswa Guest (kiswaguest.com). Fare ranges checked 25 November 2026; confirm the live fare before paying.

Madinah - Rawdah Instant AccessRawdah Instant Access and Waitlist - No Slot? Try This

The Rawdah is the blessed area inside the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, between the Prophet's house and his pulpit. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Between my house and my pulpit there is a garden of the gardens of Paradise." (Sahih al-Bukhari 1196). A permit to pray there is free, and it is booked in the Nusuk app. Most guides describe only one way to book it, but Nusuk offers three routes, and they have different rules. Knowing all three is the difference between getting in and going home without a visit.

Route 1 - The scheduled permit: Book a date and time in advance, from home, in the Nusuk app: open Praying in the Noble Rawdah, pick your name, choose a slot, and issue the permit. The scheduled permit can be used once every 365 days per person. If you cannot attend, cancel in advance: if you simply do not turn up, the booking is cancelled for you and only Instant Track is left. Entry is through the southern courtyards opposite Gate 37. Arrive early and follow the time printed on your permit; the visit lasts about 20 minutes.

Route 2 - Instant Access (Instant Track): This is the route most pilgrims do not know about. Once you are near the Prophet's Mosque, open the app and use Instant Track: new slots are released every 20 minutes through the day, subject to capacity at that moment. You can visit more than once a year this way, as long as you are near the mosque and there is space. It was announced by the Saudi Press Agency on 27 January 2025, together with the waitlist. Turn on your phone location, because the app only offers Instant Track when you are close to the mosque. If a slot appears, book it at once and go; it will not wait for you.

Route 3 - The waitlist: When no slot shows for the day you want, do not keep refreshing the page. Register on the waiting list for that day instead. Nusuk will notify you when a place opens, and you confirm your reservation from the notification. A notification is not a guarantee: the place can go to someone faster, so act the moment it arrives. Use the waitlist and Instant Track together while you are in Madinah; one of the two usually opens up.

Why 'no permits available' usually does not mean sold out: Slots are released in batches, not all at once. Pilgrims report new slots appearing through the day and fresh dates opening about a week ahead, so check the app daily rather than once and giving up. This release pattern is reported by pilgrims, not stated by Nusuk, so treat it as a habit to try, not a promise. Keep your scheduled permit as your guaranteed visit, and treat Instant Track and the waitlist as extra chances.

Timings to plan around: Women and men visit at separate times. For women, the windows announced on 20 October 2026 are after Fajr until 11:00 in the morning and after Isha until 2:00 at night; on Friday the morning window ends at 9:00. Timings change by season, so the time on your permit is the one that counts, not any timetable you read online. The app only shows the windows that apply to you.

Book the scheduled permit from home before you travel. Once you are in Madinah, try Instant Track and join the waitlist for extra visits. Never pay anyone for a Rawdah slot: the permit is free, and anyone selling one is running a scam. For the full step-by-step booking, see our scheduled permit guide. Sisters should also read the Rawdah Permit for Women guide for the women's timings and entry route, and anyone new to the app can start with our Nusuk app guide for setup.

Sources: Saudi Press Agency announcement, 27 January 2025; Nusuk platform wording as checked 10 November 2026; women's timings per the General Authority for the Care of the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques, 20 October 2026.

Hajj - Hajj 2027 RegistrationHajj 2027 Registration - Dates, Stages and What to Prepare

Hajj 2027, the 1448H pilgrimage, is expected around mid-May 2027, with the Day of Arafah most likely on 15 May, subject to moon sighting. If you are planning to go, the work starts now, not in spring. Registration on Nusuk Hajj is open, and every profile was reset for the new season, so returning pilgrims must submit their documents again. Packages are not live yet, and no 2027 prices have been announced.

What Nusuk Hajj is, and who it is for: Nusuk Hajj is the Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah platform for pilgrims from Muslim-minority countries, including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand. Pilgrims from large Muslim-majority countries, such as Pakistan, Malaysia, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia and Morocco, go through their own national quotas and schemes instead. Find out which route applies to you before you start, because the two doors have different dates and different forms.

The expected timeline: The dates below come from the preliminary timeline reported in November 2026. None of them is posted on hajj.nusuk.sa yet, and the Ministry can change them at any time. Packages are expected to be set up on about 10 December 2026. Package viewing, customisation and e-wallet linking are expected from about 24 December 2026. Booking is expected to open on about 9 January 2027. Registration, meaning account creation and document submission, is already open. Do not trust any other date you see quoted as final until it appears on hajj.nusuk.sa itself.

The ten stages inside Nusuk Hajj: Once you register, your application moves through ten tracked stages: create an account, upload your documents, fill in the application, application verification, select your preferred category, activate your e-wallet, browse service providers, select your package, book your package, and pay. Verification now takes hours to days. The e-wallet is locked for the moment, so there is nothing to pay yet, and you should never pay anyone outside your own Nusuk account.

The two files that block most people: Nusuk accepts only a passport scan and a photo in a strict size and format, and applications with the wrong files can be rejected or delayed. Prepare both files exactly as the platform asks before you start. Two more rules to know: Nusuk only accepts applicants who are 16 or older when they register, and if you register as a resident, your residence card must be valid through December 2027. If you registered in an earlier season, log in with that same account; do not create a new one.

What to do now: Create your Nusuk Hajj account and submit your documents now, while there is no rush. Subscribe to the platform updates so you hear the day packages go live. If your country runs a national scheme, check its dates separately: Pakistan's government-scheme applications for 2027 opened on 18 August 2026, for example. Do not pay anyone who promises a guaranteed 2027 package before packages go live, and do not believe any 2027 price quoted today: no prices have been published, and anyone quoting them is guessing.

This page will be updated the day the Ministry announces the opening dates. Register now, prepare your documents, and wait for the official announcement. For the wider picture, see our general Hajj 2027 guide. Our Umrah Visa article shows how Umrah visas differ from the Hajj route, and our Nusuk app guide covers Nusuk account setup.

Sources: Nusuk Hajj platform status as reported 23 November 2026; preliminary 1448 timeline as reported November 2026; Pakistan government-scheme dates as reported November 2026.

Nusuk App · CompetitionNusuk Free Umrah Competition — How Codes and Keys Work

The Nusuk Free Umrah Competition is a free quiz inside the official Nusuk app. It runs from 1 November to 20 December 2026, fifty days in total. Every day one winner is drawn for a free Umrah trip for two, and several winners are drawn for Zamzam water. You enter by answering one Islamic knowledge question a day with a key. Keys are free, and invite codes from other pilgrims give you extra keys. This guide explains how keys work, how to add a code, what the prizes include, and how to avoid scams.

How keys work: You get one free key every day inside the app, in the Games Centre under Free Umrah Competition. The key expires at the end of the day, so use it or lose it. Each key opens one of four question doors: Quran, Seerah, Makkah and the Grand Mosque, and Madinah and the Prophet's Mosque. Answer the question correctly and you are in that day's draw. Extra correct answers add extra chances in the same draw, so more keys mean more entries. You can earn extra keys by swapping invite codes. When you use someone's code, you both get one extra key. When someone uses your code, you both get one extra key too. There is one limit to remember: each pair of people can only swap once. If Nusuk says "The code already has been used", it usually means you and that person have already swapped, so copy the next code instead.

How to add a code: In the Nusuk app, tap Start the challenge and open the Keys tab. Paste the code in the "Add code to get new key" box and tap Check the code. Codes start with NG- followed by eight letters and numbers. Codes are case-sensitive, so copy the code exactly, with no spaces before or after it. Add one code at a time. On EasyNusuk, copy any code from the free codes list at the top of this page and paste it in the app. You can also share your own code with the Add your code button, so other pilgrims can use it and you both earn a key. The codes on this page are public community codes shared by users. They are not verified inside the Nusuk app, and some may already be used or expired, so try the next code if one does not work.

Where your own code is: Open the Nusuk app, go to the Free Umrah Competition, and open Keys. Your code is shown there, starting with NG-. Share it anywhere you like. Every time someone uses it, you both get an extra key.

What the prizes are: The first prize is a free Umrah trip for the winner and one companion of their choice. It includes the Umrah visa, return flight tickets, ten nights of accommodation across Makkah and Madinah, transport and guidance services, and a visit to Al-Rawdah Al-Sharifah. Fifty winners are drawn over the fifty days, so one hundred Umrah trips in total. The prize cannot be transferred to another person and cannot be exchanged for cash. The second prize is blessed Zamzam water. Ten thousand cartons are given away across the competition. Each daily Zamzam winner receives twenty cartons to share with loved ones. Delivery is only to citizens and residents in Saudi Arabia. Winners are announced every day on Nusuk's official accounts, @MyNusuk, and their names appear on the Winners page inside the game in the app. Winners are contacted by email, so keep the email address on your Nusuk account valid and check it while the competition runs. Each person can win once. Winners drawn between 21 and 30 November travel for Umrah in Ramadan, per the competition's own promotion.

Scams to avoid: The competition is free to enter. Never pay anyone for a code or a key, and never pay a person or a Facebook page that promises to enter you. Never share your Nusuk password or any verification code with anyone, not even someone who claims to be from Nusuk support. Confirm every detail inside the official app, not through links forwarded on WhatsApp or social media. If a message pressures you to pay or to share a code quickly, it is a scam. The official competition runs only inside the Nusuk app.

After 20 December 2026: The competition ends on 20 December 2026. This page will be updated the same week to say so. The free codes list on this page will stay only if a new competition is announced.

Get your free key every day, add codes from the list above, and answer the question you know best. One correct answer a day is all it takes to be in the draw. New to the app itself? Our step-by-step guide to using the Nusuk app and the complete Nusuk app guide cover setup, permits and bookings.

Sources: noblestudent.com · goodnews.com.pk · insurab.com · nusukkey.xyz. Checked November 2026.

Nusuk App · TroubleshootingNusuk OTP Not Received? How to Fix It (2026)

The OTP is the four-digit verification code Nusuk sends when you sign up or log in. When it never arrives, you cannot get into the app at all. Most OTP failures have one of four causes: a wrong number format, a visa that is too new to be synced, the wrong delivery channel, or an old account blocking the way. Work through the fixes below in order.

Check your number first: Enter your number with the full country code and no leading zero after it. A UK number starting 07 must be entered as +44 without the 0, for example 07912 345678 becomes +447912345678. Remove all spaces, dashes and brackets. Check that international SMS is switched on with your mobile company, and that the number matches the one on your visa record. Nusuk checks your details against immigration records, so a number that does not match the visa process can fail verification. One mistyped digit fails silently, so retype the number slowly and check every digit.

Wait out the visa sync delay: If your visa was issued less than 24 to 48 hours ago, Nusuk may not have your record yet. "ID not found" and "Something went wrong" during this window are often a sync delay, not a broken account. Wait a full day after the visa is issued, then try again. Do not keep creating new accounts while you wait. Each new attempt tangles the next one, and the old record is the one Nusuk remembers.

Try the email code and the web version: Newer versions of the Nusuk app offer the code by email as well as SMS. If SMS fails, choose the email option and check your spam and promotions folders, not just your inbox. Wait a minute before tapping resend. Tapping resend again and again can make the delay worse. If the app keeps failing, try the web version at nusuk.sa. Pilgrims report that one channel sometimes works when the other does not. If nothing works after repeated tries across a day, it is a server-side issue only Nusuk can fix, so contact support.

The old-account login loop: If you performed Umrah before, you may already have a Nusuk account from that trip, and a new sign-up will fail with "ID already exists" or loop back to the start. Use Recover Account, not New Account, and feed it the exact details from the web version. The recovery flow reattaches the old account instead of fighting it. If recovery still loops, email support@umrah.nusuk.sa with the subject RESET ID NUSUK and attach screenshots of your passport and visa. Do not keep creating new accounts. One identity, one account, one recovery.

When to call support: If none of the fixes above work, call Nusuk technical support on 920002814. Inside Saudi Arabia you can also call the pilgrim line 1966, or the unified contact number 930. Before you call, take a screenshot of the exact error message and note the time it happened. Never share your password or any verification code with anyone, including someone who says they are from support. Real support will never ask for them.

In most cases the fix is a number format or a one-day wait. Screenshot the error, try the fixes in order, and contact support only if the code still does not arrive after a full day. For other app problems, see Nusuk App Not Working? Common Problems & Fixes, and our Nusuk app guide and step-by-step guide to the Nusuk app cover setup and permits in full.

Sources: taqwatours.co.uk · blogs.huzi.pk · umrah.to · nusuk-keys.vercel.app. Checked November 2026.

Madinah · Rawdah Permit for WomenRawdah Permit for Women — Rules, Timings & How to Book

The Rawdah is the most sought after place of prayer in Madinah: the small, blessed area inside the Prophet's Mosque between what was the Prophet's house and his pulpit. Entry is by permit only, the permit is free, and women have their own timings, entry route and booking details. This guide covers the women's side of the visit; for the rules that apply to everyone, see our main Rawdah Permit guide.

Why the Rawdah matters: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Between my house and my pulpit there is a garden of the gardens of Paradise" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1196).

Women's visiting times: According to the schedule published by the Saudi Press Agency on 20 October 2026, women may visit the Rawdah from Saturday to Thursday after Fajr prayer until 11:00 AM, and again after Isha prayer until 2:00 AM. On Fridays the morning window is shorter: after Fajr until 9:00 AM, and after Isha until 2:00 AM. These times can change with the season and crowd levels, so treat them as a guide only. The time that counts is the one shown on your permit in the Nusuk app.

How to book, step by step:

  • Step 1: Open the official Nusuk app and sign in with your passport and visa details.
  • Step 2: Open the Rawdah section and choose the women's Rawdah Prayer Permit.
  • Step 3: Pick the date and time slot that fits your stay, and add your companions for your group.
  • Step 4: Confirm the booking. The permit is completely free, and only Nusuk issues it.
  • Step 5: Confirm your attendance in the app between 48 hours and 2 hours before your slot. If you miss this step, the booking can be lost.
  • Step 6: Your QR code appears in the app about 2 hours before the visit. Screenshot it, because the signal inside the mosque can be weak.
  • Step 7: Arrive at least 30 minutes early and follow the signs to the women's entry through the southern courtyards near Gate 37, where staff scan your code.

One visit a year, plus two backups: The scheduled Rawdah permit can be booked only once every 365 days, so choose your slot with care. If that permit is already used, or no slot is left, Nusuk offers two more routes. The Instant Track is for visitors already near the Prophet's Mosque; it opens inside the app when capacity allows. There is also a waitlist: join it and you may be offered a place when another pilgrim cancels.

Practical tips for women:

  • Wear a full, loose abaya and hijab for the visit.
  • Children are not permitted inside the Rawdah, so arrange for someone to look after them before your slot.
  • Your stay inside is short, about 10 to 15 minutes. Decide your duas before you go in, so the time is well spent.
  • You may book for a group of up to 4 companions.
  • New slots are released in batches, often on Fridays, and cancellations appear at any time. Check the app often rather than once.

If no slot shows: Do not give up after one look, and never pay an agent who promises you a permit; the permit is free and only Nusuk issues it. Keep checking the app, especially on Fridays, join the waitlist, and try the Instant Track once you are in Madinah. If the Rawdah does not work out, the city is still full of blessed places, as our Madinah Ziyarat guide shows, and sisters travelling without a mahram will find our Women Travelling Alone article helpful.

Sources: Rawdah permit guide, ksaexpats.com · Rawdah permits guide, hisartour.com · Rawdah visiting guide, visitalmadinah.com · Rawdah appointment guide, uumrahseelf.com · Women's visiting schedule: Saudi Press Agency, 20 October 2026. Checked November 2026.

Umrah · Ihram for WomenIhram for Women — Rules, What to Wear & Common Mistakes

Many sisters prepare for Umrah by asking what their Ihram clothing should look like, often picturing a special white outfit like the men's. In fact, women have no special two-piece Ihram cloth. A woman enters Ihram in her normal modest clothes, and the rules that follow are mostly about two things she must leave off, plus a few habits to adjust. This guide is the women's companion to our general Ihram Rules article, which covers the rules both genders share.

What to wear: Enter Ihram in your ordinary modest dress: a loose abaya and hijab are the usual choice. The colour is yours to choose; black, white and every other colour are all allowed. What matters is the condition of the clothing: it must be loose, not tight, and not transparent, and it should be plain, without adornment meant to attract attention. Ordinary stitched clothes, socks and closed shoes are all fine for a woman in Ihram.

The two things forbidden: The Prophet ﷺ said: "A woman in the state of Ihram must neither wear niqab nor gloves" (Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated from Ibn Umar).

Covering the face without a niqab: The ban is on the niqab, a veil tied or fitted onto the face, and on gloves covering the hands. A woman in Ihram leaves her face and hands uncovered. If non-mahram men pass by, she may still cover her face by letting her khimar or jilbab hang down over her face, untied, so the cloth falls loosely in front of it. This is what Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) described the women doing with the Prophet ﷺ during Hajj, as narrated in Sunan Abi Dawood: when riders passed, they lowered their garments over their faces, and when the men had gone, they uncovered them again.

Other rules for a woman in Ihram:

  • No perfume on the body or on the clothes, including scented soap, creams and deodorant, from the moment she enters Ihram.
  • Ghusl before Ihram is allowed and recommended for cleanliness, even though it is not a condition for the Ihram to count.
  • Menses does not prevent entering Ihram. A woman in her period makes the intention and enters Ihram like everyone else; she simply waits until she is pure before performing Tawaf.
  • She says the Talbiyah quietly, only loud enough to hear herself, not raising her voice like the men.
  • There is no idtiba for women: she keeps her right shoulder covered, and she does not take the brisk walk in the first circuits of Tawaf; she walks at her normal pace throughout.
  • After Sa'i, she ends her Umrah by shortening her hair by a fingertip's length, rather than shaving or cutting it short like the men.

Common mistakes to avoid:

  • Wearing a tied niqab in Ihram, instead of letting a loose cloth hang over the face when men pass.
  • Wearing gloves, even thin ones, while in the state of Ihram.
  • Using perfume or scented products after entering Ihram, including scented wipes and hotel soap.
  • Wearing clothes that are tight or see-through, which break the modesty that Ihram clothing is meant to keep.
  • Uncovering the face deliberately in crowds out of habit or for photographs, when the loose hanging cloth would cover it.

With these few rules kept, a woman's Ihram is simple: her everyday modest dress, an uncovered face and hands, and a quiet Talbiyah. Sisters planning the journey on their own can read our Women Travelling Alone article, and our Umrah Duas collection gathers the supplications for each stage of the rites.

Sources: Islamweb.net: Rulings for Women on Hajj and Umrah · Restrictions for a Person in the State of Ihraam · How to Perform Umrah · Women's dress in Ihram (fatwa). Checked November 2026.

Nusuk App · TroubleshootingNusuk App Not Working? Common Problems & Fixes

Nusuk is the Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah's official app for free Umrah permits and Rawdah bookings — so when it refuses to log you in, never sends the verification code, or shows no slots at all, it can feel as if the whole trip is blocked. Most of these problems are well known, and most have a simple fix. Work through the seven problems below; for the app working as it should, see our Nusuk App Guide.

Problem 1: login loop — "this ID is already registered". This usually means your details were registered on a previous visa cycle, or an agent created the account for you on an earlier trip. Do not keep creating new accounts — that only adds to the tangle. Use the app's Recover Account option to reclaim the existing account instead.

Problem 2: the OTP or verification code never arrives. Check your spam folder first. Then check the number itself: enter your mobile in full international format with no leading zero after the country code — for example +447912345678, not a number starting 07912. And the number must match the one given on your visa application; a different number is a common reason the code never comes.

Problem 3: visa sync delay. If your visa was issued less than 24–48 hours ago, the Nusuk system may not have your record yet. A "something went wrong" or "ID not found" message inside this window is usually a sync delay, not a refusal — wait a full day, then try again.

Problem 4: wrong number or name mismatch. Enter your full name exactly as it appears on your passport. Then check which number you are typing: the number starting 48 is the border number, not the visa number. Visa-on-arrival numbers start 88 when issued at a self-service machine, or 98 at the passport desk. Mixing these up is what produces error 10010016.

Problem 5: no Rawdah slots showing. Slots are released in batches — commonly around Friday and roughly 7–10 days ahead — and they can fill within seconds. Fresh seats and cancellations also appear about every 20 minutes, on the hour and at :20 and :40 past it, so keep checking rather than giving up. A standard Rawdah booking is allowed once every 365 days per person, with the Instant Track option near the mosque as the exception. Once booked, confirm your attendance from 48 hours before the appointment, and note that the QR code only appears about 2 hours beforehand. Our Rawdah Permit guide walks through the booking itself.

Problem 6: stuck or double payment. Never pay a failed transaction again immediately. Check your bank SMS first — the first payment often went through even when the app showed an error. If a refund is due, it returns to the same card you paid with.

Problem 7: the app crashes or freezes. Update the app to the latest version, clear its cache, and restart your phone. If it still misbehaves, reinstall it — or use the Nusuk web version in your browser instead.

Where to get help: Start with the in-app Help and Support section. In the Kingdom, the Ministry's Enayah Centres in Makkah and Madinah help pilgrims in person, and the toll-free pilgrim line is 1966. If your problem starts earlier — a refused visa rather than a broken app — our Umrah Visa Rejected? guide covers the common reasons and how to reapply, and the Umrah packing list helps with the rest of the journey. Community members also share free Nusuk key codes in our free codes list.

Sources: Nusuk troubleshooting file (blogs.huzi.pk) · Nusuk app guide (taqwatours.co.uk) · Rawda Essentials (mabrooressentials.com) · Nusuk app guide (umrahindex.com). Checked November 2026; server-side account and payment problems can only be fixed by Nusuk support.

Travel · Getting AroundJeddah Airport to Makkah — Taxi, Train & Bus Prices (2026)

Jeddah's King Abdulaziz International Airport (JED) is the main gateway for Makkah: from the airport to Masjid al-Haram is about 85–95 km by road, roughly 60–90 minutes without traffic. You have five real options — train, ride-hailing, airport taxi, bus, or a pre-booked transfer. The prices below are researched ranges checked in November 2026; fares vary by date, demand and season, so always confirm the live price before you pay.

OptionTimePrice
Haramain High Speed Railway54 minutes to Makkah stationEconomy about SAR 55–90 one-way (some 2026 sources report SAR 35–50); business about SAR 100–150
Uber / CareemAbout 60–90 minutes, door to doorAbout SAR 170–260 per car, more at peak times
Airport taxiAbout 60–90 minutesAround SAR 200–300 per car
SAPTCO / Northwest busAround 2 hoursAbout SAR 20–35 per person
Pre-booked private transferAbout 60–90 minutes, door to doorSedan about SAR 200–250 fixed; MPV about SAR 300–350; van about SAR 400–450

Good to know, option by option:

  • Train: the Haramain station is inside Terminal 1; book on sar.hhr.sa or the HHR app. Makkah station is in Rusaifah, about 3–4 km from the Haram, so add a taxi (SAR 20–40, 10–15 minutes) or the SAR 4 city bus for the last leg.
  • Uber / Careem: the simplest door-to-door choice — best for families, lots of luggage and late-night arrivals.
  • Airport taxi: agree the price before you get in; quotes of SAR 300–500 at the rank are common, above the usual going rate.
  • Bus: the cheapest option, but it drops you at the bus station, not your hotel, so allow for a short taxi at the Makkah end as well.
  • Private transfer: a fixed price agreed in advance, with meet and greet at arrivals — the calmest option after a long flight.

Which should you choose? The train is best for solo travellers and couples with light luggage landing at Terminal 1 in the daytime. For a family, Uber or Careem is usually simpler and often cheaper overall once the station taxi is added to the train fare. All fares rise as travel dates approach, and again in Ramadan and the Hajj season. And if you land in ihram, keep the free pilgrim shuttle in mind where it runs. Continuing on to Madinah afterwards? Our Makkah to Madinah transport guide compares the same options between the two cities. Umrah · Kosovo GuideUmrah from Kosovo — Visa & Flights Guide

Kosovo passport holders can now apply for a Saudi tourist eVisa online. Saudi Arabia added Kosovo (with Guyana) to the eVisa eligibility list on 4 October 2026, and Kosovo appears on the official Permitted Country list in the Visit Saudi eVisa Terms and Conditions (visa.visitsaudi.com). That makes Umrah from Pristina far simpler than before — no embassy visit needed for most travellers.

Visa options: Tourist eVisa — apply online at visa.visitsaudi.com. Fee SAR 535 (about US$143), including health insurance. One-year multiple-entry visa, up to 90 days per visit. Your passport must have at least 6 months' validity from your date of entry. The same visa is also available on arrival at Saudi airports on the same terms. Dedicated Umrah visa — if you prefer a package, apply through Nusuk or a licensed Umrah agent; the agent arranges the visa with hotel and transport bookings documented through Nusuk Masar. 1448H season dates: Umrah visa issuance ends 9 March 2027, last entry into Saudi Arabia 23 March 2027, and all pilgrims must depart by 7 April 2027. Plan travel inside these dates.

Flights from Pristina: There is currently no direct flight from Pristina (PRN, Adem Jashari International Airport) to Jeddah. The usual routes are Turkish Airlines via Istanbul (PRN–IST about 2 hours, IST–JED 3 hours 45 minutes) — around 6–7 hours in total with a connection; Pegasus Airlines via Istanbul Sabiha Gokcen (SAW) — the budget alternative on the same corridor; Qatar Airways via Doha — another one-stop option. Book early for Ramadan and school-holiday dates, when one-stop seats fill first.

Money and time: Kosovo uses the euro (EUR). Pristina is 2 hours behind Jeddah in winter (CET, UTC+1 vs AST, UTC+3) and 1 hour behind in summer (CEST, UTC+2). Keep the difference in mind when booking onward transport and hotel check-in times.

Health requirements: The meningococcal ACWY vaccine is mandatory for Umrah travellers and must be given at least 10 days before arrival. Polio vaccination is not compulsory for travellers from Kosovo, and yellow fever vaccination is only required if you arrive from a yellow-fever risk country. Carry your vaccination certificate with your travel documents.

Women travelling: Women of all ages from Kosovo can travel for Umrah without a mahram, under the current Saudi rules — the same rule that applies to other eVisa-eligible nationalities.

A reminder of the reward: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Umrah to Umrah expiates what is between them' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1773, Sahih Muslim 1349).
