DuasUmrah Duas — Complete Collection for the Journey

Quick answer: Umrah has only a handful of moments where the Prophet ﷺ himself taught the words: the Talbiyah on entering Ihram, "Bismillah, Allahu Akbar" at the Black Stone, "Rabbana atina…" in the last stretch of every Tawaf circuit, and the verse and dhikr on Safa. Around those fixed points, everything is open — the Multazam, the Zamzam cup, the long walk of Sa'i — for your own dua, in your own language, from your own heart. This page gathers the established duas in the order you will need them, each with its Arabic, transliteration, translation and source. For a printable one-page version spanning the whole trip, see our Umrah Dua Book.

1. The Talbiyah — on entering Ihram: From the moment you make your intention and enter Ihram, you take up the Talbiyah and keep repeating it until you reach the Kaaba and begin Tawaf. It is the pilgrim's answer to Allah's call:

لَبَّيْكَ اللَّهُمَّ لَبَّيْكَ، لَبَّيْكَ لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ لَبَّيْكَ، إِنَّ الْحَمْدَ وَالنِّعْمَةَ لَكَ وَالْمُلْكَ، لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ

"Labbayk Allahumma Labbayk, Labbayka la sharika laka Labbayk, innal-hamda wan-ni'mata laka wal-mulk, la sharika lak"

"Here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am — You have no partner — here I am. Truly all praise, all blessing and all sovereignty are Yours. You have no partner." (Sahih al-Bukhari 1549; Sahih Muslim 1184)

2. On first seeing the Kaaba: When the Kaaba first comes into view, raise your hands — the first sight is remembered as a moment when dua is accepted — and say the well-known dua reported by al-Shafi'i in al-Umm:

اللَّهُمَّ زِدْ هَذَا الْبَيْتَ تَشْرِيفًا وَتَعْظِيمًا وَتَكْرِيمًا وَمَهَابَةً

"Allahumma zid hadha al-bayta tashrifan wa ta'ziman wa takriman wa mahabah"

"O Allah, increase this House in honour, greatness, nobility and awe."

An honest note: this dua is widely loved and widely used, but scholars differ on the strength of its chain of narration — it does not carry the same certainty as the Talbiyah above. Say it if you wish, then follow it with your own dua for whatever you came carrying; nothing is lost either way.

3. During Tawaf: At the start of every circuit, facing the Black Stone, say "Bismillah, Allahu Akbar" — "In the name of Allah; Allah is the Greatest." Then, in the final stretch of each circuit, between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, recite the dua of the Qur'an:

رَبَّنَا آتِنَا فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَفِي الْآخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ

"Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan wa fil-akhirati hasanatan wa qina 'adhaban-nar"

"Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." (Qur'an 2:201; Sunan Abi Dawud 1892)

For the rest of Tawaf — what is established, what is not, and why no circuit has a dua of its own — see our Tawaf Duas article.

4. On Safa, at the start of Sa'i: As you approach Safa, first recite the words of the Qur'an:

إِنَّ الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةَ مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ

"Innas-safa wal marwata min sha'a'irillah"

"Indeed, Safa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah." (Qur'an 2:158)

Then climb Safa, face the Kaaba, raise your hands, say Allahu Akbar three times and make dua — exactly as the Prophet ﷺ did, as described in the long hadith of Jabir (RA) (Sahih Muslim 1218). Do the same on Marwah, and on every hilltop of the seven lengths.

5. At the Multazam: The Multazam is the wall of the Kaaba between the Black Stone and its door, where pilgrims press close and pour out their hearts. There is no fixed wording here — no prescribed dua you must find or lose the moment. Stand there if the crowd allows, without pushing anyone, and ask Allah for what you actually came with: forgiveness, your parents, your family, your needs in this world and the next. Sincerity is the whole of it.

6. When drinking Zamzam: Face the qiblah, say Bismillah, and before you drink, set your intention and say the dua reported from Ibn Abbas (RA):

اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ عِلْمًا نَافِعًا وَرِزْقًا وَاسِعًا وَشِفَاءً مِنْ كُلِّ دَاءٍ

"Allahumma inni as'aluka 'ilman nafi'an wa rizqan wasi'an wa shifa'an min kulli da'"

"O Allah, I ask You for beneficial knowledge, abundant provision, and healing from every disease."

The intention matters because of the Prophet's ﷺ own words: "Zamzam water is for whatever it is drunk for" (Sunan Ibn Majah 3062, graded hasan). Decide what you are asking for, then drink. The full story of the well is in our Zamzam Water article.

Dua is not a performance: You do not need Arabic to be heard. Between the fixed moments above, make dua in your own language, in your own words, from your heart — at the Multazam, between the hills of Sa'i, over the Zamzam cup. The Arabic is for the moments the Sunnah itself marked; everything around them is yours.

Practical tip: Save this page offline before you travel — phone signal inside the Haram can be weak. The permits that get you into the Haram and the Rawdah run through one app, covered step by step in our Nusuk App Complete Guide, and everything else you need to carry is on our Umrah Packing List.

Quick questions:

  • Do I have to memorise all the duas? No. The Talbiyah, the takbir at the Black Stone, "Rabbana atina" and the Safa verse are short and worth learning by heart — but the rest can be read from your phone or a booklet, or replaced with your own sincere words. No dua is wasted because it was not memorised.
  • Can I make dua in my own language? Yes — anywhere, and above all in the open moments: the Multazam, the walk of Sa'i, drinking Zamzam. Allah hears every language. The Arabic on this page is for the specific moments where the Prophet ﷺ taught specific words.
  • Is there a fixed dua for each Tawaf circuit? No. Apart from "Bismillah, Allahu Akbar" at the Black Stone and "Rabbana atina…" between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, no circuit carries its own prescribed dua. The printed dua-per-round booklets are a later help for pilgrims, not a requirement — fill the circuits with dhikr, Qur'an and your own dua.

Travel · Getting AroundMakkah to Madinah — Train, Bus & Taxi Guide

Quick answer: The two holy cities stand about 450 km apart, and there are four honest ways across: the Haramain high-speed train (about 2 hours 20 minutes, base fare SAR 162 Economy), a private car (4–5 hours door-to-door, about SAR 405–830 per vehicle), ride-hailing (about SAR 350–500), and the bus (about SAR 60–170 per person, 5.5–6.5 hours). For most pilgrims the train is the answer — the rest of this page covers when it is not, and the station taxis nobody budgets for. If you are costing the whole trip, our Umrah Cost from Pakistan breakdown shows where this leg sits in the total.

Please note — fares, not quotes: Every price below is a 2026 figure checked in October–November 2026. Train fares move with demand and how early you book; road prices are agreed with the driver before you set off. Confirm the live fare before you pay.

The four options, side by side:

OptionPriceJourney timeDoor-to-door?
Haramain trainBase fare SAR 162 Economy · SAR 455 Business, before VAT & fees; typically SAR 145–200 Economy in 2026~2 h 20 minNo — a taxi at both stations
Bus (SAPTCO, Darb Al Watan)SAR 60–170 per person5.5–6.5 hNo — city bus terminals
Private carSAR 405–830 per vehicle; luxury up to SAR 830–1,2004–5 hYes — hotel to hotel
Ride-hailing (Uber, Careem)SAR 350–500 per vehicle4–5 hYes

The Haramain train — the default choice: The Haramain High-Speed Railway runs the 449 km line between the two cities via Jeddah at speeds of up to 300 km/h, covering Makkah to Madinah in about 2 hours 20 minutes. The official base fare is SAR 162 in Economy and SAR 455 in Business, one way (sar.hhr.sa, October 2026), before the 15% VAT and fees; in practice, 2026 tickets are typically found around SAR 145–200 in Economy and SAR 240–300 in Business, depending on the train and how early you book. Book at sar.hhr.sa, in the HHR app, in the Nusuk app — the same account our Nusuk App Complete Guide walks you through — or via the call centre on 920 004 433. Our dedicated Haramain Train guide covers the stations, booking and the journey day itself in full.

Luggage, and the station gap:

  • Luggage: one large bag up to 25 kg (65 × 55 × 35 cm) plus one hand item per passenger — pack to it, and the station stops being stressful.
  • The stations are not at the Haram. Makkah station is about 3.5 km from Masjid al-Haram, a taxi of about SAR 15–30; Madinah station is about 9 km from the Prophet's Mosque, a taxi of about SAR 20–40. Add both rides — and the extra half hour at each end — to the ticket price before you compare it with a car.
  • Book early in Ramadan and Hajj. In the peak seasons the best timings sell out completely; in every season, the cheapest fares go first.

The bus — the budget backup: SAPTCO and Darb Al Watan coaches run between the two cities for about SAR 60–170 per person, taking 5.5–6.5 hours with stops on the way. The bus is rarely a first choice, but it is the reliable fallback when the trains have sold out — and for a solo pilgrim travelling light, it is by far the cheapest seat between the two cities.

Private car — best for families and groups: A car with a driver takes you hotel door to hotel door in 4–5 hours at a fixed price agreed before you set off: about SAR 405–450 for a sedan, SAR 430–550 for an SUV, SAR 530–550 for a van, and SAR 830–1,200 for a luxury vehicle. Split four to six ways, a car can cost less per head than train tickets plus station taxis — with no luggage limit and no station transfers. Agree two things before the wheels move: the full fixed price, and your stops — prayer breaks along the way, and the historic stop at Badr if your group wants it. Where you sleep at the far end matters as much as how you get there; our Makkah Hotels Near Haram guide covers the Makkah end of the journey.

Ride-hailing — Uber and Careem: Both apps work in both cities, and a Makkah–Madinah ride typically comes to about SAR 350–500 — door-to-door like a private car, booked in a minute. The catch is surge pricing: at prayer exits, on Fridays and through Ramadan the fare can climb well past that range, and drivers can be scarce for a 450 km trip at busy hours. Check the fare in the app before you commit; if it has surged, a pre-booked private car at a fixed price is usually the calmer deal.

Which option for whom:

  • Solo or a couple, in a hurry: the train — fastest by hours, and you arrive rested enough to go straight to the mosque.
  • Family or group with luggage: a private car — one fixed price, door to door, stops when you need them.
  • Tight budget, or the trains have sold out: the bus — slow, but it gets everyone there for the price of a modest meal.

However you cross, plan the days at each end as carefully as the crossing: our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide maps how crowds and prices move through the year, and if your wider journey starts or ends at the airport, our Jeddah Airport to Makkah guide and Umrah Visa Fees guide cover those legs.

Quick questions:

  • How early should I book the Haramain train? As soon as your dates are fixed. In quiet weeks, a few days ahead is usually enough; in Ramadan, the Hajj season and school holidays, book weeks ahead — popular timings sell out entirely, and the cheapest fares always go first.
  • Is the train station near the Haram? No. Makkah station is about 3.5 km from Masjid al-Haram (taxi about SAR 15–30) and Madinah station about 9 km from the Prophet's Mosque (taxi about SAR 20–40). Budget the taxi and the extra time at both ends, especially with luggage.
  • Can I take a bus at night? Yes — SAPTCO and Darb Al Watan run services through the day and into the night on this route, and many pilgrims ride overnight to save a hotel night. Confirm the exact departure time and arrival terminal when you book, and keep your valuables with you at the stops.

Makkah · Hotel GuideMakkah Hotels Near Haram — Areas & Booking Tips

Quick answer: In Makkah, distance is money. Hotels within 200 metres of the Haram (Zone 1, the Clock Tower area) cost the most but ask almost nothing of your legs; hotels 200–500 metres out (Zone 2 — Ajyad, Jabal Omar, the near end of Ibrahim Khalil Road) are the sweet spot for most pilgrims; beyond 800 metres you are in shuttle territory, where the room is cheap but the bus timetable runs your day. After the flight, the hotel is the biggest line in any package — our Umrah Cost from Pakistan breakdown shows exactly how much of the total it takes.

Please note — ranges, not quotes: Every price on this page is an approximate November 2026 nightly room range, never a fixed quote. Rates move with the season, the day of the week and how full the city is. Always confirm the live price — and the hotel's exact name and district — before you book or pay.

The four zones around the Haram:

ZoneDistanceWalkWhat it means
Zone 1 — Ultra-close0–200 m1–3 minAbraj Al Bait / Clock Tower and the streets touching the Haram. Highest prices; the right choice for elderly pilgrims, wheelchair users and families with infants
Zone 2 — Comfortable200–500 m4–7 minAjyad, Jabal Omar and the near end of Ibrahim Khalil Road. An easy walk five times a day for most people
Zone 3 — Manageable500–800 m8–12 minFine for fit walkers; think honestly about doing it five times a day, in heat, for two weeks
Zone 4 — Shuttle zone800 m–2 km+15–30 minAziziyah and the outer districts. Budget-friendly only if a frequent hotel shuttle is confirmed in writing

The main hotel areas, one by one:

  • Ajyad — directly south of the Haram, packed with 3- and 4-star hotels at Zone 1–2 distances. The catch is the slope: the walk back from the Haram is uphill, and you feel it most after Fajr.
  • Ibrahim Khalil Road / Misfalah — the flat route into King Abdulaziz Gate (Gate 1), and Makkah's budget and mid-range cluster, with plenty of Pakistani and Asian restaurants. Known names here include Anjum Hotel (~350 m), Emaar Al Khalil (~400 m) and Elaf Kinda, just 1–2 minutes from the Haram.
  • Jabal Omar — the newer west-side development: Hyatt Regency, Conrad, Hilton Suites and Marriott. The walk to the Haram is downhill, but the return climbs a steep 8–12% incline — a real consideration with elderly parents.
  • Aziziyah — the cheapest rooms in Makkah, and completely shuttle-dependent. Here the shuttle timings own your schedule: miss the bus and you miss the prayer, or pay for a taxi.

Example nightly prices (approximate, 2026, per room per night):

HotelApprox. nightly priceNotes
Pullman Zamzam (Clock Tower)from SAR 800Zone 1, inside the Abraj Al Bait complex
Al Safwa Tower 3SAR 470Twin room with breakfast for two
Maysan Al Mashaer (Ajyad)SAR 480Ajyad, Zone 2
Worth EliteSAR 345–535Price moves with season and room type
Emaar AndalusiaSAR 350–730Wide range between quiet and busy periods
Voco MakkahSAR 320–350Shuttle zone, but with a frequent hotel shuttle
Sama Al SamahSAR 150 quiet · SAR 200–220 busyAmong the cheapest rooms near the Haram

Ramadan changes everything: in Ramadan, luxury rooms can exceed SAR 3,000 a night, and Haram-view rooms cost more and sell out early. If Ramadan or Rajab is your plan, book as early as you can — our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide maps how prices and crowds move through the year.

Booking tips that protect you:

  • Ask for the walking time to a named gate — King Abdulaziz Gate (Gate 1), King Fahd Gate (Gate 79) or King Abdullah Gate (Gate 100) — never accept a bare "near Haram". Agents measure from different points; a gate name cannot be fudged.
  • Shuttles pause after prayers. Hotel shuttle buses typically stop for about an hour after each main prayer — plan your returns around it, especially in Aziziyah.
  • Wheelchair users: enter through Gate 1, 79 or 100, which have dedicated ramps — and weigh that flat entry when choosing between Ajyad's slope, Jabal Omar's incline and the flat Ibrahim Khalil Road route.
  • Get the hotel name and district in writing on the quote. "5-star near Haram" on a voucher is how pilgrims end up in Aziziyah. The name and district, in writing, before you pay.
  • No Booking, No Visa. In the Nusuk Masar era, the confirmed hotel booking is part of the visa file itself — no confirmed booking, no visa. Our Umrah Visa Fees guide explains the visa side, and the Nusuk App Complete Guide covers the app it all runs through.
  • Travelling with elderly parents? Spend on Makkah, save on Madinah. Makkah's slopes and crowds are the hard part of the trip; Madinah is flat and gentle, so a simpler hotel there hurts far less.
  • Plan the arrival too. Your hotel's district decides how the first journey feels — our Jeddah Airport to Makkah guide covers the taxi, bus and train options, and our Umrah Packing List includes the comfortable walking shoes five daily walks demand.

Quick questions:

  • How close to the Haram should my Makkah hotel be? Within 500 metres (Zones 1–2) if anyone in your group is elderly, uses a wheelchair or is travelling with infants. Fit adults can manage Zone 3 (500–800 m). Beyond 800 m, book only with a confirmed frequent hotel shuttle — and remember shuttles pause for about an hour after the main prayers.
  • Which area is best for elderly parents? Zone 1 around the Clock Tower if the budget allows; otherwise the flat Ibrahim Khalil Road route into Gate 1. Treat Ajyad's uphill return and Jabal Omar's 8–12% incline honestly, and use Gates 1, 79 or 100, which have dedicated wheelchair ramps.
  • Why do two "5-star near Haram" quotes differ so much in price? Usually because one hotel is 200 metres away and the other is 2 km away with a shuttle. Ask each agent for the walking time to a named gate and the hotel name and district in writing — the cheaper quote normally explains itself. All prices here are approximate November 2026 ranges; confirm the live price before booking.

Umrah · Pakistan Cost GuideUmrah Cost from Pakistan 2026 — Full Breakdown

Quick answer: An economy Umrah package from Pakistan, flights included, costs about PKR 245,000–320,000 per person for 7 days (quad sharing, 3-star hotels), about PKR 275,000–360,000 for 10 days and about PKR 315,000–415,000 for 15 days. With 5-star hotels next to the Haram, prices start from about PKR 395,000 for 7 days in quad sharing. This page breaks the total down line by line — flight, visa, hotels, transport and the operator's fee — so you can check any quote an agent gives you. For the journey itself, read it alongside our Umrah from Pakistan guide.

Please note — ranges, not quotes: Every figure on this page is an approximate range checked in November 2026, never a fixed price. Fares and hotel rates move with the season and the exchange rate. Always get an itemised written quote — flight, visa, each hotel, transport and fees listed separately — before you pay anything.

What each part costs (per person, November 2026):

Cost lineTypical range (PKR)Notes

Umrah visa + insurance + transport bundle45,000–65,000The visa fee itself is about SAR 300 (around PKR 22,000); mandatory insurance is about SAR 100–180

Why you cannot book it all yourself: On a Pakistani passport, the Umrah visa is only issued as part of a package through a licensed agent, with accommodation and transport booked through Nusuk Masar — the visa is never sold on its own, so there is no honest "visa only" price. The one exception: Pakistani passport holders who hold a valid US, UK or Schengen visa (usually one that has already been used) can apply for the Saudi tourist eVisa instead, at about SAR 535 including insurance (around PKR 39,600), and plan the trip independently. Our Umrah Visa Fees guide sets out both routes in full, and our Nusuk App Complete Guide explains the app every pilgrim needs either way.

The 2026 visa facts:

  • One-year, multiple-entry: the Umrah visa is now valid for 365 days from issuance, with up to 90 days of cumulative stay.
  • "No Booking, No Visa": no Umrah visa is issued without a confirmed Nusuk hotel booking behind it.

Book safely — the rules that protect you:

  • Use a verified operator only. Under the Hajj and Umrah Act 2024 (rules in force since July 2026), book only with a Ministry of Religious Affairs (MoRA) verified operator — and check the operator yourself on the verified list at mora.gov.pk before paying.
  • Pay through a bank and keep every receipt. A bank trail is your proof if anything goes wrong.
  • Beware the too-cheap package. A full package advertised far below PKR 220,000 usually leaves out the flight — the most expensive line of all.

Money-saving tips that actually work:

  • Travel off-peak. Late September to mid-November, and the post-Hajj months of Muharram and Safar, are the cheapest windows — our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide maps the seasons.
  • Share the room. Quad sharing is the single biggest saving in any package.
  • Take a shuttle hotel in Aziziyah. Makkah's shuttle-served districts cost far less than the streets beside the Haram.
  • Fly from Karachi if you can — fares from Karachi are usually the lowest in Pakistan.
  • Compare at least 3 itemised quotes before choosing an operator, and pack from our Umrah Packing List so nothing has to be bought at Haram-side prices.

Quick questions:

  • How much does Umrah cost from Pakistan in 2026? About PKR 245,000–320,000 per person for a 7-day economy package with flights (quad sharing, 3-star), rising to PKR 315,000–415,000 for 15 days — and PKR 600,000–800,000 or more in the last ten nights of Ramadan. All figures are approximate November 2026 ranges, not fixed quotes.
  • Can I book Umrah myself, without an agent, on a Pakistani passport? No. The Umrah visa is issued only inside a package from a licensed agent, with hotels and transport booked via Nusuk Masar. The exception is the Saudi tourist eVisa (about SAR 535 including insurance), open to Pakistani passport holders with a valid, usually already used, US, UK or Schengen visa.
  • Why is one operator's package so much cheaper than the rest? Usually because the flight is excluded, the hotels are far from the Haram, or the room is shared with more people. Ask for the itemised written quote, check what is actually included, and verify the operator on mora.gov.pk before you pay.

Nusuk App · Complete GuideNusuk App Complete Guide — Download, Setup, Visa, Rawdah Permit & More

Almost everything about Umrah now runs through one app. Nusuk is the official app and web platform of Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Hajj and Umrah — the single account through which pilgrims apply for visas, book permits and plan the whole journey. It replaces the old Eatmarna platform and brings together more than 130 digital services under one account. By April 2026 it had passed 51 million users from more than 190 countries (Arab News, reported by Wego). This guide covers the app in full: downloading it safely, setting up your account, what it can do, and the 2026 rules that catch pilgrims out.

Please note: EasyNusuk is an independent community website. It is not the official Nusuk site, it is not the Nusuk app, and it is not affiliated with the app or with the Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah. Visas and permits are issued only inside the official Nusuk app and through the official Nusuk websites linked at the end of this guide.

Download it — and only from the official stores: Nusuk is free on the Apple App Store and Google Play. Search for "Nusuk" (نسك) and check that the publisher is the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah before you install. Never install APK files from third-party websites — fake clones of the app exist and are built to steal passport and visa data. You can also use Nusuk in a browser at nusuk.sa. Hajj registration runs on its own separate platform at hajj.nusuk.sa — our Hajj 2027 guide explains how that side works.

Setting up your account — step by step:

  • Step 1 — Choose your language. The app works in about 10 languages, including Arabic, English, Urdu, Turkish, Malay, Indonesian, French and Hausa.
  • Step 2 — Tap Create Account.
  • Step 3 — Choose your account type: Visitor if you are an international pilgrim, or Resident if you hold a Saudi Iqama.
  • Step 4 — Enter your details: your passport number (or Iqama number for residents), your name, email address and a secure password — exactly as they appear on your documents.
  • Step 5 — Verify the OTP sent to your phone or email.

The safest moment to create the account is as soon as your visa is issued — register then, not on the day you arrive, so permit booking is already open to you. Travelling for the first time? Work through our Umrah for First-Timers guide alongside this one.

What you can do inside the app:

  • Apply for an Umrah eVisa directly, if your nationality is eligible.
  • Book your Umrah permit. The permit carries a QR code and is mandatory in 2026: officials at the gates of Masjid al-Haram scan the QR, and a valid visa alone is no longer enough to enter.
  • Book a Rawdah permit in Madinah — a separate booking from the Umrah permit. Our Rawdah Permit guide walks through it step by step.
  • Book hotels and transport for the journey.
  • Use Nusuk Wallet for payments inside Saudi Arabia.
  • Follow prayer times, maps and guidance inside the holy sites.

2026 rules to know before you travel:

  • "Any Visa Is an Umrah Visa": holders of a Saudi tourist, transit or personal visit visa can perform Umrah, as long as the visa is linked to Nusuk before arrival and a permit is issued.
  • Multiple-entry Umrah visa: launched on 20 July 2026 and valid for 365 days from issuance.
  • Enter within 30 days: once an Umrah visa is issued, you must enter Saudi Arabia within 30 days of the issue date — plan your dates before you apply.
  • Accommodation first: since June 2026, pilgrims applying for an Umrah visa through Nusuk must first book their accommodation through the official Nusuk Masar platform.
  • One Rawdah permit a year: the advance Rawdah permit is limited to one per person every 365 days, so choose your slot carefully.
  • Zero-data access: the app includes a zero-data access feature, so pilgrims can use its essential services without consuming mobile data.

Visa types and what they cost are set out in our Umrah Visa Fees guide.

Practical tips that save the day:

  • Screenshots do not work at the gates. Your entry QR code is generated live on the server and refreshes — an old screenshot will fail the scan. You need live internet as you approach the gate, so keep a Saudi eSIM set as your data line at every checkpoint.
  • Book Rawdah slots as early as your dates allow. In peak season they fill within minutes of release.
  • Start checking the app the moment your travel dates are confirmed — permits and slots reward pilgrims who book early.

Quick questions:

  • Is the Nusuk app free? Yes — the app is free to download and use, and the Umrah and Rawdah permits themselves are free for pilgrims holding a valid visa.
  • Do I need Nusuk if I already have a visa? Yes. In 2026 a visa on its own does not open the gates of Masjid al-Haram: the visa must be linked to Nusuk and a permit with a QR code issued before you enter.
  • Can I book the Rawdah without Nusuk? No — for international visitors the Rawdah permit is booked only through Nusuk, and it is a separate booking from your Umrah permit. One advance permit is allowed per person every 365 days.

Travel · Getting AroundJeddah Airport to Makkah — Taxi, Bus & Train Guide (2026 Costs)

Quick answer: King Abdulaziz International Airport (JED) in Jeddah is about 90 km from Masjid al-Haram by road, along Highway 40 — roughly 60–90 minutes by car without traffic. You have four main options: the Haramain high-speed train, Uber or Careem, an airport taxi or pre-booked private transfer, and the bus. Which one suits you depends on your terminal, your luggage, who is travelling with you, and the time your flight lands. If this leg is part of your first Umrah, read it alongside our Umrah for First-Timers guide, and see our Umrah Visa Fees guide for what the visa itself costs before you fly.

Please note — ranges, not quotes: Every fare below is an approximate range checked in November 2026. Prices change with the season and demand — Ramadan and peak Umrah weeks push every option up — so always confirm the live fare with the official operator before you pay: in the Haramain app or at sar.hhr.sa for the train, in the Uber or Careem app for a car, and at the official rank or counter for taxis and buses.

1 — The Haramain high-speed train (fastest): The Haramain station sits inside Terminal 1 at Jeddah airport, and the train reaches Makkah station in 54 minutes, stopping once at Jeddah Al-Sulaimaniyah on the way. Trains run roughly 06:05–22:35, about hourly. Economy fares in 2026 are typically SAR 55–90 one way — across dates, times and how full the train is, the range runs about SAR 40–120 — and business class is roughly SAR 100–150. Book on the official site, sar.hhr.sa, or in the HHR app, and book early: fares are priced dynamically, so the cheapest seats go first. One catch at each end. The train only helps if you land at Terminal 1 — from any other terminal you first need a taxi or the airport shuttle to reach the station. And Makkah station is in Ar-Rusayfah, about 3.5 km from Masjid al-Haram, so add a 10–15 minute taxi (about SAR 20–40), the SAR 4 city bus, or the free shuttle when it runs for the last leg. Our Haramain Train guide covers the same railway's Makkah–Madinah route, booking and luggage rules in full.

2 — Uber or Careem (simplest door to door): Both apps pick up at Jeddah airport and take you straight to your hotel door for about SAR 170–260 per car. For a family of four with suitcases, that often works out close to four train tickets plus the station taxi — with none of the lifting. You need a working SIM or eSIM and mobile data to order the ride, and fares surge at peak times, so the same trip costs more on a busy evening than at midday. For late-night arrivals, ride-hailing and taxis are the reliable options: the last train leaves around 22:35, but the apps run through the night.

3 — Airport taxi or pre-booked private transfer: The official taxi rank outside arrivals charges about SAR 200–300 per car to Makkah. Agree the full price before you get in — and use the official rank, not the touts who approach travellers inside the terminal, who often quote SAR 300–500 for the same ride. A pre-booked private transfer starts from about SAR 220 for a sedan: the driver waits at your terminal, helps with the luggage, and drops you at your hotel door at a fixed price agreed before you land — the calmest option after a long flight, and the one we suggest for elderly parents.

4 — The bus (cheapest): The Northwest Bus NW28 runs from the airport to Makkah for about SAR 25–35 per person (listed at SAR 33), taking about 2 hours, roughly hourly from 01:00 to 23:59 — it is also the only public transport that runs deep into the night. SAPTCO coaches cover the route for about SAR 20–45 per person in 2–3 hours. Both drop you at a bus station in Makkah, not at your hotel, so add a short taxi for the final stretch — even so, the bus stays the cheapest way in for a solo traveller with time to spare.

The options side by side (per person unless stated, as of November 2026):

OptionTypical costTimeDoor to door?Best for

Uber / CareemSAR 170–260 per car60–90 minYesFamilies, lots of luggage

Private transferFrom SAR 220 per car60–90 minYesElderly parents, late arrivals

Practical tips for the journey:

  • Get connected before you leave the airport. Buy a Saudi SIM or activate an eSIM in the terminal — you need data for Uber and Careem, for the Nusuk app, and for maps, and airport Wi-Fi ends at the door.
  • Keep small cash in riyals. The bus fare and the short station taxi are easiest with small notes; not every driver or counter takes a card quickly at busy times.
  • Allow extra time in Ramadan and peak season. The highway and the streets around the Haram slow down sharply, and every fare in this guide rises — a 60-minute drive can take two hours.
  • Travelling with elderly parents or children? Prefer a pre-booked car or a ride app: one seat, no changes, no carrying bags between platforms. Our Umrah Packing List helps you keep medicines and documents in your hand luggage for the ride.
  • Confirm your hotel's exact location. Fares vary with where in Makkah you are dropped — a Clock Tower hotel and an Aziziyah hotel are different journeys, so show the driver the exact address, ideally in Arabic on your phone.

Quick questions:

  • What is the cheapest way from Jeddah airport to Makkah? The bus. The Northwest Bus NW28 costs about SAR 33 per person and SAPTCO coaches about SAR 20–45, against SAR 55–90 for the train and SAR 170+ for a car. Buses take about 2–3 hours and drop you at a Makkah bus station, so add a short taxi to your hotel — it is still the cheapest door-to-door total.
  • Is there a train from Jeddah airport to Makkah? Yes — the Haramain high-speed train runs from a station inside Terminal 1 to Makkah station in 54 minutes, roughly hourly from about 06:05 to 22:35. Economy is typically SAR 55–90 one way; book at sar.hhr.sa. Makkah station is about 3.5 km from the Haram, so finish with a taxi (about SAR 20–40) or the SAR 4 city bus.
  • How long does the taxi take at night? About 60–90 minutes, and often closer to an hour once the roads empty. Taxis and Uber/Careem run through the night, which makes them the practical choice for landings after the last train at around 22:35 — agree the fare, or check the app price, before you set off.

Madinah · Rawdah Permit GuideHow to Get a Rawdah Permit — Step by Step

The Rawdah — the blessed area inside the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, between the Prophet's ﷺ house and his pulpit — is entered by permit only. The permit is completely free, and for visitors from outside Saudi Arabia it is booked only through the official Nusuk app. The Tawakalna app serves Saudi citizens and residents; if you are travelling in for Umrah, Nusuk is your route. No agent can book the permit for you, and nobody should charge you for it.

Why pilgrims long for the Rawdah: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1196; Sahih Muslim 1391).

How to book — step by step:

  • Step 1 — Download the official Nusuk app, and check the publisher is the Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah.
  • Step 2 — Register with your passport number and your visa number and phone, exactly as they appear on your documents. Our Nusuk App Guide walks through registration screen by screen.
  • Step 3 — On the Home screen, tap Rawdah.
  • Step 4 — Choose Men or Women. The two have separate visiting times, and a permit booked under the wrong category will not scan at the gate.
  • Step 5 — Pick a green (available) date and time slot — greyed-out slots are full.
  • Step 6 — Confirm the booking.
  • Step 7 — Save the permit and screenshot the QR code. Signal inside the mosque can be weak, and the screenshot opens the gate when the app will not load.
  • Step 8 — On the day, arrive 20–30 minutes early and join the queue for your slot.

One permit a year — and the Instant Track: Under the rule announced in December 2025 by the authority that runs the Two Holy Mosques, each person can hold one advance Rawdah permit every 365 days. If you are already in Madinah, the Nusuk Instant Track can offer same-day slots when you are near the Prophet's Mosque, subject to capacity on the day.

When slots are released: New slots appear in batches, typically on Thursday and Friday mornings around Fajr (Madinah time), and only 1–2 weeks ahead. They go quickly — once your Madinah dates are close, check the app regularly, especially on those mornings.

Confirm, cancel, and how long you get: You must confirm your attendance in the app between 48 hours and 2 hours before the visit. If you cannot attend, cancel in the app — a missed appointment can block future bookings. Men and women visit in separate periods (the Saudi Press Agency published the current visiting periods on 20 October 2026), and a visit lasts about 20–45 minutes, so prepare your duas before you go in. While you are in the city, our Madinah Ziyarat Guide plans the rest of your days.

Quick questions:

  • Is the Rawdah permit free? Yes — completely free, and for international visitors it is issued only through the official Nusuk app. Tawakalna is for Saudi citizens and residents.
  • How often can I book? One advance permit every 365 days under the December 2025 rule. Once you are in Madinah, the Instant Track may offer a same-day slot when you are near the mosque, subject to capacity.
  • What happens if I cannot attend? Confirm your attendance between 48 hours and 2 hours before the visit, and cancel in the app if you cannot go — missed appointments can block future bookings.

Sources: Nusuk — Official Site ↗ · Saudi Press Agency — Rawdah visiting periods, 20 October 2026 · Saudi Life Guide — Nusuk App Guide 2026 · Sahih al-Bukhari 1196 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1391 — Sunnah.com ↗

Umrah · When to GoBest Time to Perform Umrah — Weather, Crowds & Cost Guide

Umrah can be performed at almost any time of year, but the month you choose decides three things: how hot Makkah feels, how crowded the Haram is, and how much the trip costs. Here is the year in short — the coolest months, the busiest weeks, the cheapest windows, and the stretch that balances all three.

The reward that drives the crowds: The Prophet ﷺ said that Umrah in Ramadan is equal to Hajj in reward (Sahih al-Bukhari 1782) — which is why Ramadan is both the most blessed and the most crowded time to go.

Coolest — winter, December to February: These are Makkah's mildest months, with daytime highs around 29–32°C and nights near 18°C; January is the coolest month of the year. Tawaf and the walk to your hotel stay comfortable even for elderly pilgrims and children. One caution: Rajab (December 2025 – January 2026) is a winter peak — the weather is at its best, but so are the crowds and the prices.

Most crowded and most expensive — Ramadan: Ramadan 1447 is expected around 17/18 February to 18/19 March 2026. It is the busiest and priciest time of the year — in Ramadan 2025 the Grand Mosque received a record 25 million worshippers in the first 10 days alone. If price matters, avoid the last 10 nights of Ramadan and the school-holiday weeks, when family trips push fares and hotel rates to their peak. Our Umrah in Ramadan guide covers the month in full.

Cheapest — late September to mid-November, and the post-Hajj months: The lowest prices and the lowest crowds come in late September to mid-November and in the post-Hajj months of Muharram and Safar (June–August 2026). The trade-off is heat: those summer months regularly reach 40–44°C, so plan Tawaf for the early morning or the night, and rest through the middle of the day.

The best balance — mid-October to mid-November 2026: If you want one window that balances weather, crowds and cost, this is it: temperatures are falling, the Haram is calmer than in the winter peak, and prices have not yet climbed for December. Pair it with our Umrah Cost 2026 breakdown to budget the trip.

Who should go when:

  • Families with elderly parents or young children: choose winter — the mild weather is worth the higher price. See our Umrah for Elderly & Disabled guide for facilities and pacing.
  • Budget travellers: choose the summer and post-Hajj months — the lowest crowds and prices of the year, if you can handle 40–44°C heat.
  • Seeking the Ramadan reward: go, but book months ahead, pace yourself around fasting, and expect the fullest Haram of the year.

Quick questions:

  • What is the coolest month for Umrah? January — winter days run about 29–32°C with nights near 18°C, the gentlest weather of the year in Makkah.
  • When is Umrah cheapest? Late September to mid-November, and the post-Hajj months of Muharram and Safar (June–August 2026) — the lowest crowds and prices, but serious summer heat.
  • When is it most crowded? Ramadan — above all the last 10 nights — and the school-holiday weeks. Ramadan 1447 falls around 17/18 February to 18/19 March 2026.

Sources: Wego Blog — Umrah month-by-month guide · Saudi National Center for Meteorology — Makkah climate averages · Sunaan — Best Time for Umrah 2026 guide · Sahih al-Bukhari 1782 — Sunnah.com ↗

Madinah · Ziyarat GuideMasjid al-Qiblatain — The Mosque of Two Qiblas

About 5 km north-west of the Prophet's Mosque stands a white mosque with a story no other mosque on earth can tell. Masjid al-Qiblatain — the Mosque of the Two Qiblas — was built by Sawad ibn Ghanam ibn Ka'ab in 2 AH (623/624 CE), and it was here, in the middle of a prayer, that the direction of Muslim prayer changed forever: from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Makkah. Pilgrims visit it on almost every Madinah stay. Be clear about its place, as with all ziyarat: visiting Qiblatain is voluntary, not a rite of Umrah — there is no permit, no ticket and no prescribed ritual, only one of the great turning points of the Seerah. Our Madinah Ziyarat Guide shows where it fits into your days in the city.

The day the Qibla changed: For the first part of his time in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ and the believers prayed facing Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem, as the earlier prophets had done. In 2 AH — the majority dating is mid-Rajab, though some reports say 15 Sha'ban — the command came down while the Prophet ﷺ was leading prayer in this mosque:

فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبْلَةً تَرْضَاهَا ۚ فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ

"We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram" (Qur'an 2:144).

One prayer, two directions: Al-Bara' ibn Azib narrates that the first prayer the Prophet ﷺ offered facing the Kaaba was Asr. A man who had prayed with him then passed a congregation of the Ansar who were still praying toward Jerusalem; he testified that he had just prayed with the Prophet ﷺ facing Makkah — and they turned around in the middle of their prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari 40). Sahih Muslim 526 records the same turn taking place during Fajr. A congregation that began its prayer toward one qibla and finished it toward another — that is why this mosque carries the name it does.

Two mihrabs — and what remains of them: For centuries the mosque kept two mihrabs, one facing Jerusalem and one facing Makkah, a physical record of the change. In the 1987 rebuild under King Fahd, the Jerusalem-facing mihrab was removed so that no one could mistake it for a direction of prayer; in its place a small marker mihrab was installed under a secondary false dome, kept as history. The Makkah-facing mihrab was retained, and it alone is the qibla of the mosque today.

What to see and do today:

  • Pray two rak'ahs of Tahiyyat al-Masjid — the greeting of the mosque — facing the Makkah mihrab, as in any mosque. There is no special prayer prescribed for this place; its honour is the event that happened here.
  • Look for the marker mihrab under the smaller dome: it marks the old Jerusalem direction. It is history only — a reminder of the first qibla and of the day it changed. Prayer is only ever toward Makkah.
  • Take a quiet minute with the story. The congregation that turned mid-prayer did so on one man's truthful report — a lesson in trusting the word of the truthful and obeying a command the moment it reaches you.
  • Combine the visit. Qiblatain pairs naturally with Mount Uhud and Masjid Quba in a single Madinah ziyarat round; our Madinah Ziyarat Guide lays out the order, and our Makkah Ziyarat guide covers the matching visits in the first city.

Getting there: The mosque lies about 5 km north-west of the Prophet's Mosque — roughly 10 to 15 minutes by taxi or ride-hailing car. Most pilgrims hire a car for the full Madinah round (Qiblatain, Quba and Uhud together), typically about SAR 150–200 per vehicle at 2026 operator fares, agreed before you set off. Go in the early morning or late afternoon to avoid the midday heat, and allow 30 to 45 minutes at the mosque itself.

Quick questions:

  • Why is it called the Mosque of Two Qiblas? Because a prayer was prayed here in 2 AH that began facing Jerusalem and, when the command of Qur'an 2:144 arrived mid-prayer, finished facing the Kaaba in Makkah (Sahih al-Bukhari 40; Sahih Muslim 526).
  • Can I pray facing the old Jerusalem marker? No. The marker mihrab is kept as history only. Since 2 AH the qibla of the whole ummah is the Kaaba, and every prayer at Qiblatain is offered facing the Makkah mihrab.
  • Do I need a permit or ticket? No. Masjid al-Qiblatain is a neighbourhood mosque open to visitors — walk in respectfully outside the busiest prayer-time crush, greet the mosque with two rak'ahs, and leave it as you found it.

Sources: Qur'an 2:144 · Sahih al-Bukhari 40 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 526 — Sunnah.com ↗

Umrah · Women TravellersUmrah for Women Travelling Alone — 2026 Rules & Practical Guide

For decades, a woman planning Umrah had to plan around one condition first: a mahram — a male guardian — had to travel with her before a visa would be issued. That condition no longer exists. Since October 2022, Saudi Arabia has allowed women to perform Umrah without a mahram, and women now travel alone or in women-only groups in large numbers. This guide sets out the 2026 rules exactly as they stand, the two visa routes, the honest note about scholarly difference, and the practical steps and safety habits that make a solo journey smooth.

The 2022 change — the rule today: In October 2022, the Minister of Hajj and Umrah, Tawfiq Al-Rabiah, announced that women may perform Hajj or Umrah without a male guardian (reported by Arab News, 11 October 2022). The Ministry of Hajj and Umrah's own FAQ answers the question directly: asked whether a woman can perform Umrah without a mahram, it replies, "Yes, it is allowed." The rule applies to adult women of all ages. One limit stands: women under 18 travel with a parent or guardian.

Two visa routes:

  • Tourist eVisa: If your nationality is eligible — for example the UK, US or EU countries — the Saudi tourist eVisa allows Umrah, and the application asks no mahram details at all. It is also multiple-entry, which suits sisters who hope to return.
  • Umrah visa through an operator: Pilgrims from countries such as Pakistan, India and Bangladesh use the traditional Umrah visa, arranged through a licensed operator or the Nusuk platform. One honest caution: some operators still impose their own conditions on women travelling alone, even though the Saudi rule does not — so confirm with your operator before you book. Our Umrah Visa Fees 2026 guide breaks down the costs, and pilgrims travelling from Pakistan should read Umrah from Pakistan for the operator route step by step.
Scholars differ — stated neutrally: The visa rule is a travel rule, not a fatwa. On the religious question of a woman travelling without a mahram, scholars have long differed: the Shafi'i and Maliki schools allow the journey when she travels in safe, trustworthy company, while the Hanafi school holds that a mahram is required. EasyNusuk presents both positions without deciding between them — speak to a trusted scholar who knows your circumstances before you decide.

The practical guide — step by step:

  • Passport: Your passport must be valid for 6+ months from travel. Check the date before anything else is booked.
  • Visa: Take one of the two routes above. The Umrah visa fee is SAR 300 plus insurance; our Umrah Visa Fees 2026 guide sets out what the total usually comes to.
  • Book through Nusuk: Book your hotel and transport through Nusuk where your visa route requires it, and keep every booking saved offline on your phone.
  • Permits in the Nusuk app: Book your Umrah permit in the Nusuk app before you travel, and in Madinah book your Rawdah permit — women have their own visiting times and entrance, as our Rawdah Permit guide explains.
  • Vaccinations: Requirements change — check the current vaccination rules on Nusuk before you travel and carry the certificates with your documents.
  • Pack with the journey in mind: Our Umrah Packing List covers documents, medicines and the small things solo travellers rely on most, and first-time pilgrims should work through Umrah for First-Timers before departure.

Ihram clothing for women: A woman enters ihram in her ordinary modest dress — there is no special two-garment ihram for women as there is for men. A clean abaya and hijab in any colour is her ihram; what she avoids while in ihram is a sewn face veil (niqab) and gloves, following the Prophet's ﷺ instruction for women in ihram (Sahih al-Bukhari 1838). Our Ihram Rules guide covers what to wear and what to avoid in full.

Safety tips for travelling alone:

  • Stay near the Haram: Choose a hotel a short, well-lit walk from Masjid al-Haram in Makkah and from the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah — the single biggest practical safety decision you will make.
  • Travel in women-only company where you can: Join a women-only group or sisters from your hotel for ziyarat trips and the journey between the two cities; the women's sections of both mosques are busy and supervised at all hours.
  • Keep documents and phone ready: Carry copies of your passport, visa and permits, keep your phone charged with a power bank in your handbag, and save your hotel's address card.
  • Share your live location with family at home, send them your itinerary before you fly, and check in each day — small habits that let everyone relax.

Quick questions:

  • Can a woman perform Umrah without a mahram in 2026? Yes. Saudi Arabia removed the mahram requirement in October 2022; the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah's FAQ confirms "Yes, it is allowed" for adult women of all ages. Girls under 18 travel with a parent or guardian.
  • Which visa should a woman travelling alone apply for? Eligible nationalities (UK, US, EU and others) can use the tourist eVisa, which asks no mahram details. Other nationalities — Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and more — use the Umrah visa through a licensed operator or Nusuk; confirm the operator's own conditions before booking.
  • Does the Saudi rule settle the religious question? No — it is a travel rule. Scholars differ (Shafi'i and Maliki allow travel in safe, trustworthy company; Hanafi requires a mahram), so consult a trusted scholar about your own situation.

Sources: Ministry of Hajj and Umrah — official FAQ · Arab News, 11 October 2022 · Nusuk — Official Site ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 1838 — Sunnah.com ↗

Umrah GuideWhat to Do After Umrah — Keeping the Spirit Alive at Home

Umrah ends at the airport, but its real test begins at home. The journey is accepted by Allah, not by the photos you post. The days in Makkah and Madinah filled your heart; the weeks after you land decide whether that light stays. Here is how to carry Umrah into ordinary life — with gratitude, small steady habits, and sincerity.

Gratitude first: Before anything else, thank Allah for choosing you for the journey. Gratitude is not only a feeling — Allah ties it to increase:

لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ

"La'in shakartum la-azidannakum"

"If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favour]" (Surah Ibrahim 14:7, Sahih International).

And He pairs gratitude with remembrance:

فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ وَاشْكُرُوا لِي وَلَا تَكْفُرُونِ

"Fadhkuruni adhkurkum washkuruli wa la takfurun"

"So remember Me; I will remember you. And be grateful to Me and do not deny Me." (Surah al-Baqarah 2:152, Sahih International).

What your Umrah earned you: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Umrah to Umrah is an expiation for what is between them, and the Hajj mabrur (accepted Hajj) has no reward except Jannah" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1773; Sahih Muslim 1349).

Scholars explain that this expiation covers the minor sins; major sins still need their own sincere repentance. So let the return home begin with istighfar, settling any rights you owe to people, and a clean page.

Keep the habits small and steady: Do not try to bring all of Makkah home at once. Pray the five prayers on time, read a little Qur'an every day — even a single page — and keep the morning and evening adhkar you started in Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The most beloved deeds to Allah are those that are most consistent, even if they are small" (Sahih al-Bukhari 6464). A page a day kept for a year outweighs a burst that fades within a week.

Share the experience without showing off: Tell your family what you learned and how the journey changed you — not how many photos you took. Keep acts of worship off social media: sincerity (ikhlas) is what protects the reward of the whole trip, and the prayer nobody saw is safe from showing off.

Stay connected to the Haramain spirit: Listen to lectures from the scholars of Makkah and Madinah, keep in touch with the friends you made on the trip, and keep your Zamzam and dates as a reminder, not a trophy. And let the heart plan ahead: our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide helps you plan a return trip, and our Hajj 2027 guide sets out the next, greater goal.

Practical follow-ups in the first days home:

  • Thank the people who helped you travel — the family who covered for you, the agent who arranged it, the group leader who guided you.
  • Share Zamzam water and dates with loved ones who could not go.
  • Sort your photos, and keep a short written journal of the duas that were answered — you will want it on hard days.
  • Make dua that Allah accepts your Umrah — acceptance is His gift, and it is asked for like everything else.

If old habits creep back: Do not despair. A slip after Umrah is not the end of the story — repent, restart, and remember that Allah's mercy is wider than any slip. And if you are preparing a companion for their first journey, our Umrah for First-Timers guide is the one to share with them.

Quick questions:

  • How do I know if my Umrah was accepted? No one can know for certain. The sign the scholars mention is a life that improves afterwards — better prayer, cleaner habits, a softer heart.
  • Can I go for Umrah again soon? Yes — there is no waiting period. See the Best Time to Perform Umrah guide for when to go.
  • What should I do with leftover Zamzam water? Share it with family and friends; it keeps its blessing at home.

Sources: Qur'an 14:7 ↗ · Qur'an 2:152 ↗ (Sahih International translation) · Sahih al-Bukhari 1773 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1349 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 — Sunnah.com ↗

DuasUmrah Dua Book — Essential Duas for the Whole Journey

One page to save or print before you travel: the essential duas of Umrah, from leaving home to coming back, each with its Arabic, transliteration and meaning — so you are never stuck for words at the moments that matter most.

1. Before travel — boarding the plane: Say Allahu Akbar three times, then recite the verse the Prophet ﷺ recited when setting out on a journey:

سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لَهُ مُقْرِنِينَ وَإِنَّا إِلَى رَبِّنَا لَمُنْقَلِبُونَ

"Subhanal-ladhi sakhkhara lana hadha wa ma kunna lahu muqrinin, wa inna ila Rabbina lamunqalibun"

"Glory be to Him who has made this subservient to us, for we could never have done it ourselves, and to our Lord we will surely return." (Qur'an 43:13–14, recited by the Prophet ﷺ when setting out — Sahih Muslim 1342)

Then continue with the rest of the travel dua: "Allahumma inna nas'aluka fi safarina hadhal-birra wat-taqwa, wa minal-'amali ma tarda. Allahumma hawwin 'alayna safarana hadha, watwi 'anna bu'dah. Allahumma antas-sahibu fis-safar, wal-khalifatu fil-ahl. Allahumma inni a'udhu bika min wa'tha'is-safar, wa ka'abatil-manzar, wa su'il-munqalabi fil-mali wal-ahl." — "O Allah, on this journey of ours we ask You for righteousness and piety, and for deeds that please You. O Allah, make this journey easy for us and shorten its distance. O Allah, You are our Companion on the journey and the One who looks after our family. O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the hardship of travel, from distressing sights, and from returning to find harm in our property or family." (Sahih Muslim 1342)

2. Entering Makkah:

اللَّهُمَّ هَذَا حَرَمُكَ وَأَمْنُكَ، فَحَرِّمْنِي عَلَى النَّارِ، وَأَمِّنِّي مِنْ عَذَابِكَ يَوْمَ تَبْعَثُ عِبَادَكَ، وَاجْعَلْنِي مِنْ أَوْلِيَائِكَ وَأَهْلِ طَاعَتِكَ

"Allahumma hadha haramuka wa amnuka, fa-harrimni 'alan-nar, wa amminni min 'adhabika yawma tab'athu 'ibadak, waj'alni min awliya'ika wa ahli ta'atik"

"O Allah, this is Your Sanctuary and place of safety. Forbid me from the Fire, protect me from Your punishment on the Day You raise Your servants, and make me of Your friends and the people of Your obedience." (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah 7549; al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman 3969)

3. First sight of the Kaaba:

اللَّهُمَّ زِدْ هَذَا الْبَيْتَ تَشْرِيفًا وَتَعْظِيمًا وَتَكْرِيمًا وَمَهَابَةً، وَزِدْ مَنْ شَرَّفَهُ وَكَرَّمَهُ مِمَّنْ حَجَّهُ أَوِ اعْتَمَرَهُ تَشْرِيفًا وَتَكْرِيمًا وَتَعْظِيمًا وَبِرًّا

"Allahumma zid hadhal-bayta tashrifan wa ta'dhiman wa takriman wa mahabah, wa zid man sharrafahu wa karramahu mimman hajjahu awi'tamarahu tashrifan wa takriman wa ta'dhiman wa birra"

"O Allah, increase this House in honour, greatness, nobility and awe. And increase those who honour and revere it, among those who perform Hajj or Umrah to it, in honour, nobility, greatness and righteousness." (al-Bayhaqi, Sunan 5/73; Ibn Khuzaymah 4/212, graded Hasan)

Scholars say the first sight of the Kaaba is a moment when dua is accepted — raise your hands and ask for whatever is in your heart. If you cannot remember the wording, say Allahu Akbar three times and make your own personal dua.

4. During Tawaf — between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone:

رَبَّنَا آتِنَا فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَفِي الْآخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ

"Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan wa fil-akhirati hasanatan wa qina 'adhaban-nar"

"Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." (Qur'an 2:201)

The Prophet ﷺ said this dua between the two corners (Sunan Abi Dawud 1892, graded Hasan by al-Albani), and it was also his most frequent dua (Sahih al-Bukhari 6389). For the full set of Tawaf supplications, see our Tawaf Duas article and the Tawaf Guide.

5. At Safa and Marwah (Sa'i): On first approaching Safa, recite this verse once:

إِنَّ الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةَ مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ

"Innas-Safa wal-Marwata min sha'a'irillah"

"Indeed, Safa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah" (Qur'an 2:158) — then say "Abda'u bima bada'allahu bihi" ("I begin with what Allah began with").

Then, on top of each hill, facing the Kaaba, say Allahu Akbar three times, then say the following three times, making your own personal dua between each repetition:

لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ. لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ، أَنْجَزَ وَعْدَهُ، وَنَصَرَ عَبْدَهُ، وَهَزَمَ الْأَحْزَابَ وَحْدَهُ

"La ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-hamd, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir. La ilaha illallahu wahdahu, anjaza wa'dah, wa nasara 'abdah, wa hazama al-ahzaba wahdah"

"None has the right to be worshipped except Allah, alone, without a partner. To Him belongs all sovereignty and praise. He is over all things omnipotent. None has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone. He fulfilled His promise, aided His slave, and single-handedly defeated the confederates." (Sahih Muslim 1218)

There is no fixed dua for the walk between the hills — ask Allah for anything from your heart as you walk. Our Sa'i Guide walks through the rite step by step.

6. Drinking Zamzam:

اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ عِلْمًا نَافِعًا وَرِزْقًا وَاسِعًا وَشِفَاءً مِنْ كُلِّ دَاءٍ

"Allahumma inni as'aluka 'ilman nafi'an wa rizqan wasi'an wa shifa'an min kulli da'"

"O Allah, I ask You for beneficial knowledge, abundant provision, and healing from every disease." (Reported from Ibn Abbas (RA) — al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak 1739; Sunan al-Daraqutni 2738; Musannaf 'Abd al-Razzaq 9112, with a good chain)

Remember the hadith: "The water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for" (Sunan Ibn Majah 3062). Face the qiblah, say Bismillah, and drink in three sips. The full story of the well is in our Zamzam: Virtues and History article.

7. Leaving Makkah — returning home:

آيِبُونَ تَائِبُونَ عَابِدُونَ لِرَبِّنَا حَامِدُونَ

"Ayibuna ta'ibuna 'abiduna li-rabbina hamiduna"

"We return, repenting, worshipping, and praising our Lord." (Sahih Muslim 1342 — the Prophet's ﷺ dua on returning from a journey)

Practical tip: Save this page offline or print it before you travel — phone signal inside the Haram can be weak. For everything else you need to carry, see our Umrah Packing List, and if this is your first journey, our Umrah for First-Timers guide walks through the whole trip in order.

Quick questions:

  • Do I have to memorise all of these? No. Only the Tawaf dua between the corners and the Sa'i dhikr are specifically reported; for everything else, sincere personal dua in your own words is accepted.
  • Can I read duas from my phone during Tawaf? Yes, many pilgrims do. Keep your focus, and do not block others.
  • Is there a fixed dua for each round of Tawaf? No — except the Rabbana atina dua between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, which is said on every round.

Sources: Qur'an 43:13–14 ↗ · Qur'an 2:201 ↗ · Qur'an 2:158 ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1342 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1218 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sunan Abi Dawud 1892 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sunan Ibn Majah 3062 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 6389 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah 7549 · al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman 3969 and Sunan 5/73 · Ibn Khuzaymah 4/212 · al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak 1739

Madinah · Ziyarat GuideMount Uhud & the Martyrs of Uhud — History, Virtues & Visiting Guide

About 5 km north of Masjid an-Nabawi stretches a long ridge of red rock, some seven kilometres from end to end: Mount Uhud. No mountain on earth is loved the way this one is loved — and the plain at its foot holds one of the hardest days in the Seerah, the Battle of Uhud, and the graves of seventy of the finest of the Companions. Pilgrims come here on almost every Madinah stay. Be clear about its place, as with all ziyarat: visiting Uhud is voluntary, not a rite of Umrah. There is no permit, no ticket and no prescribed ritual — only history, grief, gratitude and lessons that still speak. Our Madinah Ziyarat Guide shows where an Uhud visit fits into your days in the city.

The mountain that loves us: Anas (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said of Uhud: "This is a mountain that loves us and is loved by us" (Sahih al-Bukhari 4083). He ﷺ said it on the road home, as the mountain came into view — the very ground where he had been wounded and his beloved uncle killed. For him, seeing Uhud meant being home; and the scholars note that he loved it for the martyrs it holds and the lesson it taught.

The Battle of Uhud — Shawwal, 3 AH: A year after their defeat at Badr, the Quraysh of Makkah marched on Madinah with an army of about 3,000 men. The Prophet ﷺ went out to meet them beneath Uhud with about 700 men, after Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his followers turned back on the road. The Muslims took the high ground, with the mountain guarding their backs — and at first, the day was theirs: the Quraysh line broke and their camp was overrun. Then came the moment the whole visit turns on.

The archers' lesson: Before the battle, the Prophet ﷺ stationed fifty archers on a small hill guarding the pass, under Abdullah ibn Jubayr (RA), with an order that could not have been plainer. Al-Bara (RA) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ told them: "Do not leave this place; if you should see us conquering the enemy, do not leave this place, and if you should see them conquering us, do not come to help us" (Sahih al-Bukhari 4043). When the enemy fled, most of the archers went down for the spoils, against their commander's reminder. Khalid ibn al-Walid — not yet a Muslim — led the Quraysh cavalry through the empty pass and fell on the Muslims from behind. The day reversed in minutes. The Qur'an itself addresses that moment: "…until you lost heart and disputed about the matter and disobeyed, after He had shown you what you loved" (Qur'an 3:152). The hill is still there, and the lesson with it: a clear command set aside for a moment's gain can undo everything.

Hamza and the seventy: Seventy Muslims were martyred that day. Among them was Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib (RA), the Prophet's ﷺ uncle and foster-brother, struck down by the spear of Wahshi — remembered ever since as Sayyid al-Shuhada, the Master of the Martyrs. With him fell Mus'ab ibn Umayr (RA), the standard-bearer, and Abdullah ibn Jubayr (RA) himself, who died at his post with the few archers who stayed. The martyrs were buried where they fell, at the foot of Uhud, and the Prophet ﷺ returned in later years to visit them and pray for them — which is why the visit you are making is one he made first.

What you will see today:

  • The mountain itself — the long, red, bare ridge filling the northern horizon. The visit is made at its foot; the main mountain has no visitor path and climbing it is not part of the visit.
  • The Martyrs' Cemetery (Shuhada Uhud) — the enclosed graveyard on the plain where Hamza (RA) and the seventy rest. Visitors stand outside the fence, greet the martyrs with salam and make du'a for them, looking across to the mountain they died beneath.
  • The Archers' Hill (Jabal al-Rumah) — the small hill opposite the cemetery, where the fifty archers stood. Visitors climb it — a short, easy climb — for the view across the whole battlefield: cemetery below, mountain behind, the pass the cavalry came through plain to see.
  • Masjid Sayyid al-Shuhada — the large mosque beside the cemetery, named in honour of Hamza (RA); pray your regular prayers here if the time comes in.
  • Masjid al-Mustarah — on the road back towards the city, marking the place where the Prophet ﷺ rested and prayed on his return from the battle, wounded, carrying the day's grief with him.

Visiting etiquette:

  • Greet them as the Prophet ﷺ taught us to greet the people of the graves — with salam and du'a for their forgiveness and wellbeing, and a moment's thought for your own return to Allah. The counterpart visit in the city is Jannatul Baqi, and the two belong to the same spirit.
  • No prayer is prescribed at the graves themselves. Make du'a standing at the fence; offer your prayers in the mosque.
  • Take nothing and leave nothing: no soil, no stones, no rubbing of the fence or the ground, no writing on the rocks. Keep the plain clean.
  • Keep it quiet. This is a graveyard before it is a landmark — lower your voice, and keep group talks brief and away from the fence where others are making du'a.

Practical tips: Uhud lies about 5 km north of the Prophet's Mosque — ten to fifteen minutes by car. There is no permit, ticket or booking of any kind; you simply go. Most pilgrims fold it into one Madinah ziyarat round with Masjid Quba and Masjid Qiblatain — a hired car for the full Madinah round typically costs about SAR 150–200 per vehicle at 2026 operator fares, agreed before you set off. Go in the early morning or late afternoon: the plain has almost no shade, and the midday heat on open rock is severe. Allow 45 minutes to an hour — time at the cemetery, a climb up the Archers' Hill, and a quiet look at the mountain before you leave.

Quick questions:

  • Do I need a permit to visit Mount Uhud? No. There is no permit, ticket or Nusuk booking for Uhud — it is an open ziyarat site about 5 km north of the Prophet's Mosque. Simply travel there, visit the martyrs' cemetery and the Archers' Hill, and make du'a.
  • Who is buried at Uhud? The seventy martyrs of the Battle of Uhud (3 AH), among them Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib (RA), the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, known as the Master of the Martyrs; Mus'ab ibn Umayr (RA); and Abdullah ibn Jubayr (RA), commander of the archers. They lie in the enclosed cemetery at the foot of the mountain, and visitors greet them from outside the fence.
  • Can I climb Mount Uhud? The visit centres on the cemetery and the small Archers' Hill opposite it, which visitors climb for the view over the battlefield. The main ridge of Uhud has no visitor path, and climbing it is not part of the visit — the mountain is honoured from below, where the martyrs lie.

Sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 4083 · Sahih al-Bukhari 4043 · Qur'an 3:152 · Sahih al-Bukhari 4083 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Mount Uhud — Makkah Live ↗ · Ziyarat taxi fares as published by Madinah operators, November 2026

Umrah · Cost GuideHow Much Does Umrah Cost in 2026? — Complete Budget Breakdown

"How much does Umrah cost?" is the first question every pilgrim asks — and the honest answer is that there is no single price. Two choices decide most of your budget: when you go and how close you sleep to the Haram. Everything else is smaller than those two. This breakdown goes through the journey line by line — visa, flights, hotels, food, transport, permits and the small extras — with the ranges pilgrims are actually paying in 2026, so you can build a budget that holds. If you are planning the trip itself, read it alongside our Umrah for First-Timers guide.

Please note — ranges, not promises: Every figure below is a range checked in November 2026, not a quote. Prices move with the season (Ramadan alone can add roughly 30–50%), your departure city and your operator. The Saudi riyal is pegged at about SAR 3.75 to USD 1, so riyal-to-dollar conversions are stable; conversions into rupees and other currencies move daily. Confirm the live price of every line before you pay.

The budget at a glance (per person unless stated, as of November 2026):

Cost lineTypical rangeNotes
Umrah visa + mandatory insuranceSAR 400–480Before agent fees; tourist eVisa about SAR 535
Hotels in MakkahSAR 150–2,500+ per room / nightDistance from the Haram decides — see below
Hotels in MadinahSAR 120–1,800 per room / nightGenerally a little cheaper than Makkah
FoodSAR 45–130 per dayEconomy to standard eating — see below
Haramain train, Makkah ↔ MadinahSAR 150–200 one wayEconomy; Business about SAR 250–300
Private car, Makkah ↔ MadinahSAR 400–550 per vehicleSplit between passengers
Nusuk Umrah & Rawdah permitsFreeNever pay anyone for the permits themselves
Zamzam to take homeAbout SAR 12.50One sealed 5-litre container at the airport

1 — The visa: The dedicated Umrah visa costs about SAR 400–480 in government fee and mandatory insurance, before your agent's service charge; the tourist eVisa costs about SAR 535 but is multiple-entry for a year. Our Umrah Visa Fees 2026 guide breaks both down line by line. Pilgrims from Pakistan cannot apply directly and go through a licensed operator — all-in visa costs there run about PKR 48,000–65,000.

2 — Flights: The most variable line of all, set by your departure city, airline and how early you book. It is also why complete packages differ so widely: full Umrah packages from Pakistan generally run PKR 220,000–500,000+ per person depending on season and hotel tier, as our Umrah from Pakistan guide sets out. Wherever you fly from, the same rule holds: fares climb steeply in Ramadan, Rabi al-Awwal and school holidays, and booking early is the single biggest saving most pilgrims ever make.

3 — Hotels, the biggest lever: In Makkah, price follows metres from Masjid al-Haram. Off-peak 2026 ranges per room, per night: on the Haram plaza and in the Clock Tower complex, about SAR 900–2,500+; 300–600 m out (Ajyad, Misfalah), about SAR 350–700; 700 m–1.5 km in the shuttle zone, about SAR 150–350. Madinah runs a little cheaper: plaza-facing 5-star about SAR 800–1,800; Markaziyah, 200–500 m, about SAR 300–600; 600 m and beyond, about SAR 120–280. Two warnings from every honest operator: rates are quoted per room, so a SAR 400 room is SAR 100 per person in quad sharing — sharing is where packages get cheap — and the same room can cost several times more in the last ten nights of Ramadan.

4 — Food: Both cities are ringed with pilgrim restaurants, and a filling meal costs about SAR 15–30. Budget about SAR 45–70 a day eating economically — pilgrim restaurants, bakeries, dates and Zamzam between meals — or SAR 90–130 a day for a standard mix with hotel breakfasts. Many packages include some or all meals; check what yours actually covers before budgeting twice for the same food.

5 — Getting around: Between the two cities, the Haramain high-speed train runs about SAR 150–200 one way in Economy (about SAR 250–300 in Business), booked at sar.hhr.sa — our Haramain Train guide covers booking and stations. A private car for the same journey costs about SAR 400–550 per vehicle, and a taxi from Jeddah airport to a Makkah hotel about SAR 200–350 per vehicle — per vehicle, not per person, so families often find the car cheaper than four train seats. Short rides inside each city run about SAR 20–50; agree the fare before you get in.

6 — The free lines, and one small one: Your Umrah permit and Rawdah permit in the Nusuk app are completely free — anyone charging for the permit itself is charging for their time, not a government fee. And the journey's best-value souvenir: one factory-sealed 5-litre container of Zamzam from the official counters at Jeddah or Madinah airport costs about SAR 12.50, and most airlines carry it free, on top of or within your baggage allowance — confirm your airline's rule before you fly.

What a whole trip adds up to: Worked per-person estimates for a 10-night Umrah split between Makkah and Madinah, flights included, come out at roughly SAR 3,600–4,900 on an economy basis (quad sharing, shuttle-zone hotels), SAR 5,800–7,900 at standard (triple or twin sharing, 4-star walking distance), and SAR 11,600–16,900+ for premium (twin sharing, 5-star facing the Haram). Treat these as planning bands from published 2026 operator benchmarks, not quotes — your own total will land inside or outside them depending on your city, season and room.

Money-saving tips that actually work:

  • Travel off-peak. The quiet months after Hajj season and outside Ramadan and school holidays are dramatically cheaper — our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide maps the seasons, weather and crowds month by month.
  • Book early, especially flights and trains. Haramain fares and airfares both reward the early booker and punish the late one.
  • Share the room. Quad sharing quarters the per-person hotel cost — the biggest single saving after the season itself.
  • Trade metres for money, honestly. A shuttle-zone hotel at SAR 150–350 with a reliable free shuttle beats a SAR 700 room you resent paying for — but price in the walking if you are travelling with elderly parents.
  • Eat where pilgrims eat. The restaurants one street back from the Haram feed you well for SAR 15–30 a meal; the hotel buffet is a treat, not a routine.
  • Pack properly and buy nothing in a panic. Ihram, sandals, medicines and documents bought calmly at home cost a fraction of the same items beside the Haram — the Umrah Packing List is the checklist to work from.

Quick questions:

  • How much does Umrah cost in total in 2026? For a 10-night trip split between Makkah and Madinah with flights included, published 2026 benchmarks put it at roughly SAR 3,600–4,900 per person on an economy basis, SAR 5,800–7,900 at standard, and SAR 11,600–16,900+ for premium Haram-facing hotels. Ramadan adds roughly 30–50%. Your departure city, season and room sharing move the total more than anything else.
  • How much does Umrah cost from Pakistan? Full packages generally run PKR 220,000–500,000+ per person by season and hotel tier. The visa alone, through a licensed operator with mandatory insurance, is typically PKR 48,000–65,000. The SAR–PKR rate moves daily, so confirm the exact figure with your operator before paying.
  • Are the Nusuk permits really free? Yes. The Umrah permit and the Rawdah permit booked in the official Nusuk app cost nothing at all — they are separate from your paid visa. If someone charges you "permit fees", you are paying for their service, not for a government charge.

Makkah · Ziyarat GuideMakkah Ziyarat — Historic Places to Visit in Makkah

Your Umrah happens inside Masjid al-Haram — but the city around it is the stage of the Seerah itself. The mountain where the Prophet ﷺ hid on the Hijrah, the cemetery where Khadijah (RA) rests, the mosque where the jinn heard the Qur'an: all of them stand within a short drive of the Haram, and together they are known as the Makkah ziyarat — the visits. Be clear about their place, as with our Jabal al-Noor guide: ziyarat is voluntary, not part of Umrah. Your Umrah is complete without a single visit; these places are for learning, reflection and love of the history, and no special rites are prescribed at any of them.

The cave that sheltered the Hijrah: When the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA) hid from the Quraysh search parties in the Cave of Thawr, Allah recorded the moment in the Qur'an: "…when they were both in the cave, and he said to his companion: Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us" (Qur'an 9:40). They stayed in the cave for three nights before travelling on to Madinah — the journey that begins the Islamic calendar.

Jabal Thawr — the mountain of the Hijrah: About 5 km south of Masjid al-Haram stands Jabal Thawr, with the Cave of Thawr near its summit. The climb is harder than Jabal al-Noor — steeper, rougher and with less of a made path — and takes most climbers one and a half to two and a half hours. Many pilgrims, wisely, look up at the mountain from below and make du'a there instead; the view carries the story just as well. If you do climb, go at first light, carry plenty of water, and read the honest climb advice in our Jabal al-Noor & Cave Hira guide — it applies here twice over.

Jannat al-Mualla — the cemetery of Makkah: A short distance north of the Haram — walkable for most, a few minutes by car — lies Jannat al-Mualla, Makkah's historic cemetery. Here rest Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA), the Prophet's ﷺ first wife and the first believer; his grandfather Abdul Muttalib; his uncle Abu Talib; and his infant sons Qasim and Abdullah. Greet the people of the graves as the Prophet ﷺ taught, and make du'a for them and for your own departed. Entry arrangements at the cemetery change from time to time, so follow the signs and the staff at the gate on the day. Its counterpart in the second city is covered in our Jannatul Baqi guide.

Two stops near the Haram:

  • Masjid al-Jinn — a small, working mosque near Jannat al-Mualla, marking the place where a group of jinn listened to the Prophet ﷺ reciting the Qur'an and believed: "Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened and said, 'Indeed, we have heard an amazing Qur'an'" (Qur'an 72:1). Pray two rak'ah if it is open, and move on — it is a short stop.
  • The Prophet's birthplace — in the Suq al-Lail area, a short walk from the Haram, stands the building known as the Prophet's ﷺ birthplace, today housing a library. It is seen from outside only; pause, reflect on where the story began, and do not treat the spot itself as a rite.

The Hajj sites, on a quiet day: A ziyarat drive usually continues east through the plains your Hajj guides describe: Mina, with its sea of white tents and the pillars of the Jamarat; Muzdalifah, the open plain where pilgrims sleep under the sky; and Arafat, with the small white-pillared hill of Jabal al-Rahmah at its heart. Outside the Hajj season a driver can take you through all three in one sweep.
