During Hajj itself the whole area is restricted to the pilgrims performing it — see our Hajj 2027 guide for the season and its rules.

Masjid Aisha at Taneem: Many tours end at Masjid Aisha in Taneem, about 7.5 km from the Haram — the Miqat point where the Prophet ﷺ sent Aisha (RA) to enter Ihram for her Umrah. Pilgrims staying in Makkah who wish to perform a second Umrah go out to Taneem, enter Ihram there, and return. Our Miqat guide explains the boundary and the rules in full.

How to do the tour well:

  • Hire a car and driver, or join an organised ziyarat tour. The full round of outer sites takes about 3 to 4 hours by car. Agree the route and the price before you set off.
  • Start after Fajr or after Asr. The mountains and plains have almost no shade; our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide shows how much the season changes the heat.
  • Keep every visit simple: look, learn, reflect, and make du'a in your own words. No prayers are prescribed at these places, and nothing should be touched, taken or written on the rocks and walls.
  • Match the day to your group. With elderly parents or small children, take the flat stops — the cemetery, Masjid al-Jinn and the drive through the Hajj sites — and leave both mountain climbs out. Our Madinah Ziyarat Guide plans the matching days in the second city.

Quick questions:

  • Is Makkah ziyarat part of Umrah? No. Ziyarat means visiting the historic places of Makkah — Jabal Thawr, Jannat al-Mualla, Masjid al-Jinn and the rest. It is voluntary and rewarded as learning and reflection, but it is not one of the rites, and your Umrah is complete without it.
  • How long does a Makkah ziyarat tour take? About 3 to 4 hours by car for the standard round of outer sites, without climbing. Add two hours or more for each mountain if you climb Jabal al-Noor or Jabal Thawr. Most pilgrims hire a driver or join an organised tour and start after Fajr.
  • Who is buried in Jannat al-Mualla? Makkah's historic cemetery holds Khadijah (RA), the Prophet's ﷺ first wife; his grandfather Abdul Muttalib; his uncle Abu Talib; and his infant sons Qasim and Abdullah. Visit to greet the people of the graves and make du'a, following the entry arrangements in force at the gate.

Sources: Qur'an 9:40 · Qur'an 72:1 · Makkah Ziyarat Guide — Quba Travels ↗ · Makkah Ziyarat Guide — Zikr Cabs ↗ · Site distances and visiting details as listed November 2026; confirm entry rules on the day

Kaaba · Sacred PlacesThe Hateem (Hijr Ismail) — Part of the Kaaba: History, Virtues & How to Pray There

On the north-western side of the Kaaba stands a low, semicircular wall of white marble, about 1.3 metres high, marked by three golden lanterns. Pilgrims call it the Hateem, or Hijr Ismail — and the ground it encloses is unlike any other patch of the Mataf: it is part of the Kaaba itself. That one fact explains everything about the place — why Tawaf must pass outside it, and why a short prayer inside it is one of the most sought-after moments of a pilgrimage.

Praying inside the Kaaba — without entering it: Aisha (RA) said: I wanted to enter the House and pray inside it, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took me by the hand and led me into the Hijr, and said: "Pray in the Hijr if you want to enter the House, for it is part of the House — but your people ran short of funds when they rebuilt the Kaaba, so they left it outside the House" (Sunan Abi Dawud 2028; also Jami' at-Tirmidhi 876 and Sunan an-Nasa'i 2912).

Why part of the Kaaba stands outside its walls: When Ibrahim (AS) raised the Kaaba, its foundations included the area of the Hijr. When the Quraysh rebuilt the Kaaba before Islam, they resolved to use only purely lawful money — and it ran out. Rather than mix in unlawful wealth, they built the walls inside Ibrahim's foundation line and left the remaining strip, about three metres wide next to today's wall, outside, marking it with the low wall so people would know it still belonged to the House. The Prophet ﷺ told Aisha (RA) that, had the Quraysh not been so new to Islam, he would have rebuilt the Kaaba on Ibrahim's foundations — the Hijr inside, the door at ground level (Sahih al-Bukhari 1586; Sahih Muslim 1333). Out of care for their hearts, he left it as it was — and so it stands today.

The Tawaf rule — the reason this matters for your Umrah: Because the Hijr is part of the Kaaba, Tawaf is only complete if you circle outside the whole Hateem wall. A round that cuts through the Hijr, or across its wall, does not count, because you have circled inside the House rather than around it. In the crowd this is the easiest Tawaf mistake to make — the flow of people can carry you towards the gap at either end of the wall. Keep the wall on the outside of your circuit, as our Tawaf Step by Step guide explains round by round.

Praying inside the Hateem:

  • What to pray: Two rak'ah of voluntary (nafl) prayer. Prayer in the Hijr is prayer inside the Kaaba, and the scholars hold it recommended — the Prophet ﷺ himself prayed two rak'ah inside the Kaaba in the year of the Conquest (Sahih al-Bukhari 505; Sahih Muslim 1329). For the obligatory (fard) prayers, join the congregation in the mosque instead, as he ﷺ did.
  • How to enter: Through the open gaps at either end of the semicircular wall. There is no booking and no permit — only patience. Go at the quieter hours, outside the press of Tawaf peaks, and never push: a prayer reached by harming others has lost its point before it begins.
  • What you will notice: Above the enclosed area, the Kaaba's golden rain-spout — the Meezab-e-Rahmat, the Spout of Mercy — pours the roof's rainwater down into the Hijr. Tradition also holds that Ibrahim (AS) built a shelter here for Ismail (AS) and his mother Hajar, and it is widely said that mother and son are buried beneath this ground — one more reason pilgrims treat the small enclosure with such reverence.
  • A moment from the Seerah: It was standing in the Hijr, on the night journey of al-Isra, that the Prophet ﷺ described Jerusalem to the doubting Quraysh as Allah displayed it before him (Sahih al-Bukhari 3886).

Make the most of the minutes you get: Space inside the Hijr is small and the wait is real, so spend the prayer itself unhurriedly and keep your du'a long rather than your stay. Ask for everything — this is du'a offered, in effect, from inside the House of Allah. Afterwards, the natural continuations are the two rak'ah at Maqam-e-Ibrahim described in our Tawaf guide and the duas gathered in Tawaf Duas. If you are travelling with family, our Umrah for First-Timers guide shows where a quiet visit to the Hateem fits into a first journey without rushing the rites.

Quick questions:

  • Is the Hateem really part of the Kaaba? Yes. The strip of ground beside the Kaaba's north-western wall lies on the foundations of Ibrahim (AS). The Quraysh rebuild left it outside the walls when their lawful funds ran out, and the Prophet ﷺ confirmed to Aisha (RA): "it is part of the House" (Sunan Abi Dawud 2028).
  • Can I walk through the Hateem during Tawaf? No. Every round of Tawaf must pass outside the Hateem wall; a round that cuts through the Hijr does not count, because the Hijr is part of the Kaaba and Tawaf must circle the whole House. Watch for the gaps at both ends of the wall in the crowd.
  • What should I pray inside the Hateem? Two rak'ah of voluntary (nafl) prayer, followed by your own du'a. Praying in the Hijr counts as praying inside the Kaaba itself. Enter through the gaps at either end of the wall at a quiet time, and pray the obligatory prayers with the congregation in the mosque.

Sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 2028 · Sahih al-Bukhari 505, 1586 & 3886 · Sahih Muslim 1329 & 1333 · Praying in Hijr Ismail — IslamQA ↗ · Hijr Ismail / Hateem — The Pilgrim ↗

Makkah · Ziyarat GuideJabal al-Noor & Cave Hira — Visiting Guide

North-east of Masjid al-Haram rises a steep, bare mountain with an unmistakable double-humped summit: Jabal al-Noor, the Mountain of Light. Near its top sits a small cave, Ghar Hira — the Cave of Hira — the place where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ used to withdraw in solitude, and where the first words of the Qur'an were revealed to him. Climbing it is one of the most loved ziyarat (visits) in Makkah. One thing to be clear about from the start: the climb is not part of Umrah. Your Umrah is complete without it; this is a voluntary visit to a place of history, done for reflection, not a rite.

What happened in the cave: Aisha (RA) narrated the beginning of the revelation: the Prophet ﷺ would go to the cave of Hira and devote himself to worship there for many nights, until the angel came to him in the cave and said "Read!" — bringing the first revealed words of the Qur'an: "Read, in the name of your Lord who created — created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen" (Qur'an 96:1–4; the full narration is in Sahih al-Bukhari 3).

The mountain and the cave, in numbers:

  • Jabal al-Noor stands about 642 metres high, roughly 5 km from Masjid al-Haram — a short taxi ride from the Haram area.
  • The Cave of Hira is tiny: about 3.7 metres long and 1.6 metres wide, sitting some 270 metres above the foot of the mountain. Only a few people can be inside at once, and at busy times you queue on the rocks outside.
  • The climb is about 1,750 steps. The path is stepped and paved most of the way, but it is steep and there is little shade.

The climb, honestly: A fit walker reaches the top in 30 to 45 minutes; most pilgrims take one to two hours with rests, and there is no shame in taking longer. Go at your own pace, stop often, and carry water — you will want more than you expect. Wear shoes with real grip (see our Umrah Packing List), and keep bags and food tucked away: monkeys live on the mountain and are quick to snatch anything edible in the open. At the summit the whole of Makkah spreads out below you, and through a gap in the rocks beside the cave the Haram can be seen in the distance — the same view the Prophet ﷺ knew, with a very different city beneath it.

When to go: Climb early in the morning, ideally setting off at or just after Fajr, or late in the afternoon — never in the midday heat, which on bare rock is dangerous as well as miserable. The mildest months are November to February; our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide compares the seasons. Nights on the mountain are popular in Ramadan, but the path is steep: go in daylight unless you are with people who know it well.

At the top — keep it simple: The cave is a place to look, reflect and remember what began there. No specific prayer or ritual inside the cave is prescribed, and the visit does not need one: pilgrims commonly pray two rak'ah nearby if there is space, make du'a, and begin the walk down. Treat the place with care — leave no litter, write nothing on the rocks, and be patient with the crowd at the cave mouth. At the foot of the mountain, the Hira Cultural District now houses exhibitions on the story of the revelation, worth an hour if you have it.

Who should think twice: The climb is genuinely demanding. If you are travelling with elderly parents, anyone with heart, knee or breathing problems, or very small children, weigh it carefully — our Umrah for Elderly & Disabled guide covers the gentler options, and there is no obligation here at all: the mountain can be honoured from below. Many families split up, with the younger members climbing while everyone else visits the exhibitions at the base.

Getting there: Taxis and ride-hailing cars from the Haram area take around 15 to 20 minutes depending on traffic; agree the fare or use the app meter, and arrange the return before you start climbing, as cars at the base can be scarce at peak times. If this is your first journey, read our Umrah for First-Timers guide for where a ziyarat day fits around the rites, and our Madinah Ziyarat Guide for the visits waiting in the second city.

Quick questions:

  • Is visiting Cave Hira part of Umrah? No. It is a voluntary ziyarat — a visit to a historic place — not one of the rites of Umrah or Hajj. Your Umrah is complete without it, and no specific prayer inside the cave is prescribed.
  • How long does the climb take? The stepped path is about 1,750 steps. Fit walkers take 30 to 45 minutes; most pilgrims take one to two hours with rests. Start early in the morning, carry water and wear shoes with grip.
  • Can elderly pilgrims climb Jabal al-Noor? For most, honestly, no — the climb is steep, exposed and demanding, and there is no lift or cart. Elderly pilgrims and anyone with mobility, heart or breathing problems are better served by the facilities described in our Elderly & Disabled guide, and lose nothing religiously by skipping the climb.

Sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Qur'an 96:1–5 · Mountain and cave dimensions as recorded for Jabal al-Noor and Ghar Hira, November 2026

Travel · Getting AroundHaramain High-Speed Train — Makkah to Madinah Guide

Almost every Umrah journey has the same long leg in the middle: Makkah to Madinah, some 450 km of desert highway. By coach or car that drive takes around five hours. The Haramain High-Speed Train does it in about two — air-conditioned, seated, and with the desert passing at up to 300 km/h. Opened in 2018 and built for pilgrims above all, it has quietly become the easiest way to travel between the two holy cities. This guide covers the stations, booking, luggage and the small details that matter on the day. Our Umrah for Elderly & Disabled guide already recommends it for older travellers; here is the full picture for everyone.

The five stations:

  • Makkah — in the Rusaiyfah district, a short drive from Masjid al-Haram.
  • Jeddah (Al Sulaymaniyah) — the city's main Haramain station.
  • King Abdulaziz International Airport — a station inside Jeddah's airport, so you can step off a flight and onto the train.
  • King Abdullah Economic City — serving KAEC and Rabigh.
  • Madinah — on the eastern side of the city, a short drive from the Prophet's Mosque.

Journey times: Makkah to Madinah takes about 2 hours on the through services, against roughly 5 hours by road. Makkah to Jeddah airport is under an hour, which makes the train a realistic option straight after landing — or for the return to your flight home.

Booking, in brief:

  • Book on the official Haramain (HHR) website or app, or through Saudi Arabia Railways. You choose your train, class and seat, pay by card, and receive an e-ticket with a QR code — keep it on your phone and carry your passport or ID, as staff check them together.
  • Two classes: Economy and Business, both air-conditioned with allocated seating; Business adds wider seats and lounge access at the main stations. Fares vary with class, season and how early you book — the cheapest tickets go first, above all in Ramadan and the school holidays, so book as soon as your dates are fixed.
  • Arrive early: plan to be at the station at least 30 to 45 minutes before departure. Ticket gates and boarding close shortly before the train leaves, and the stations are large — the walk to the platform takes longer than you think.

Luggage: The standard allowance is one large bag (up to 25 kg) plus a hand bag per passenger; oversized and extra items are restricted, and bags are screened at the station entrance like at an airport. Confirm the current allowance when you book, keep medicines and documents in your hand bag, and label everything — stations at prayer times and peak hours are busy places. Our Umrah Packing List helps you travel light enough for all of this to be easy.

The last stretch — station to Haram: Neither terminus is at the mosque door. At both ends you finish the journey by taxi, ride-hailing car or shuttle bus — around 10 to 20 minutes depending on traffic and prayer times. Build that time into your plans, especially if you are heading to a booked Rawdah slot (see our Rawdah Permit guide) or a departing flight. Travellers from Pakistan will find how the train fits a package itinerary in our Umrah from Pakistan guide.

Coming from Jeddah airport for Umrah? Mind the Miqat: If you land at Jeddah and take the train straight to Makkah to begin Umrah, remember that the line carries you across the Miqat boundary quickly, and the train does not stop for Ihram. The common, safe practice is to enter Ihram before you board — many pilgrims change and make their intention at the airport. Our Miqat guide explains the boundary and the rules in full; if your exact case is unusual, ask a qualified scholar before you travel.

Train or road — which should you choose? For most pilgrims the train wins on time, comfort and rest: you arrive in Madinah ready to go to the Prophet's Mosque, not worn out from five hours on a coach. Private cars keep one advantage — door-to-door travel, which can matter with very elderly passengers, lots of luggage or small children (see our Umrah with Kids guide). If you do take the road, the same journey is covered in the travel sections of our Umrah for First-Timers guide. And once you arrive, our Madinah Ziyarat Guide plans your days in the second city.

Quick questions:

  • How long is Makkah to Madinah by Haramain train? About 2 hours on through services, at speeds of up to 300 km/h — against roughly 5 hours by coach or car on the highway.
  • How do I book Haramain train tickets? On the official Haramain (HHR) website or app, or through Saudi Arabia Railways. Pick your train and class (Economy or Business), pay by card, and travel on the e-ticket QR code with your passport or ID. Book early in Ramadan and holiday periods — the cheapest fares sell out first.
  • Are the stations close to the Haram? Not at the door: Makkah station (Rusaiyfah) and Madinah station are each a short taxi, ride-hailing or shuttle ride — roughly 10 to 20 minutes — from the mosque. Arrive at the station 30 to 45 minutes before your train, and allow the same margin at the other end.

Sources: Haramain High Speed Railway (HHR) official booking channels and Saudi Arabia Railways — stations, journey times and luggage rules as listed November 2026; confirm fares and allowances when you book

Umrah · Accessibility GuideUmrah for Elderly & Disabled — Wheelchair, Facilities & Tips

Age and disability are no barrier to Umrah. The Two Holy Mosques run some of the most complete accessibility services of any religious site in the world: free wheelchairs around the clock, bookable electric carts, step-free routes and dedicated lanes, all arranged so that an elderly parent or a pilgrim with limited mobility can complete every rite with dignity. This guide gathers what is available in Makkah and Madinah, what it costs, and the practical tips that make the journey easier. If this is also your first Umrah, read it alongside our Umrah for First-Timers guide.

Seated Tawaf is valid: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself performed Tawaf riding his camel (Sahih al-Bukhari 1633), and scholars take this as clear evidence that performing Tawaf seated, in a wheelchair or a cart, is valid for whoever needs it. And Allah says: "Allah does not burden a soul beyond what it can bear" (Quran 2:286). Scholars differ on some of the details, so for your own exact situation, ask a qualified scholar before you travel.

Free manual wheelchairs, day and night: Inside Masjid al-Haram, manual wheelchairs are free, 24/7, from service counters near the major gates, including the King Abdulaziz Gate, Gate 74 and the Ajyad Gate. They are for use inside the mosque only and must be returned to a counter when you finish; a family member or companion does the pushing. Step-free access is built in: 32 gates have ramps, among them gates 68, 74, 79, 84, 89, 90, 93 and 94.

Electric carts through the Tanaqol app: The powered option is booked through Tanaqol, the official app of the General Authority for the Care of the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques. The current prices are:

  • Full Umrah (Tawaf and Sa'i): 300 SAR
  • Tawaf only: 50 SAR
  • Sa'i only: 50 SAR
  • Pilgrims aged 65 and over: 50% off, so a full Umrah costs 150 SAR
  • Free for people with verified disabilities and for children under six

Pickup and drop-off points are at Al-Marwah (Gate 25), Al-Arqam (Gate 16), Ajyad (Gate 5) and Al-Shabika (Gate 66), and for Tawaf itself, golf carts run on the Mataf roof. Prices can change, so confirm in the Tanaqol app before you go.

Tawaf and Sa'i in a wheelchair:

  • Sa'i has a dedicated middle wheelchair lane running between Safa and Marwah, away from the fastest walkers.
  • Upper-floor Tawaf is calmer and far less crowded than the ground-floor Mataf, and the upper floors are reached by lift and escalator.
  • A free cart-loan service operates at exits 309 and 343.
  • An official wheelchair-pusher service works at the entrances. Use the official counters only, and politely decline unauthorised pushers who approach you.

In Madinah: Masjid an-Nabawi holds more than 2,500 free mobility carts, issued through the Doors Management Office, so wheelchair help in the Prophet's Mosque is just as organised as in Makkah. Book the Rawdah slot itself through the Nusuk app, exactly as our Nusuk App Guide and Rawdah Permit guides explain.

Renting a chair privately: Private companies rent out electric wheelchairs with hotel delivery at roughly SAR 100 to 120 per day, or about SAR 700 per week. On a longer stay this can be simpler than collecting and returning a mosque chair every day. Prices vary by company and season, so confirm before you book.

Practical tips from experienced families:

  • Travel in the mild months. November to February brings the gentlest weather; our Best Time to Perform Umrah guide compares the seasons.
  • Rest between the rites. Sit for 15 to 20 minutes and drink Zamzam between Tawaf and Sa'i instead of pushing straight on.
  • Choose the hotel by distance, not by stars. A simple hotel close to the Haram is worth more than a grand one far away: every metre saved is energy saved. Our Umrah Packing List covers the small things that help on the road.
  • Carry medicines in your hand luggage, together with a doctor's note explaining them, and keep the note with your passport and visa papers (see Umrah Visa 2026).
  • Take the Haramain train between Makkah and Madinah: about 2 hours, against roughly 5 hours by coach, and far kinder on an elderly traveller.

Quick questions:

  • Is Tawaf in a wheelchair valid? Yes. The Prophet ﷺ performed Tawaf riding his camel (Sahih al-Bukhari 1633), and scholars hold that Tawaf performed seated, in a wheelchair or an electric cart, is valid for whoever needs it. For the details of your own case, ask a qualified scholar.
  • Where do I get a free wheelchair in Masjid al-Haram? From the service counters near the major gates, including the King Abdulaziz Gate, Gate 74 and the Ajyad Gate. The chairs are free and available 24/7, for use inside the mosque only, and must be returned; a companion does the pushing.
  • How much do the electric carts cost? Through the Tanaqol app: 300 SAR for a full Umrah, 50 SAR for Tawaf only and 50 SAR for Sa'i only. Pilgrims aged 65 and over pay half (150 SAR for a full Umrah), and carts are free for people with verified disabilities and for children under six. Prices can change, so confirm in the Tanaqol app before you go.

Sources: General Authority for the Care of the Affairs of the Two Holy Mosques: Tanaqol electric cart service and the wheelchair services of Masjid al-Haram and Masjid an-Nabawi (prices as listed November 2026; confirm in the Tanaqol app before travel) · Sahih al-Bukhari 1633 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Quran 2:286

Umrah · Miqat GuideMiqat — Where to Enter Ihram (All 5 Miqat Locations & Rules for Air Travellers)

Every road to Makkah crosses an invisible line: the Miqat — the boundary points fixed by the Prophet ﷺ where a pilgrim travelling for Hajj or Umrah must enter Ihram. You may not pass your Miqat heading for the Sacred House without Ihram, so knowing which Miqat is yours — and what to do on a plane — matters before you ever leave home. For what Ihram itself involves once you enter it, read our Ihram Rules guide next.

Who fixed the Miqat? Ibn Abbas (RA) narrated: "The Prophet ﷺ designated Dhul Hulayfah as the Miqat for the people of Madinah, Al-Juhfah for the people of Sham (Syria), Qarn al-Manazil for the people of Najd, and Yalamlam for the people of Yemen. These Miqats are for the people of those places and for everyone who comes through them intending Hajj or Umrah. Whoever lives inside these boundaries enters Ihram from where he is, and the people of Makkah enter Ihram from Makkah itself" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1524; Sahih Muslim 1181).

The five Miqat, one by one:

  • Dhul Hulayfah — the Miqat for the people of Madinah and everyone who passes through Madinah on the way to Makkah. Also called Abyar Ali (Bir Ali), it lies about 9 km from the Prophet's Mosque; its mosque, Masjid Bir Ali, has washing and changing facilities, and almost every Madinah-to-Makkah pilgrim stops there to enter Ihram.
  • Al-Juhfah — the Miqat for pilgrims coming from Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa along that route. It stands near the modern town of Rabigh on the Red Sea coast road.
  • Qarn al-Manazil — the Miqat for the people of Najd — the Riyadh region — and for Gulf travellers approaching Makkah on the Taif road. It is located at as-Sayl al-Kabir, northeast of Makkah.
  • Yalamlam — the Miqat for the people of Yemen and for everyone arriving from the south, including many sea and air routes from Asia whose path crosses it before reaching Jeddah.
  • Dhat Irq — the Miqat for the people of Iraq and those coming from beyond it in the northeast (reported in Sunan Abi Dawud 1739).

The simple rule underneath: use the Miqat of your route. If your journey passes one of the five — by road, sea or air — that one is yours, wherever you originally come from. If you live between a Miqat and Makkah, you enter Ihram from your own home. Our Umrah for First-Timers guide shows where this step sits in the full order of the rites.

Rules for air travellers — read this before you fly:

  • Your Miqat is the point your flight path crosses. Most flights into Jeddah cross Yalamlam (or Qarn al-Manazil on some routes) shortly before landing — so your Ihram begins in the air, not at the airport. Jeddah itself lies inside the Miqat line, so waiting until you land is too late if you intend Umrah straight away.
  • Prepare on the ground. Take ghusl before you travel, and either wear the Ihram garments from home or change into them early in the flight — not in a rush in the aisle. What you still need at that point is only the intention and the Talbiyah.
  • Listen for the announcement. Airlines on Umrah routes usually announce that the plane is approaching the Miqat, often about 30 minutes beforehand. When it comes — or a little before, to be safe — make your intention for Umrah and announce the Talbiyah: "Labbayk Allahumma labbayk..." From that moment the rules of Ihram apply to you.
  • Sleeping through it? Set an alarm for the expected crossing time, or ask the crew or a travelling companion to wake you — the crossing into Ihram should be a conscious, deliberate moment.

If you pass the Miqat without entering Ihram: the correct step is to go back to the Miqat (or to any Miqat) and enter Ihram from there. If returning is genuinely not possible, the majority of scholars hold that you enter Ihram where you are and a dam (a sacrificial animal in the Haram) is owed. Do not guess with something like this — if it happens to you, ask a qualified scholar about your exact situation, and keep our Umrah Packing List habit of preparing early so it does not happen at all.

What about the people of Makkah? Makkah's own residents enter Ihram from Makkah itself — from their homes — for Hajj, exactly as the hadith above states. For Umrah, a person already in Makkah goes out to the nearest land outside the Haram boundary (the Hal) — most commonly Masjid Aisha at Tan'im, about 7 km away — following the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to Aisha (RA) (Sahih Muslim 1211). Before any of this, make sure the paperwork side is settled: our Umrah Visa 2026 guide and the Nusuk App Guide cover visas, permits and bookings.

Quick questions:

  • Which Miqat do I use if I fly to Jeddah? The one your flight crosses — for most Jeddah flights that is Yalamlam. Make your intention and say the Talbiyah on the plane before the crossing; the crew normally announce it in advance.
  • Can I wear the Ihram clothes at home and enter Ihram later? Yes. Wearing the garments is not itself Ihram — Ihram begins with the intention and the Talbiyah. Many pilgrims wear the cloth from home and enter Ihram on the plane as it approaches the Miqat.
  • I am visiting Madinah first — where is my Miqat? Dhul Hulayfah (Bir Ali). You enter Ihram there when you leave Madinah for Makkah, not when you first land in Saudi Arabia.

Sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1524 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1181 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sunan Abi Dawud 1739 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1211 — Sunnah.com ↗

Umrah · When to GoBest Time to Perform Umrah — Months, Weather & Crowds Guide

Umrah can be performed at almost any time of the year — unlike Hajj, it is not tied to fixed days. But "any time" is not "all times are equal": Makkah's weather, the crowds in the Haram and hotel prices swing enormously from month to month. The best time for you depends on what you value most — mild weather, spiritual intensity, quiet, or cost. Here is the honest month-by-month picture.

The reward never sleeps: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Umrah in Ramadan is equal to Hajj" — and in another narration, "equal to Hajj with me" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1782; Sahih Muslim 1256). And he ﷺ said: "Umrah to the next Umrah is an expiation for whatever (sins) are between them" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1773; Sahih Muslim 1349) — so every season carries its own blessing.

The best weather window — November to February: These are Makkah's mild months. Daytime temperatures sit around 25–30°C, evenings are cool enough for a light layer, and Tawaf and the walk between the Haram and your hotel stay comfortable even for the elderly. If your group includes parents, grandparents or small children, plan for this window first. The one caution: late December brings school holidays worldwide, so crowds grow and prices jump even though the weather is at its best.

Ramadan — the greatest reward, the greatest crowds: Because an Umrah in Ramadan carries the reward described above, Makkah fills to its limits — above all in the last ten nights, when the Haram stays packed through the night for Qiyam and the search for Laylatul Qadr. Hotels near the Haram reach their highest prices of the year, and permits and good rooms go early. Go in Ramadan for the reward with your eyes open: book months ahead, pace yourself around fasting, and read our Umrah in Ramadan guide before you commit.

Summer — May to August, handle with care: Makkah's summer heat regularly reaches 40–45°C and beyond at midday. Tawaf on the open Mataf and the walk to the hotel become genuinely hard, especially for the elderly, children and anyone with health conditions. If summer is your only option: perform Tawaf in the early morning or at night, carry water constantly, rest in the heat of the day, and pack exactly as our Umrah Packing List describes for hot weather. The compensation is real, though — outside the school holidays, summer weeks can be quieter and cheaper.

The Hajj closure — Umrah stops: There is one season when Umrah is simply not available: as Hajj approaches, Umrah visa issuing winds down, existing Umrah pilgrims are required to leave, and Umrah permits pause so the holy cities can receive the Hajj pilgrims. The Umrah season then reopens after Hajj, in the new Islamic year. Never plan an Umrah that touches the Hajj days themselves — see our Hajj 2027 guide for the season's dates and how the two pilgrimages differ.

School holidays — the hidden crowd driver: Whenever schools close in the big sending countries — late December to early January, spring breaks, and the long summer holidays — family Umrah trips surge, Haram crowds swell, and prices follow. If your dates are flexible, travelling in term-time weeks is the single easiest way to find a calmer, cheaper Umrah. Families travelling in those peak weeks should plan with our Umrah for First-Timers guide and book everything early.

Month-by-month, in short:

  • Muharram – Safar (season reopens after Hajj): The quietest Haram of the year at first, but still hot — a good pick for heat-tolerant pilgrims who want space and lower prices.
  • Rabi al-Awwal – Jumada al-Akhirah (roughly autumn into early winter): Cooling steadily, moderate crowds — for many, the sweet spot of the whole year.
  • Rajab – Sha'ban: Mild weather and a spiritual build-up towards Ramadan; crowds grow week by week as Ramadan nears.
  • Ramadan: Maximum reward, maximum crowds and prices — book far ahead, especially for the last ten nights.
  • Shawwal: A post-Ramadan lull with warm but manageable weather; often good value.
  • Dhul Qa'dah – Dhul Hijjah: The season winds down and then closes for Hajj — do not plan Umrah here.

So, when should you go? For weather and comfort: November to February. For reward: Ramadan, accepting the crowds. For quiet and value: the weeks just after the season reopens, or term-time weeks in autumn. Travelling from Pakistan? Our Umrah from Pakistan guide adds the flights, visa and package details for your route. Whichever month you choose, an Umrah performed sincerely is never wasted — the calendar only changes the conditions, not the acceptance.

Quick questions:

  • Which is the least crowded time for Umrah? The weeks right after the Umrah season reopens following Hajj, and term-time weeks in mid-January to February, are usually the quietest — though "quiet" in Makkah is always relative.
  • Can I perform Umrah during Hajj season? No. Umrah visas and permits pause as Hajj approaches, and Umrah pilgrims must leave before Hajj begins. Umrah resumes after Hajj, in the new Islamic year.
  • What is the best time for elderly parents? November to February, when Makkah's weather is mildest. Avoid the summer heat and, if possible, the peak crowds of Ramadan's last ten nights.

Sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1782 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1256 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 1773 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1349 — Sunnah.com ↗

Madinah · Jannatul BaqiJannatul Baqi — Visiting the Cemetery of Madinah

On the eastern side of Masjid an-Nabawi in Madinah lies a quiet field of sand and small stones that holds more history than almost any place on earth: Jannatul Baqi, also called Baqi al-Gharqad, the cemetery of Madinah since the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Thousands of the Companions are buried here, among them Uthman ibn Affan (RA), the third caliph, and the wives of the Prophet ﷺ — the Mothers of the Believers — with one exception: Khadijah (RA) rests in Makkah, in the cemetery of Jannatul Mu'alla. A visit to Baqi belongs in every Madinah stay; our Madinah Ziyarat Guide shows how it fits into the wider round of visits.

The Prophet's own visits: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ visited Baqi regularly, often late at night, and prayed for its people. Aisha (RA) narrates that when it was her night, he would go out to Baqi towards the end of the night and say his du'a for them, including: "O Allah, forgive the people of Baqi al-Gharqad" (Sahih Muslim 974).

The du'a on entering a graveyard: Greet the people of Baqi the way the Prophet ﷺ taught his companions to greet the people of the graves:

السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ أَهْلَ الدِّيَارِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُسْلِمِينَ، وَإِنَّا إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ بِكُمْ لَاحِقُونَ، نَسْأَلُ اللَّهَ لَنَا وَلَكُمُ الْعَافِيَةَ

"As-salamu 'alaykum ahla ad-diyari min al-mu'minina wa al-muslimin, wa inna in sha Allahu bikum lahiqun, nas'alullaha lana wa lakum al-'afiyah"

"Peace be upon you, O dwellers of these abodes from among the believers and Muslims; and we — if Allah wills — will join you; I ask Allah for well-being for us and for you" (Sahih Muslim 974, narrated by Buraydah RA).

Why visit graves at all? The Prophet ﷺ said: "I used to forbid you from visiting graves, but now visit them, for they remind you of the Hereafter" (Sahih Muslim 977). Baqi is not a sightseeing stop — it is a reminder that the greatest generation ended in this same sand, and that we follow them.

Visiting Baqi — the practical side:

  • Opening times. Baqi usually opens briefly after the Fajr and Asr prayers, when the gates are opened for men to enter, greet the people of Baqi and make du'a. Times are controlled by the mosque authorities and can change — ask at the Haram or check on the day.
  • Women pay their respects from outside the boundary — from the gates and the surrounding courtyard of Masjid an-Nabawi, where Baqi lies in full view; the greeting and du'a above are said from there.
  • What you will see. The graves today are simple, unmarked mounds of sand and earth, each with small stones — no names, no structures. You will not be able to identify the grave of any individual Companion; visit the whole cemetery with one greeting and one du'a for all of its people.
  • Combine your Madinah days well. Baqi sits right beside the Haram, so it pairs with your Rawdah Permit visit on the same day, and with a trip out to Masjid Quba. First-time visitors should read Umrah for First-Timers for the order of the Madinah days, and the Umrah Packing List for what to carry — you need nothing for Baqi but a quiet heart.

Etiquette in Baqi — please keep it:

  • Keep your voice low. It is a graveyard, not a gathering place; speak softly, if at all.
  • Make du'a only to Allah. Ask Allah to forgive the people of Baqi and to grant you a good end — never ask anything from the dead; supplication is worship, and worship is for Allah alone.
  • No wailing or loud lamentation over the graves.
  • No touching, kissing or climbing on graves, and do not take sand or stones from them.
  • No littering — leave the cemetery exactly as you found it, and follow the instructions of the staff at the gates.

Quick questions:

  • Who is buried in Jannatul Baqi? Thousands of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, including Uthman ibn Affan (RA) and the Mothers of the Believers — the Prophet's wives — except Khadijah (RA), who is buried in Jannatul Mu'alla in Makkah. The graves today are simple unmarked mounds, so individual graves cannot be picked out.
  • When can I visit Baqi, and can women visit? The gates usually open briefly after Fajr and Asr prayers for men to enter. Women greet the people of Baqi and make du'a from outside the boundary, by the gates and the courtyard of Masjid an-Nabawi. Times are set by the mosque authorities and may change.
  • What should I say when I enter a graveyard? The du'a the Prophet ﷺ taught: "Peace be upon you, O dwellers of these abodes from among the believers and Muslims; and we — if Allah wills — will join you; I ask Allah for well-being for us and for you" (Sahih Muslim 974). Then make du'a to Allah for them — and for yourself.

Sources: Sahih Muslim 974 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 977 — Sunnah.com ↗

Umrah · Pakistan GuideUmrah from Pakistan — Complete Guide 2026

Every year, hundreds of thousands of Pakistanis travel for Umrah — but the Pakistani route has its own rules, and the first one surprises many people: Pakistani passport holders cannot apply for an Umrah visa directly on Nusuk. Your application must go through a licensed Umrah tour operator attested by Pakistan's Ministry of Religious Affairs, working with a Saudi-approved service provider. Anyone offering you a "direct" or "visa-only, no operator" route is not following the system. This guide walks through the whole journey — visa, costs, flights and permits — and if it is your first time, read it alongside Umrah for First-Timers.

The hotel booking rule (Nusuk Masar) — read this first: Since 10 June 2025, under the Nusuk Masar rule, a confirmed hotel booking with a Booking Reference Number (BRN) is mandatory before any visa is issued. Visa-only applications are not accepted — your operator books the hotels through the Masar system first, then the visa follows. This is why honest operators quote packages, not bare visas.

What it costs (2026):

  • Saudi government visa fee: SAR 300 — about PKR 22,300 at recent rates.
  • All-in visa cost from Pakistan: typically PKR 48,000–65,000, including the mandatory medical insurance and the operator's processing.
  • Full Umrah packages: generally PKR 220,000–500,000+, depending on the season and the hotel tier — distance from the Haram is the biggest price driver. Our Umrah Visa Fees 2026 guide breaks the costs down further, and Umrah Visa 2026 covers the visa types.
  • A warning on numbers: the SAR–PKR rate moves daily, so every rupee figure here is a guide, not a promise — confirm the exact amount with your operator before you pay.

Documents and timing:

  • Passport valid at least 6 months from your date of entry — check it before you book anything.
  • Entry window: 30 days from issuance — you must enter Saudi Arabia within 30 days of the visa being issued (this changed in October 2025), so do not apply too early.
  • The Hajj pause: Umrah visas pause about 10–15 days before Hajj and resume after Hajj — plan around it.
  • The 1448 AH season opened with visas from 31 May 2026 and entry from 1 June 2026.

Vaccinations:

  • Polio (OPV) is required for Pakistani travellers — get the drops and keep the record.
  • Meningococcal ACWY: Saudi Arabia suspended the mandatory requirement in February 2025, but many operators and health guidance still list it. Check the current rule with your operator, and if you have the certificate, carry it.
  • Your certificate, digitally: the NADRA digital vaccination certificate is available through the NIMS portal for PKR 100 — carry a printout as well as the digital copy.

Flights: Direct and one-stop flights run from Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad to Jeddah or Madinah — PIA, Saudia and Airblue, plus the Gulf carriers. Flying into Madinah and out of Jeddah (or the reverse) saves a long road transfer. Book early — fares climb steeply in the peak months.

After you arrive: Your visa came through an operator, but your permits are your own job: use the Nusuk app for your Umrah permit and your Rawdah visit slot — our Nusuk App Guide and Rawdah Permit guides walk through both, step by step. Women can travel for Umrah without a mahram under current Saudi rules — see Women Travelling Alone for Umrah for the details and safety advice. For money, carry Saudi riyals in cash plus your bank cards; for luggage, the Umrah Packing List covers everything, including the documents folder.

Best time to go: November to February for the coolest weather and the easiest Tawaf. Ramadan carries unmatched reward — but it is the busiest and priciest season of the year, so book it many months ahead.

Quick questions:

  • Can I apply for an Umrah visa myself on Nusuk from Pakistan? No. Pakistani passport holders cannot apply directly on Nusuk — your application must go through a licensed Umrah tour operator attested by Pakistan's Ministry of Religious Affairs, working with a Saudi-approved service provider. Since 10 June 2025 your operator must also hold a confirmed hotel booking (BRN) on Nusuk Masar before the visa can be issued.
  • How much does Umrah from Pakistan cost in 2026? The Saudi government visa fee is SAR 300 (about PKR 22,300); the all-in visa cost from Pakistan is typically PKR 48,000–65,000 with mandatory medical insurance and processing; full packages generally run PKR 220,000–500,000+ by season and hotel tier. The SAR–PKR rate moves daily — confirm the exact figure with your operator.
  • Which vaccinations do Pakistani pilgrims need? Polio (OPV) is required. The meningococcal ACWY requirement was suspended by Saudi Arabia in February 2025, but many operators still list it — check the current rule with your operator and carry your certificate if you have one. Your NADRA digital vaccination certificate is available via the NIMS portal for PKR 100.

Sources: Pakistan Ministry of Religious Affairs (licensed Umrah operator rules) · Nusuk Masar confirmed-hotel-booking (BRN) requirement, in force from 10 June 2025 · Saudi Umrah visa fee schedule · NADRA NIMS vaccination certificate service — PKR amounts are guides; confirm the exact cost with your operator on the day, as the SAR–PKR rate changes daily.

Umrah · Ramadan GuideUmrah in Ramadan — Virtues, Booking & Tips

Of all the months in which to stand before the Kaaba, none carries a promise like Ramadan. Umrah at any time of year wipes away sins and poverty, but an Umrah performed while fasting, praying Taraweeh and chasing Laylatul Qadr is something pilgrims save for years to experience. Here is what the Prophet ﷺ said about it, what it does and does not replace, and how to plan the trip well. If this is your first journey, read our Umrah for First-Timers guide alongside this one.

The promise: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Umrah in Ramadan is equivalent to Hajj" — and in one narration, "equivalent to Hajj with me" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1782; Sahih Muslim 1256). He said this to a woman of the Ansar who had missed Hajj with him because her family had only two camels, and he directed her to perform Umrah in Ramadan instead.

Equal in reward — not a replacement for Hajj: Read the hadith carefully. The scholars explain that Ramadan Umrah equals Hajj in reward, not in what it discharges. It does not replace the obligatory Hajj: a Muslim who performs Umrah in Ramadan and later becomes able to perform Hajj still owes Hajj, exactly as before. IslamQA (fatwa 104926) states this plainly, and the scholars of the four madhhabs hold that the virtue in the hadith is general — it is not limited to that one woman, nor to someone who missed Hajj; it applies to anyone who performs Umrah in Ramadan. So go for the multiplied reward, and keep Hajj itself on your plans for when Allah enables it — our Hajj 2027 guide shows how that journey is booked.

Planning a Ramadan Umrah — what is different:

  • Book 5–6 months ahead. Ramadan is the busiest Umrah season of the year. Flights and hotels — above all the hotels near the Haram — fill fast and prices climb steeply, especially for the last ten nights. Sort your visa early too: see Umrah Visa 2026 for the visa types and Umrah Visa Fees 2026 for what it costs.
  • You still need a Nusuk Umrah permit. Ramadan changes nothing here: you need one Umrah permit for each performance of Umrah, booked in the Nusuk app, and you show the permit's QR code at the checkpoint. Book your slot as soon as your dates are fixed — Ramadan slots go quickly. Our Nusuk App Guide walks through the booking step by step.
  • Taraweeh crowds. The Haram fills to the streets for Maghrib, Isha and Taraweeh. Arrive about 90 minutes before Maghrib or Isha to secure a place inside; arriving at the adhan often means praying in the outer courtyards or the road.
  • Flip your day around. Rest and sleep in the daytime — after Fajr and again after Dhuhr if you can — and give the nights to worship: Taraweeh, Tahajjud, Qur'an and du'a. Fighting the crowds on no sleep helps no one.
  • The last ten nights. These are the peak of the month and the peak of the crowds. In them falls Laylatul Qadr, better than a thousand months — increase du'a and i'tikaf-style devotion, and expect the Haram to be at its fullest on the odd nights.
  • Iftar and Suhoor. Break your fast simply — dates and Zamzam are distributed in the Haram, and many pilgrims iftar in the courtyard before Maghrib prayer. Eat a real Suhoor before Fajr even if you must wake for it; you will need the strength for a day of fasting and walking. Keep iftar light if you plan to stand long in Taraweeh.
  • Pack differently for Ramadan. Take a lighter Ihram — the nights are long in worship and the days warm. Pack dates for iftar on the move and a refillable water bottle for Zamzam and for keeping hydrated between Iftar and Suhoor. Our full Umrah Packing List covers everything else.

Quick questions:

  • Does Ramadan Umrah replace Hajj? No. It equals Hajj in reward, as the Prophet ﷺ said (Sahih al-Bukhari 1782; Sahih Muslim 1256), but it does not lift the obligation of Hajj. If Hajj becomes possible for you later, it remains due — IslamQA fatwa 104926 confirms this.
  • Do I need a Nusuk permit in Ramadan? Yes. You need one Umrah permit per performance of Umrah, booked in the Nusuk app, and you present its QR code at the entrance — Ramadan is no exception, and slots fill faster than in any other month.
  • When should I book? Five to six months before Ramadan if you can. Hotels near the Haram sell out first and prices rise sharply, above all for the last ten nights — and your Nusuk Umrah slot and visa should be arranged just as early.

Sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1782 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1256 — Sunnah.com ↗ · IslamQA fatwa 104926 (Ramadan Umrah equals Hajj in reward but does not replace the obligatory Hajj)

Madinah · Masjid QubaMasjid Quba — Virtues, History & How to Visit

Before there was a Prophet's Mosque, there was Quba. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived at the outskirts of Madinah during the Hijrah, he stayed with Banu Amr ibn Awf and laid the first stones of a mosque there — the first mosque in Islam. It is a short trip from the Haram in Madinah, and the reward promised for praying in it is unlike any other mosque visit on your journey. It fits naturally into a wider day of visits — see our Madinah Ziyarat Guide for the full route.

Founded on taqwa: Allah says of it: "A mosque founded on piety (taqwa) from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in" (Qur'an 9:108) — revealed about Masjid Quba, whose people loved to purify themselves thoroughly, and Allah praised them for it in the same verse.
Two rak'ahs here, an Umrah's reward: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever purifies himself in his house, then comes to the Quba Mosque and offers a prayer therein, will have a reward like that for Umrah" (Sunan Ibn Majah 1412, graded hasan; also Jami' at-Tirmidhi 324, graded hasan). Note the condition woven into the words: the purification — wudu — is done at home first, then you come and pray.

The Prophet's own habit: After settling in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ used to go to Quba every Saturday, sometimes walking and sometimes riding, and pray two rak'ahs there (Sahih al-Bukhari 1193; Sahih Muslim 1399), and he encouraged his companions to do the same. Saturday was his habit, not a condition: the hadith of Ibn Majah sets no day, so a prayer at Quba on any day of the week earns the same promised reward. If your ziyarat day falls on a Saturday, you are simply closer to his exact practice.

How to visit — the practical side:

  • Where it is: Masjid Quba stands about 3.5 km south of the Prophet's Mosque — roughly 10 minutes by taxi or bus. Taxis wait around the Haram; agree the fare or check the meter before you set off.
  • Make wudu at your hotel first. The hadith's wording ties the reward to purifying yourself in your house — for the traveller, your hotel room — then going to Quba and praying. Wudu facilities exist at the mosque if you need them, but come ready.
  • Pray two rak'ahs on arrival — or join a congregational prayer if one is under way; either fulfils the "offers a prayer therein" of the hadith.
  • Combine it with a ziyarat trip. Quba pairs naturally with Mount Uhud and Masjid al-Qiblatain in a single half-day circuit — the order and stories are laid out in our Madinah Ziyarat Guide.
  • Women and children are welcome. Quba has provision for families, and the reward of the prayer is for everyone who comes purified and prays.
  • No permit is needed. Unlike the Rawdah — which requires a booked slot, as our Rawdah Permit guide explains — Masjid Quba is open to walk in and pray; just avoid the busiest prayer-time crush if you are with small children. If you are packing for the Madinah days, our Umrah Packing List has the essentials, and first-time pilgrims should start with Umrah for First-Timers.

Quick questions:

  • Does praying at Quba really equal Umrah reward? Yes — that is the Prophet's ﷺ own words: whoever purifies himself at home, comes to Masjid Quba and prays there receives a reward like that of Umrah (Sunan Ibn Majah 1412, hasan; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 324, hasan). Like Ramadan Umrah, it is a reward, not a performed Umrah — it does not take the place of the rites in Makkah, nor of Hajj itself.
  • Do I need a Nusuk permit for Quba? No. Masjid Quba needs no permit and no booking — make wudu at your hotel, travel the roughly 3.5 km from the Prophet's Mosque, and pray two rak'ahs. Permits on the Madinah side are for the Rawdah only.
  • Which day should I visit? Any day. The Prophet ﷺ habitually went on Saturdays (Sahih al-Bukhari 1193; Sahih Muslim 1399), and visiting on Saturday follows his practice most closely — but his habit was not a condition, and the promised reward applies on whichever day you go.

Sources: Sunan Ibn Majah 1412 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Jami' at-Tirmidhi 324 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 1193 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1399 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Qur'an 9:108

Umrah · Tawaf SupplicationsTawaf Duas — What to Recite During Tawaf

Ask many pilgrims what to recite during Tawaf and they will show you a booklet with a different du'a printed for each of the seven circuits. Here is the honest answer, and it sets most people free: there is no fixed du'a prescribed for each circuit of Tawaf. The Prophet ﷺ never assigned one supplication to the first round, another to the second, and so on. The dua-per-round booklets are a later convention, written as a help for pilgrims — they are not from the Sunnah, as works such as Fiqh as-Sunnah and fatwas on IslamOnline make clear. What follows is what is established. For the walk itself — where to start, how to count — see our Tawaf Step by Step guide.

At the Black Stone, at the start of every circuit: Face the Black Stone, and if you can reach it without pushing, touch or kiss it; otherwise point towards it with your right hand. Say: "Bismillah, Allahu Akbar" — "In the name of Allah; Allah is the Greatest." Fiqh as-Sunnah also records a longer opening du'a you may say at the first circuit: "Allahumma imanan bika wa tasdiqan bikitabik wa wafa'an bi'ahdika wa ittiba'an li sunnat nabbiyyika, bismillahi wallahu akbar" — "O Allah, [I circle Your House] believing in You, affirming Your Book, fulfilling my covenant with You, and following the Sunnah of Your Prophet; in the name of Allah, and Allah is the Greatest."

Between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone: In the final stretch of every circuit, recite the du'a of the Qur'an: "Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan wa fil-akhirati hasanatan wa qina 'adhaban-nar" — "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and shield us from the punishment of the Fire" (Qur'an 2:201; Sunan Abu Dawud 1892).

Two corners that wipe away sins: The Prophet ﷺ said that touching the Black Stone and the Yemeni Corner (Rukn Yamani) erases sins (Musnad Ahmad, graded sahih by al-Albani in Sahih al-Jami' 2194). Note the difference between them: the Yemeni Corner is touched with the hand if you can reach it — it is not kissed, and no takbir is said there; if you cannot reach it, simply walk past without pointing at it.

For the rest of the walk: Everything else is open. Fill your Tawaf with dhikr (SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah, La ilaha illa Allah), recitation of the Qur'an, blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and above all your own personal du'as — in your own words and your own language. Tawaf is one of the great moments of a pilgrim's life to ask Allah for everything: forgiveness, healing, provision, your family, the whole Ummah. When Tawaf ends, Umrah continues with Sa'i Step by Step; if you are on your first journey, our Umrah for First-Timers guide walks through the whole order, and the Ihram Rules and Hajj 2027 guides cover the sacred state you are in and the greater pilgrimage ahead.

What to avoid:

  • Pushing or shoving to reach the Black Stone — harming a fellow pilgrim cancels the spirit of the act; pointing from a distance is enough.
  • Treating booklet du'as as obligatory, or feeling your Tawaf is incomplete without them — it is not.
  • Kissing the Yemeni Corner, or saying takbir there — it is touched only.
  • Raising your voice in group chanting that disturbs those around you; Tawaf is a quiet, personal conversation with Allah.

Quick questions:

  • Is there a fixed dua for each round of Tawaf? No. No specific du'a is prescribed for each of the seven circuits; the per-round du'as in printed booklets are a later convention, not the Sunnah. Say the takbir at the Black Stone, recite Qur'an 2:201 between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, and spend the rest in your own du'a and dhikr.
  • Can I make dua in my own language? Yes. Personal supplication in any language is encouraged throughout Tawaf — Arabic is not a condition for your own du'as.
  • What if I cannot reach the Black Stone? Point towards it with your right hand, say "Bismillah, Allahu Akbar", and keep walking with the flow. Do not push through the crowd — the pointing carries the same meaning.

Sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1892 (the du'a between the two corners) — Sunnah.com ↗ · Fiqh as-Sunnah (the opening du'a, and that no per-circuit du'a is prescribed) · Sahih al-Jami' 2194 (touching the two corners erases sins)

Zamzam · Virtues & HistoryZamzam Water — Virtues, History & How to Drink It

Every pilgrim drinks it, and most carry a bottle of it home like treasure: Zamzam, the water of the well beside the Kaaba. Its story begins with Hajar (AS), left in the empty valley of Makkah with her infant son Ismail (AS). When the baby cried with thirst, she ran between Safa and Marwa searching for water — the walk pilgrims still repeat in Sa'i — until, by Allah's mercy, water gushed from the ground at the child's feet, and she held it back, saying "Zam, zam" — "hold, hold" (Sahih al-Bukhari 3364). That spring has flowed ever since. If you are preparing for your first journey, our Umrah for First-Timers guide shows where Zamzam fits in the order of the rites.

Its virtues: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for" (Sunan Ibn Majah 3062). He ﷺ also said of it: "It is blessed; it is food that nourishes" (Sahih Muslim 2473a, narrated by Abu Dharr RA), and: "The best water on the face of the earth is the water of Zamzam" (Sahih al-Jami' 3302).

A note on the famous hadith, honestly: Sunan Ibn Majah 3062 is graded hasan in the Darussalam edition, but scholars have differed over its grading across the centuries. So take it the way the scholars advise: as a strong encouragement to drink Zamzam with a sincere intention — for healing, for knowledge, for provision, for whatever good you ask — not as a guaranteed promise that works by itself. Pair the intention with du'a, and leave the outcome to Allah.

How to drink it, the Sunnah way:

  • Face the Qibla if you can, and say Bismillah.
  • Drink in three sips, pausing to breathe between them — do not drain the cup in a single breath.
  • Drink your fill, until you are properly satisfied — not just a token sip.
  • Praise Allah afterwards (Alhamdulillah), then make your du'a.
  • Sprinkle some on your head, face and chest, as the Prophet ﷺ did with Zamzam.

The du'a of Ibn Abbas (RA): Whenever he drank Zamzam, Ibn Abbas (RA) would say: "Allahumma inni as'aluka 'ilman nafi'an, wa rizqan wasi'an, wa shifa'an min kulli da'" — "O Allah, I ask You for beneficial knowledge, plentiful provision, and healing from every disease" (recorded in IslamQA fatwa 1698). Use his words, or ask in your own. Many pilgrims pause for Zamzam straight after Tawaf, while their du'as are still warm.

Taking Zamzam home: Sealed Zamzam is sold at official sales points at Jeddah and Madinah airports for departing pilgrims. Under the Saudi civil aviation (GACA) rule, a pilgrim travelling on an Umrah or Hajj visa may take one sealed 5-litre bottle, which travels as checked baggage, handled separately — never pack loose bottles inside a suitcase, as airlines do not accept them. Whether that bottle is carried free or counts inside your normal allowance differs by airline and airport, so confirm with your airline before you fly. Our Umrah Packing List covers the rest of the journey-home luggage rules, and Hajj 2027 covers the same allowance in Hajj season.

Quick questions:

  • Can I drink Zamzam with an intention? Yes — that is exactly what the hadith encourages. Drink it intending a good you are asking Allah for — healing, knowledge, provision — and make du'a as you drink.
  • Is Zamzam mentioned in the Quran by name? No. The well is not named in the Qur'an; its story and virtues come to us from the Sunnah, above all Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 and Sahih Muslim 2473a.
  • Can I take Zamzam home? Yes. Buy the sealed 5-litre bottle at the official airport sales point when you depart; it is checked in separately under the Zamzam allowance. Loose bottles inside a suitcase are not accepted.

Sources: Sunan Ibn Majah 3062 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Zamzam: The Blessed Water — Its Story and Its Virtue — IslamQA ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 · Sahih Muslim 2473a

Umrah · Ihram RulesIhram Rules — What to Wear & What to Avoid

Ihram is both a sacred state and the clothing pilgrims wear for Hajj and Umrah. You enter it at the Miqat with the intention (niyyah) and the Talbiyah, and from that moment a set of rules applies until you exit Ihram. Most mistakes come from the clothing rules, so here they are plainly. If you are preparing for your first journey, start with our Umrah for First-Timers guide, then come back to this page.

For men — two unstitched cloths:

Men wear two pieces of plain, unstitched white cloth: the izar (lower wrap) and the rida (upper sheet).

What a man in Ihram may wear: The Prophet ﷺ was asked what a man in Ihram may wear and said: "He must not wear shirts, turbans, trousers, hooded cloaks, or leather socks, except for one who cannot find sandals; he may wear leather socks, but he should cut them below the ankles. And do not wear any clothing that has been touched by saffron or safflower" — Sahih al-Bukhari (1542); also Sahih Muslim (1177).

So: no underwear, no stitched shirts or trousers, no cap or turban — the head stays uncovered — and no socks or closed shoes; open sandals or flip-flops are fine. A belt or money pouch around the waist, a watch and glasses are allowed; they are not clothing.

For women — normal modest dress, face and hands uncovered:

Women wear their normal modest clothes (abaya and hijab). Two things are specific to Ihram: a woman in Ihram must not wear a face veil (niqab) and must not wear gloves (Sahih al-Bukhari 1838). If non-mahram men are nearby, she may screen her face with a loose cloth that does not touch it. Socks and closed shoes are fine for women.

Rules for everyone in Ihram:

  • No perfume on the body or clothes — use unscented soap, shampoo and deodorant while in Ihram.
  • No cutting hair or nails.
  • No hunting.
  • No marriage contract, proposal or arrangement while in Ihram.
The spirit of Ihram: Allah says in the Qur'an: "Hajj is [during] well-known months, so whoever has made Hajj obligatory upon himself therein, there is [to be for him] no sexual relations and no disobedience and no disputing during Hajj" (Qur'an 2:197).

If you break a rule by mistake:

Do not panic. If it was forgetful or accidental, remove the cause and carry on; scholars say forgetfulness is excused. For a deliberate breach, fidyah is prescribed — fasting three days, feeding six poor people, or offering a sacrifice (Qur'an 2:196). Ask a qualified scholar about your own case rather than guessing.

Practical tips:

  • Practise tying the izar at home before you travel; use a belt or safety pins so it cannot slip.
  • Choose light white cotton, and pack a spare set — our Umrah Packing List covers what else to bring.
  • Carry unscented toiletries from home — scented hotel soap counts as perfume.
  • Put your Ihram on before the Miqat, not in the plane aisle at the last minute.

Once you are in Ihram, the rites begin with Tawaf Step by Step. Planning further ahead? See the Hajj 2027 guide for dates and registration, and the Nusuk App Guide for permits and bookings.

Quick questions:

  • Can men wear underwear in Ihram? No. Nothing stitched or shaped to the body is allowed for men in Ihram, including underwear.
  • Can women wear socks in Ihram? Yes. Socks are allowed for women; only the face veil and gloves are prohibited.
  • Can I wear a watch or sunglasses in Ihram? Yes. A watch, glasses, sunglasses and a waist belt/pouch are all allowed.

Sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1542 — Hadith Unlocked ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 1838 · Sahih Muslim 1177

Umrah · Family GuideUmrah with Kids — Tips for Families Travelling with Children

Yes, children can perform Umrah — at any age, even as babies. A woman once lifted her small child to the Prophet ﷺ and asked, "Is there Hajj for this one?" He said: "Yes, and you will have a reward" (Sahih Muslim 1336a). A child's Umrah is voluntary and rewarded, and the parent who brings them shares the reward. It does not replace the obligatory Hajj they will owe after puberty. New to Umrah yourself? Read our Umrah for First-Timers guide first.

What counts for a child:

Scholars agree a child's Hajj and Umrah are valid and rewarded, but they do not count as the obligatory Hajj — that must be done again after reaching puberty. The pen is lifted from a child until puberty (Sunan Abi Dawud 4403), so if a young child breaks an Ihram rule there is no fidyah on them. If you carry your child during Tawaf, scholars say one Tawaf suffices for both the carrier and the child.

Ihram for children:

Dress boys in Ihram cloths like the adults; dress girls in normal modest clothes. Keep it simple and comfortable — the point is the experience, not perfection.

In the Haram with little ones:

  • Use the upper floors for Tawaf with a stroller; the ground-floor mataf gets very crowded.
  • A baby carrier often works better than a stroller in crowds.
  • Go at quieter times — after Fajr or late at night. Our Tawaf Step by Step and Sa'i Step by Step guides show what each rite involves.
  • Keep children hydrated and take breaks; short, calm visits beat long, tired ones.
  • Give older children a small job: carrying the Zamzam bottle or remembering a dua.

Safety and paperwork:

Every child needs their own passport and Umrah visa, including babies. Put an ID wristband on your child with a parent's name and phone number, and agree a meeting point in case you get separated. Our Umrah Packing List will help you pack for the whole family.

Make it memorable:

Teach older children the Talbiyah and a short Tawaf dua before you travel. Let them see the Kaaba first from a quiet spot rather than in a rush. A child's first Umrah is often the memory that brings them back as adults. Mothers travelling without a mahram can also read our guide on Women Travelling Alone for Umrah.

Quick questions:

  • What age can a child do Umrah? Any age, from newborns upward.
  • Does a baby need their own Umrah visa? Yes. Every traveller, including infants, needs a passport and visa.
  • Are strollers allowed in Masjid al-Haram? Yes, in most areas; use the upper floors and avoid the crowded ground-floor mataf.

Sources: Sahih Muslim 1336a — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sunan Abi Dawud 4403

Hajj · Hajj 2027 GuideHajj 2027 — Dates, Registration & Complete Guide

Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam and the journey of a lifetime — and for Hajj 2027 (1448 AH), the planning starts now. This guide brings together the expected dates, how registration through Nusuk Hajj works, and a short summary of the rites, so you can prepare early and calmly.

Please note — the dates are estimates: Every Gregorian date in this guide comes from the Umm al-Qura calendar and is an estimate only. The days of Hajj are confirmed only by the official sighting of the Dhul Hijjah moon, announced by Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court. If the moon is sighted a day earlier or later, every date below moves with it.

The expected dates for Hajj 2027:

  • Hajj days: Friday 14 May to Wednesday 19 May 2027 — corresponding to 8–13 Dhul Hijjah 1448 AH
  • Day of Arafah (9 Dhul Hijjah): Saturday 15 May 2027 — the greatest day of Hajj
  • Eid al-Adha (10 Dhul Hijjah): Sunday 16 May 2027
The call to Hajj: Allah says in the Qur'an: "And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass" (Qur'an 22:27). And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever performs Hajj for the sake of Allah and does not commit any obscenity or wrongdoing, returns as pure as the day his mother gave birth to him" — narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1521) and Sahih Muslim (1350).

Registration — only through Nusuk Hajj: For pilgrims from countries served by the programme, Hajj registration and packages are handled only through the official Nusuk Hajj platform — hajj.nusuk.sa. As of checks in late September 2026, the 1448 AH season had not yet opened. Registration is expected to open in autumn 2026 (October–December), with package sales following in early 2027 — but no opening date has been officially announced, so check hajj.nusuk.sa directly and beware of anyone quoting you a "confirmed" date or price. Pilgrims from countries not served by Nusuk Hajj (such as Pakistan and India) continue to apply through their own national Hajj schemes and licensed operators.

How registration works — step by step:

  • Step 1 — Create and verify your Nusuk profile: Register on hajj.nusuk.sa with your personal details exactly as they appear on your passport, and complete the verification steps. (If you are new to Nusuk, our Nusuk App Guide explains how the platform and app work.)
  • Step 2 — Passport: You need a passport valid for at least 6 months beyond your return date — renew early if yours expires before the end of 2027.
  • Step 3 — Photo: Upload a recent passport-style photograph that meets the portal's specification.
  • Step 4 — Health and vaccination requirements: Complete the health declaration and the vaccination requirements as announced for the season — check the portal for the exact list when registration opens.
  • Step 5 — Choose a package: When sales open, compare the official packages (category, hotels in Makkah and Madinah, Mina camp, transport) and select the one that fits your budget and mobility.
  • Step 6 — Pay through the portal: Payment is made inside Nusuk Hajj — never to an agent's personal account.
  • Step 7 — Hajj visa: Once your package is confirmed and paid, your Hajj visa is issued electronically through Nusuk.

The rites of Hajj — a short summary:

  • Before the days begin: Enter Ihram at the Miqat with the intention for Hajj and the Talbiyah on your lips.
  • 8 Dhul Hijjah — Mina: Travel to Mina and spend the day and night there in prayer.
  • 9 Dhul Hijjah — Arafah: The heart of Hajj. Stand at Arafah from noon until sunset in du'a and repentance — "Hajj is Arafah." After sunset, move on without praying Maghrib there.
  • The night — Muzdalifah: Spend the night under the open sky at Muzdalifah, pray Maghrib and Isha together, rest, and collect your pebbles.
  • 10 Dhul Hijjah — Eid day: Stone the large Jamarah (Jamrat al-Aqabah), offer the sacrifice, shave or trim the hair, then perform Tawaf al-Ifadah (and Sa'i) in Makkah.
  • 11–13 Dhul Hijjah — Days of Tashreeq: Stay in Mina and stone all three Jamarat each day after noon.
  • Before leaving Makkah: Perform the Farewell Tawaf (Tawaf al-Wada) as your last rite.
About prices — read this before you pay anyone: No Hajj 2027 pricing has been confirmed yet. Official package prices are published only inside Nusuk Hajj when sales open. Anyone advertising fixed "Hajj 2027 packages" with guaranteed prices or guaranteed visas before then is not selling through the official channel — do not pay unofficial agents, and never pay for registration itself, which is free on the portal. For what the separate Umrah journey costs, see our Umrah Visa Fees 2026 guide and the full Umrah Visa 2026 guide.

Quick questions:

  • When is Hajj 2027? Hajj 2027 is expected from 14 to 19 May 2027 (8–13 Dhul Hijjah 1448 AH), with the Day of Arafah on Saturday 15 May and Eid al-Adha on Sunday 16 May 2027. These are Umm al-Qura calendar estimates — the final dates depend on the official Dhul Hijjah moon sighting.
  • How do I register for Hajj 2027? Only through the official Nusuk Hajj platform at hajj.nusuk.sa: create and verify your profile, add a passport valid at least 6 months beyond your return and a passport-style photo, complete the health and vaccination requirements as announced, then choose a package and pay through the portal — your Hajj visa is issued via Nusuk. The 1448 season had not opened as of late September 2026 and is expected to open in autumn 2026; check the portal directly for the announcement.
  • How much does Hajj 2027 cost? Nobody knows yet — no 2027 pricing is confirmed. Prices appear only inside Nusuk Hajj when package sales open in early 2027. Treat any price quoted before then, especially by unofficial agents, as a warning sign.

Sources: Nusuk Hajj — hajj.nusuk.sa ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 1521 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1350 — Sunnah.com ↗

Umrah · First-Timers GuideUmrah for First-Timers — Step-by-Step Guide for Your First Umrah

Your first Umrah is a journey you will remember for the rest of your life — and it is simpler than it looks from the outside. Umrah has four essential acts: entering Ihram, Tawaf around the Kaaba, the two rak'ah prayer, and Sa'i between Safa and Marwa, finished by shaving or trimming the hair. This guide walks a first-timer through every step, in order, with the practical tips nobody tells you until you are already there.

Why go, and go again: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Umrah to Umrah expiates what is between them (of sins), and there is no reward for an accepted Hajj except Paradise" — narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari (1773) and Sahih Muslim (1349).

Your first Umrah — step by step:

  • Step 1 — Enter Ihram at the Miqat. Before crossing the Miqat (the boundary around Makkah for your direction of travel — your flight or group will announce it), bathe if you can, put on your Ihram garments, pray two rak'ah, and make your niyyah (intention) for Umrah. Then begin the Talbiyah: "Labbayk Allahumma labbayk..." — "Here I am, O Allah, here I am." You are now in Ihram, and its rules apply until your Umrah is complete.
  • Step 2 — Enter Makkah. Settle into your hotel, rest if the journey was long — there is no need to rush to the Haram exhausted — then enter Masjid al-Haram with your right foot, saying the du'a for entering a mosque. Lower your gaze until you reach the Mataf, then look up: your first sight of the Kaaba. Make du'a from your heart at that moment.
  • Step 3 — Tawaf: 7 circuits of the Kaaba. Begin at the Black Stone corner (follow the green light on the wall opposite it), with the Kaaba on your left, and walk seven full circuits, ending back at the Black Stone line. Our Tawaf Step by Step guide covers every detail, and Tawaf Duas gathers what to recite as you walk.
  • Step 4 — Two rak'ah at Maqam Ibrahim. After the seventh circuit, pray two rak'ah behind Maqam Ibrahim if you can do so without crowding others — anywhere in the mosque is valid when it is busy.
  • Step 5 — Drink Zamzam. Go to a Zamzam dispenser, drink your fill facing the Qibla, and make du'a — Zamzam is drunk for whatever intention you drink it with.
  • Step 6 — Sa'i: 7 lengths between Safa and Marwa. Walk to Safa, face the Kaaba and make du'a, then walk to Marwa — that is one length. Seven lengths in total, ending at Marwa. Walk at your own pace; men jog lightly only between the two green markers. Our Sa'i Step by Step guide walks you through it.
  • Step 7 — Shave or trim the hair (halq/taqsir). Finally, men shave the head (halq) — the more rewarded option — or trim evenly all over; women trim a fingertip's length from the ends of their hair. With this, your Umrah is complete and you leave the state of Ihram. May Allah accept it.

Practical tips for first-timers:

  • Best times to go: The quietest months are usually just after Hajj season and in the weeks outside Ramadan and school holidays; the quietest hours in the Haram are mid-morning and the middle of the night. Ramadan is the most rewarded time — and the most crowded.
  • What to carry in the Haram: A small drawstring bag for your shoes (keep them with you — racks are easy to lose), your phone, a small bottle for Zamzam, and your hotel's address card. Travel light; everything else stays in the room. Our Umrah Packing List covers the full suitcase.
  • Agree a meeting point: Before entering, fix a landmark meeting point with your companions (a gate number works well) — phone signal inside can be patchy and batteries die.
  • Sisters travelling without a mahram: The visa rules changed in 2022 — see our guide on Women Travelling Alone for Umrah for the rules, permits and safety tips.

Common first-timer mistakes:

  • Passing the Miqat without Ihram: If you fly into Jeddah intending Umrah, you cross the Miqat in the air — enter Ihram before it (most pilgrims put on Ihram at home or at the departure airport and make niyyah when the captain announces the Miqat). Crossing without Ihram means returning to a Miqat or offering a sacrifice — ask before you travel, not after you land.
  • Losing count of the circuits: Tawaf is exactly seven. Count on your fingers or a small counter, and if you become unsure, build on the lower number you are certain of and complete the rest.
  • Rushing Sa'i: Seven lengths is about 3 kilometres of walking. Pace yourself, rest on the benches when you need to, sip Zamzam along the way — there is no prize for finishing exhausted, and the elderly and children in the crowd deserve your patience.

Quick questions:

  • How long does a first Umrah take? The rites themselves usually take about 2–3 hours at a calm pace — Tawaf, the two rak'ah, Zamzam and Sa'i — longer in Ramadan and Hajj season crowds. There is no time limit; go gently.
  • What is the correct order of the Umrah steps? Ihram at the Miqat with niyyah and Talbiyah, then Tawaf (7 circuits from the Black Stone), two rak'ah at Maqam Ibrahim, drinking Zamzam, Sa'i (7 lengths between Safa and Marwa), and finally shaving or trimming the hair. The order matters — do not cut your hair before Sa'i.
  • Can I perform Umrah on the day I arrive? Yes — many pilgrims do, once they have settled in and rested a little. If you arrive exhausted or unwell, resting first and performing Umrah later the same day or the next morning is perfectly fine; your Ihram simply continues until you complete it.

Sources: Nusuk — Official Site ↗ · Sahih al-Bukhari 1773 — Sunnah.com ↗ · Sahih Muslim 1349 — Sunnah.com ↗

Umrah Visa · Fees & CostsUmrah Visa Fees 2026 — Cost, Types & How to Apply

Before the flights and the hotels, every Umrah journey starts with one question: what does the visa itself cost? In 2026 there are four realistic routes — the tourist eVisa, visa on arrival, the dedicated Umrah visa and the free stopover visa — and they are priced differently. Which one is yours depends mostly on your passport. The figures below were checked on 16 November 2026.

Please note: Visa fees change often. Treat the amounts here as a guide for planning, and always confirm the final amount on the official portal — visa.visitsaudi.com for the tourist eVisa and umrah.nusuk.sa for the Umrah visa — before you pay.

The fees at a glance:

Visa / itemFeeNotes
